title: Teacher who survived Oregon school attack says she had no chance to protect children
summary: A teacher wounded in last week’s attack on a special education classroom at an Oregon elementary school says she never had a chance to try to shelter any of the children inside
story: A teacher wounded in last week’s attack on a special education classroom at an Oregon elementary school says she never had a chance to try to shelter any of the children inside
A teacher wounded in last week's attack on a special education classroom at an Oregon elementary school says she never had a chance to try to shelter any of the children inside.

In a statement issued by a family friend, Becky Drury said Wednesday that she ran to see what was going on when she realized something was happening — but immediately saw the shooter and rushed back to the classroom.
“I turned to shut the door behind me, but the shooter was already there,” Drury said. “Before I could do anything more, he shot me at close range and I fell to the ground.”

Her left hand was nearly severed by a gunshot, and her right arm was struck as well. Unable to get up or defend herself or others, she said, “I did the only thing I could do, which was to pretend to be dead in the hope he would not shoot me again.”

Three children — ages 5, 8 and 11 — and a teacher were killed at Silver Rail Elementary in Bend, Oregon, last Thursday when a former student there, 16-year-old Griffin J. John II, blasted his way through locked doors with a shotgun and attacked the classroom. Another student was critically injured.

Authorities said another teacher threw her phone at the gunman and then tackled him and wrestled with him for control of the weapon, likely saving lives before the gunman was shot by a father who followed him into the building.
Some news reports had suggested that Drury threw herself on top of one student to protect her. Drury, who remains hospitalized, said she wanted to correct the record.
“Accurate, respectful reporting is a truly important service that will help heal the wounds inflicted by that awful day,” she said.
School reopened in the district Wednesday for the first time since the shooting. Dozens of officers were on hand at each school to welcome children back, the Bend Police Department said.

In a social media post, the department said it continues investigating the attack, including serving search warrants at the attacker's home, as well as on his electronic devices and his social media accounts on a variety of platforms.

The statement said police have confirmed that the pump-action shotgun used in the attack had been legally purchased. The Associated Press previously reported it had been purchased by the suspect's mother, according to a law enforcement source who was not authorized to discuss the investigation. But investigators said they were still looking into how the boy obtained it.

title: Carney says Trump’s tariffs hurt Americans as US Embassy alleges Canadian interference
summary: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney says that U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs have raised costs for American families and upended decades of trade as he unveiled a $6.2 billion plan to protect Canada’s manufacturing heartland
story: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney says that U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs have raised costs for American families and upended decades of trade as he unveiled a $6.2 billion plan to protect Canada’s manufacturing heartland

TORONTO -- Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Wednesday that U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs have driven up costs for American families and upended a decades-old trade relationship as he unveiled a multibillion-dollar plan to shield Canada’s manufacturing heartland from the trade war.

Carney also said he spoke with Trump for “quite some time” about issues including trade, as the U.S. Embassy in Canada accused Canadian politicians of seeking to influence American politics ahead of next month’s midterm elections. Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford rejected suggestions of improper interference.
Trump has openly said he wants automakers to move production from Canada to the United States, threatening an industry deeply integrated across the border for decades.

“U.S. tariffs have upended a trade bargain that’s existed for decades,” Carney said. “They’ve raised costs for American families while putting Ontario workers and businesses at a disadvantage and under a cloud of uncertainty.”

Carney said an integrated North American auto industry would benefit both countries but acknowledged that it may no longer be a priority for Washington. “Their approach has changed,” he said. “So must ours.”

Carney said the conversation covered Iran, the Middle East and some trade issues. They discussed Ukraine days earlier. He gave no indication of a breakthrough but said Canada remains ready to negotiate.
Trade negotiations collapsed in August after the countries appeared close to a deal. Trump subsequently imposed 50% tariffs on about $20 billion in Canadian goods, prompting Canadian retaliation.

“It’s clear that Canada’s relationship with the United States has changed permanently,” Ford said. “No matter what happens in the midterms, no matter who sits in the White House, we’re not going back to the way things were.”

Trump’s trade war and repeated threats to make Canada the 51st U.S. state have fueled a surge in Canadian nationalism. Carney has made reducing Canada’s dependence on the United States a priority, setting a goal of doubling exports to other markets over the next decade.
Carney and Ford announced the 8.7 billion Canadian dollar ($6.2 billion) plan to support steelmakers, automakers and critical mineral development in Ontario, Canada’s manufacturing heartland.
The plan includes CA$5.2 billion ($3.7 billion) over five years for steelmakers and CA$2.5 billion ($1.8 billion) for automakers, including CA$1.5 billion ($1.1 billion) from Ottawa.
The announcement comes as U.S.-owned steelmaker Cleveland-Cliffs announced layoffs at its Hamilton, Ontario, plant, highlighting the toll of Trump’s tariffs on Canadian manufacturing.
Also Wednesday, the U.S. Embassy issued a fact sheet accusing Canadian politicians of seeking to interfere in American elections.

The statement singled out Industry Minister Mélanie Joly for discussing retaliatory tariffs targeting Republican states and Ford for airing a U.S. advertisement featuring former President Ronald Reagan criticizing tariffs. Trump abruptly canceled trade talks with Canada after the ad aired during the World Series in October 2025.
The embassy also cited 11 Canadians charged with illegally voting in U.S. elections between 2012 and 2026, without linking the cases to Canada’s government.

The administration has launched a whole-of-government effort to investigate and prosecute noncitizen voting, something election experts and administrators characterize as a comparatively small issue. The Department of Justice says that since the start of 2026 it has arrested more than 200 people for illegally voting as noncitizens in past elections, a vanishingly small number compared to the country's tens of millions of regular voters.

“The items featured in the U.S. embassy’s ‘fact sheet’ are not genuine examples of foreign interference and the implicit assumption that Canada could significantly alter the outcome of the midterms is absurd,” said Daniel Béland, a political science professor at McGill University in Montreal.
“Accusing Canada of foreign interference ahead of the midterms could pave the way to ‘Blame Canada’ rhetoric after the electoral results are in.”
Carney said Canada was responding to U.S. tariffs, while Ford denied any interest in interfering in American elections.
Carney said Canadian auto exports to the U.S. have fallen more than 10%, while U.S. exports to Canada have dropped more than 20%.
“Tariffs make both our industries weaker and reduce choice for our families,” Carney said.

title: Prosecutor says he'll seek death penalty for mom charged with murder in twins' deaths
summary: An Idaho prosecutor is seeking the death penalty against a woman charged with murder in the deaths of her twin toddlers last year
story: An Idaho prosecutor is seeking the death penalty against a woman charged with murder in the deaths of her twin toddlers last year
BOISE, Idaho -- An Idaho prosecutor is seeking the death penalty against a woman charged with murder in the 2025 deaths of her twin toddlers.

Andrea Shaw, 23, has pleaded not guilty and has said the 18-month-old twins became sick and died after receiving flu shots and routine childhood vaccinations. But Payette County Prosecutor Mike Duke wrote in court documents that an autopsy revealed symptoms consistent with smothering and wrote that suffocation “is the only conceivable explanation” for their deaths.
Deputy prosecuting attorney Ryon Sirucek notified the court of his intent to seek the death penalty last week.

In the court document, Sirucek said the state would try to show that four aggravating factors make capital punishment appropriate in the case: That more than one murder was committed at the time; that the killings were especially heinous, atrocious or cruel; that the defendant showed “utter disregard” for human life and that she would likely pose a continuing threat to society.

Shaw’s attorney, Joseph Filicetti, did not immediately respond to a voicemail and text message requesting comment. In July, Filicetti wrote in a text message that Shaw “denies anything and everything” and that the state “cannot prove” the criminal charges.

The twins were found dead in their shared bed May 1, 2025, according to court records. They had been vaccinated eight days earlier, and the day after their vaccinations Shaw took them to the emergency room, reporting that they were lethargic and felt feverish. The doctor felt the symptoms were a reaction from the vaccinations, and the twins were given Tylenol and a popsicle and sent home, according to the court records.

A few days after the twins' deaths, Shaw went on an internet show produced by Children's Health Defense, an anti-vaccine group founded by Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. He has not been affiliated with the group since December 2024, when he formally resigned as chairman to join President Donald Trump’s administration.
Medical experts point out that the childhood vaccines at issue — hepatitis A, influenza and DTaP — are safe and effective for kids and recommended by various medical groups.

Shaw is also a plaintiff in a federal lawsuit brought by Children’s Health Defense and others against the American Academy of Pediatrics, accusing the organization of racketeering and lying about the safety of vaccinations. The American Academy of Pediatrics has asked the court to dismiss the lawsuit, calling it the “latest missive in a campaign targeting” the academy and its “use of science-backed evidence in vaccine policy.”
A grand jury indicted Shaw on the murder charges in July, and she is being held without bond. A trial has been set for January.
AP reporter Josh Kelety contributed.

title: 6 people arrested for allegedly running a marriage fraud ring, authorities say
summary: Federal prosecutors announced they have broken up a fraudulent marriage ring in Massachusetts that conducted dozens of bogus ceremonies with immigrants over the past decade and netted participant millions of dollars
story: Federal prosecutors announced they have broken up a fraudulent marriage ring in Massachusetts that conducted dozens of bogus ceremonies with immigrants over the past decade and netted participant millions of dollars
Wedding rings were exchanged, and photos of a smiling bride and well-dressed groom made it look like these were legitimate marriages.

But federal authorities argued Wednesday that the ceremonies were part of an elaborate, decade-long marriage fraud ring that netted a half-dozen people in Massachusetts millions of dollars. Prosecutors charged six people, including the alleged ringleader Jennifer Gonzalez, with conducting as many as 20 marriages to help immigrants obtain legal status.

The other five were allegedly paid by Gonzalez to take part in the marriages — several of them taking part in multiple nuptials. Each marriage cost an immigrant from $38,000 to $40,000. All face charges including harboring illegal aliens, conspiracy to harbor illegal aliens, conspiracy to commit marriage fraud and marriage fraud.

“What an affront the alleged conduct revealed here today must be to those who play by the rules," U.S. Attorney Leah Foley told reporters. "To see a for-profit business whose sole purpose is helping people cheat and skip the line by simply paying for it must be so offensive and disheartening to those who follow our country’s laws.”
Five of the six were arrested Wednesday morning and are expected to appear in federal court later in the day. A sixth defendant is currently in state prison serving a sentence for a firearms crime.

“Ms. Gonzalez got rich off selling the American Dream all the while investing her money in another country,” Foley said, detailing how Gonzalez allegedly used profits from the marriage ring to buy businesses and real estate in the Dominican Republic. She is an American citizen.
An attorney for Gonzalez, 43, of Fall River, Massachusetts, could not be reached for comment.

The arrests are the latest effort to crack down on marriage fraud and come as the Trump administration has increased restrictions on both legal and illegal immigration and reduced the avenues available for people to enter the country or become a citizen.

In August, 11 people were charged with participating in a multimillion-dollar scheme to help hundreds of Chinese nationals fraudulently obtain green cards through sham marriages to U.S. citizens. In that scheme, American citizens were paid as much as $30,000 to enter into bogus marriages with immigrants seeking lawful permanent resident status. The decade-long scheme netted tens of millions of dollars.

Three years ago, a similar scheme was prosecuted in Massachusetts. Marcialito Biol Benitez, a 49-year-old Philippine national living in Los Angeles, pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit marriage fraud and immigration document fraud. Benitez admitted operating a large-scale marriage fraud agency in which he arranged marriages between foreign nationals and American citizens.

In the latest case, prosecutors said the investigation was ongoing. They allege in the court documents that some of the defendants lied on applications for Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, by falsely claiming they never had been married. Gonzalez is also accused of spending $120,000 she received in SNAP benefits. Prosecutors also accused the defendants of engaging in housing and unemployment fraud.
None of the immigrants who entered into the marriages have been charged.

“Marriage fraud undermines the processes that ensure honest, lawful individuals can marry United States citizens and enjoy everything the United States has to offer to them,” John Soares, assistant special agent in charge, Homeland Security Investigations in New England, told reporters. “Fraudsters, like the individuals arrested today, make that process more difficult.”

title: Supreme Court rebuffs Trump admin restrictions on medical care for trans inmates
summary: The Supreme Court has rejected a Trump administration appeal seeking to immediately enforce medical care restrictions for transgender people in prison
story: The Supreme Court has rejected a Trump administration appeal seeking to immediately enforce medical care restrictions for transgender people in prison
WASHINGTON -- The Supreme Court on Wednesday refused to allow the Trump administration to immediately enforce new medical restrictions for transgender people in prison.

The decision leaves in place a lower-court block on the policy. It was adopted after an executive order from President Donald Trump, who has taken several steps to roll back transgender rights during his second term.
Justice Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas would have allowed the policy to be enforced.
The Supreme Court has previously allowed other policies for transgender people to move ahead for now, including restrictions on military service and passport sex markers.

Trump's order called on the Bureau of Prisons to revise its medical care policies so that federal funds aren’t spent “for the purpose of conforming an inmate’s appearance to that of the opposite sex.”
The new policy would halt surgeries, taper off hormones and end social accommodations like makeup and wigs. Prisons would continue to offer mental health services.

Attorneys for transgender inmates challenged the policy in court and U.S. District Judge Royce Lamberth ordered treatments to continue. Lamberth, who was nominated to the bench by President Ronald Reagan, pointed out that untreated gender dysphoria can cause severe side effects like depression, anxiety and suicidal thoughts.
The Trump administration appealed, arguing that treatments raised security concerns and “could no longer be justified.” A divided appeals court panel left the order in place.

About 600 inmates were receiving hormone therapy in 2025, the agency said in court records. Withdrawing care would have significant effects on their bodies and mental health, their lawyers said. The government has not detailed evidence of security problems linked to hormone therapy for transgender inmates over the 30 years it has been provided, they wrote.

The conservative-majority Supreme Court has previously upheld state laws banning certain medical treatments for transgender youth, and restricting sports participation by transgender athletes in women’s sports.

title: Chemical tank explodes in Ohio, forcing evacuations
summary: A chemical tank exploded in Toledo, Ohio, forcing hundreds of residents to evacuate or shelter in place due to fears of a toxic release
story: A chemical tank exploded in Toledo, Ohio, forcing hundreds of residents to evacuate or shelter in place due to fears of a toxic release

TOLEDO, Ohio -- A chemical tank exploded in Toledo, Ohio, forcing hundreds of residents to evacuate their homes or shelter in place due to fears of a toxic release, and the mayor warned Wednesday that it may still be explosive.

A sheriff's deputy was injured when he responded to the explosion around 9:30 p.m. Tuesday and was able to drive himself to the hospital, Mayor Wade Kapszukiewicz said at a news conference Wednesday morning.
MC Tank Transport said the tank contained glycidyl methacrylate, which it described as “an industrial chemical used to make certain plastics, paints and coatings perform better.”
Kapszukiewicz said the chemical is liquid inside the tank but becomes a gas when released. Video from the area showed a large plume in the sky.

“There is still concern that the tank is emitting this chemical and it has the potential within 12 hours of the incident to be explosive,” the mayor said, adding that it can hold 5,500 gallons of the chemical in liquid form. He said officials don’t know what caused the explosion.

People who come into contact with glycidyl methacrylate may feel as if their eyes, nose, mouth and skin are burning, the city fire department said. Overexposure can lead to headache, dizziness, tiredness, nausea and vomiting.

“It’s really toxic if you touch it, if you ingest it,” Karim Baroudi, director of the Toledo-Lucas County Health Department, said during the news conference. “Now we’re trying to kind of determine how much of a toxicity is in the air that the people are breathing so we can give better guidance.”

Baroudi advised residents to close their windows and that those who “feel irritation in the eyes, heavily breathing, just take a shower for now.” The fire department said those who experience symptoms should contact a medical professional.
First responders, hazmat and safety teams are not approaching the tank because of the risk of more explosions, and will reassess conditions later Wednesday morning, Kapszukiewicz said.

The city ordered people within a 1-mile (1.6-kilometer) radius of the explosion to evacuate their homes and businesses Tuesday night. More than 900 people live within the evacuation zone, and it was believed that all of them had left by Wednesday morning, the mayor said. A shelter-in-place order was issued for residents beyond the evacuation zone within a 3-mile (4.8-kilometer) radius.

It was very foggy early Wednesday in the city of about 265,000 people, hindering visibility and delaying efforts to use drones to monitor the site. Kapszukiewicz reassured residents outside the evacuation zone that the fog was unrelated to the chemical explosion. The National Weather Service said the fog was expected to lift by mid-morning.

Arkansas-based MC Tank Transport said in a statement the company is working with the fire department and other emergency authorities. Company representatives were on their way to Toledo, Kapszukiewicz said.

“Our immediate and overriding concern is the safety of area residents, emergency responders and our employees,” it said. “Our immediate and overriding concern is the safety of area residents, emergency responders and our employees.”
McCormack reported from Concord, New Hampshire. Associated Press writer Dave Collins in Hartford, Connecticut, contributed.

title: Taxpayers are funding private school tuition. It's helping classical Christian schools expand
summary: Conservatives are banding together to grow classical Christian schools by leveraging new taxpayer-funded scholarships
story: Conservatives are banding together to grow classical Christian schools by leveraging new taxpayer-funded scholarships

HURST, Texas -- Keith Castello spends a lot of time praying about available real estate. Driving in his white pickup under a glaring Texas sun, the classical Christian school administrator points out empty office parks, a shopping mall, and an old church — all locations he is scouting for new Christian schools.
Demand is booming, he says. And part of that demand comes from a new state incentive: taxpayer money for kids who attend Christian schools.

This summer, Texas began rolling out $1 billion in public funding that eligible families can put toward private education expenses. Republican-controlled state legislatures around the country have approved a cascade of similar programs in the past six years, alarming public school advocates.

These programs mean half of school-age children in the United States are now eligible to apply for state money to attend private schools. In the U.S., most private schools are religious. Securing public money for them raises issues over church-state separation but fulfills a longstanding goal for Christian conservatives, who lobbied for this funding.

“I have been praying for 28 years for things that are coming to fruition right now,” said Castello, who is launching three classical Christian schools this fall under his Kyrie Christian Academy brand.

Those suburban Texas schools are part of a larger network, the Association of Classical Christian Schools, which has ties to the Trump administration and was founded by Doug Wilson, a conservative Idaho pastor and writer. The schools offer a liberal arts education, with an added emphasis on virtue and a biblical worldview.

The annual ACCS conference in June in Atlanta buzzed with talk of the historic shift in school funding, which bolsters a conservative Christian push to remake the education landscape. Critics worry it will drain public schools, which educate students of all religious backgrounds and political persuasions. When students leave their public school, state money allocated to educate each student goes away too.

Conservatives are banding together to leverage these expanding taxpayer-funded scholarships. Last year, ACCS formed a coalition with some powerful conservative groups, including Turning Point Education and the Heritage Foundation. Their goal is to convert or create 5,000 new classical Christian schools in the next decade with 1.5 million students nationwide.

The aim, according to ACCS President David Goodwin, is to take a share of public funding and educate future leaders through Christian schools. “It sounds like a very ambitious goal, but this money has never been there before,” he said.

The Association of Classical Christian Schools calls its campaign the “Battle for the American School.” It’s a riff on the 2022 bestselling book Goodwin co-wrote with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who sent his children to ACCS schools before joining President Donald Trump’s cabinet. Their book, “Battle for the American Mind,” extols classical education and critiques the prevailing public school model.
Hegseth remains a booster: The Pentagon recently introduced a form of classical education into government-run schools on military bases.

The ACCS version of classical Christian education is proudly erudite: The Oxford-educated Christian writer C.S. Lewis is a lodestar, and students study the “great books.” Its teaching methods draw from ancient and medieval sources with a strong focus on Western Christian history.

The schools have their roots in a radical source. Wilson, the founder of ACCS, is a self-described Christian nationalist who has made headlines for preaching at a Pentagon worship service and advocating for the repeal of women’s voting rights. For more than four decades, he has also been a pioneer in classical Christian education.
In 1981, he helped start the Logos School in Moscow, Idaho, one of the first in the modern classical Christian movement. He founded ACCS in 1994.
At the June conference, Wilson told a packed ballroom of 1,000 ACCS leaders they can’t opt out of the culture wars.
Education is “the central cultural battle,” he argued. He repeated for emphasis the refrain: “Classical Christian education is a hot center of the conflict of our time.”

On a Wednesday in August, the school year begins at Covenant Christian Academy, an ACCS school in the Dallas-Fort Worth suburbs. Well-behaved children in lower grades file into chapel in the cafeteria, all wearing blue oxford shirts, the girls in blue-and-white plaid skirts and dresses. The principal gives a talk on the virtue of prudence.

By the time these students are in fifth grade, they will study Latin, in a building where bulletin boards now feature quotes from Cicero and St. Augustine. In their final year, they will present a senior thesis. Most will go on to college, many at public universities, some at Christian colleges.

Castello was at Covenant Christian Academy for 20 years. While he was headmaster, the academy expanded its campus and grew from 275 students to more than 600. Though he is a product of public schools — good ones, he’s quick to note — he is now a foot soldier in this battle for private education.

When he began his teaching career after seminary, he loved how academics came alive at schools like Covenant: “Every class was grounded on the word of God, it was rooted in truth, it was meant to be transformative in the lives of students.”

But private schools can be financially out of reach for families. It was a struggle for Castello and his wife to afford Covenant for their two sons. He knew most members of his Southern Baptist church could not pay the tuition, now around $20,000, so he helped raise scholarship money and ramped up financial aid.
Now that Texas offers money for private school tuition, he encourages parents to use it.

When Gwen Albaugh’s husband died from cancer three years ago, Castello secured a scholarship for her two children to attend Covenant. She said, “I know that they are somewhere that they are being taught the foundational work, whether that be academics or faith-wise, and I’m able to now provide for our family.”
After Texas launched its education savings accounts this year, Albaugh’s children were among at least 78 Covenant students who qualified for the program.
For years, Democrats and rural Republicans in Texas blocked efforts to create education savings accounts.
“They were worried, I think rightfully, about what it would do to public schools in rural areas,” said Douglas Harris, an economist at Tulane who studies school choice.
Advocates also warned these programs entwine government and religion by diverting taxpayer money to Christian schools.

“It’s an abject violation of religious freedom to force a taxpayer to fund a school that discriminates against their faith,” said Rachel Laser, head of the advocacy group Americans United for Separation of Church and State.

Classical education, popular among conservatives, was already on the rise before more taxpayer funds became available. It exists in many forms, in religious schools outside ACCS, homeschooling groups, secular and charter schools. Many classical Christian schools go a step further in their focus on reclaiming and promoting Western Christian culture.

ACCS is an accrediting body and the oldest network of classical Christian schools. Its membership includes about 500 schools, but it has grown by nearly 200 schools since 2019. Goodwin, its president, credits a pandemic-era mistrust of public education, when debates ignited over school closures, books, race, sexuality and gender identity.
Not all ACCS schools accept government money, but many that do now advertise state funding options on their websites.

“What we’re trying to do is take enough of the public school share that we can change the country’s direction with powerful leadership coming out of these classical Christian schools,” Goodwin said in a promotional video.

Wilson echoed that idea. “We are training and educating leaders,” he told The Associated Press. “We teach them how to analyze, how to take arguments apart, how to understand what your opponent is saying and represent it accurately.”

Wilson can be a provocateur, suggesting homosexuality should be criminalized and criticizing Muslim immigration to the U.S. His Idaho church prefers heads of households, usually men, to vote. He describes his politics as “slightly to the right” of Confederate Gen. J.E.B. Stuart.
Castello labels some of Wilson’s statements as “vilely offensive.” He compares Wilson to a family elder, one who deserves respect, but also has some reprehensible views.

ACCS is less pugilistic than its founder. It includes socially conservative Christians across denominations and hasn’t adopted Wilson’s more fringe beliefs. Schools agree to a statement of faith, including that same-sex relationships and gender transitions are off-limits, but families may not be aware of Wilson’s teachings or influence. He still advises the ACCS board, though, and his books are required reading in some of its schools.

Wilson is part of the reason three mothers pulled their children this year from a San Diego-area Christian school, which pursued an affiliation with ACCS. They opposed his patriarchal, controversial views and were concerned when students received humanities coursework Wilson wrote.

In one of the texts students read, a commentary on C.S. Lewis, Wilson defends the author’s “historic Christian understanding of the relationship of men and women.” He calls Islam and Hinduism “false religions.”
Sarah Stankorb, an author who covered Wilson in her book “Disobedient Women,” said ACCS schools are “definitely a mode of transmission into the Doug Wilson pipeline.”

At Coram Deo Academy, an ACCS school where Castello served as vice president of operations until last year, more than 360 students out of 2,000 have been approved for Texas Education Freedom Accounts, or TEFA.

Coram Deo could potentially receive $3.5 million in TEFA funds this year, equal to nearly 17% of its budget, according to Scott Head, the school’s chief financial officer. The taxpayer funds are also on track to cover half of the school’s financial aid budget.

The Texas program prioritizes low-income students and those with disabilities, but its income limits this year go up to $165,000 for a family of four, opening the door to middle-income families. Eligible students can receive at least $10,474 for private school, which covers Coram Deo’s average tuition. The school’s hybrid model keeps costs lower because students are homeschooled part of the week.
Nathanael Wydner graduated from Coram Deo, but he and his wife Candice could not afford to send both of their children on his salary alone. They cried when they got off the TEFA waitlist.
“This year and probably for years to come, it’s everything. It’s the only way that this works for us,” Wydner said.
At one of Castello’s startup schools, 22 out of 25 students are using TEFA this year.
The Rev. Victor Shahat, head of St. Clement Orthodox Christian Academy, said, “I can’t imagine without TEFA we can open the school this year at all.”

The TEFA program is not conducive to startups, since vendor schools must be in operation for two years. Castello qualified because he ran a microschool for seven years at a tennis club for the owners’ children. His Kyrie organization now serves as a TEFA conduit for three new locations.
Castello said the influx of taxpayer money “completely transforms the possibility” of increasing access to Christian education.
“We’re on a massive inflection point in the Christian school movement,” Castello tells a sanctuary full of Christian-school parents one Monday evening.

Standing behind the lectern, cowboy boots under his dress slacks, he predicts Texas will increase the funding for its education savings accounts — an outcome that may hinge on whether the Republican or Democrat wins the governor’s race this November. He tells the audience about a new federal tax credit, which will also send money to private schools.
There are murmurs of approval and “amens” when he mentions how Christian schools will benefit.

Hours earlier, Castello had walked through his newest school, Southlake Christian Academy, located in a church. Supplies crowded an office, and the sound of drilling echoed as contractors installed security cameras.
The campus opened with six students this year, but Castello has big plans for it. A longtime coach, he hopes to add athletic facilities, and he has brought on a real estate consultant.
He plans to talk to lawmakers about making it easier for private schools like his to buy shuttered public school buildings.
He has heard the critiques that these programs will hurt public schools. He counters that he and other private school parents still pay taxes that support public education.
“I’m not against the public schools,” Castello said, though he doesn’t see them as religiously neutral, calling them “secular humanist schools.”
The line between public and private schools is blurring.
“If private schools are being funded by taxpayer funds, then what is the difference between public and private?” he asked.

title: Tom Skerritt, known for roles in "Alien," "Picket Fences," dies at 93
summary: Tom Skerritt died of natural causes, his family said in a statement.
story: Tom Skerritt, the actor known for his roles in "Alien," "Top Gun" and TV's "Picket Fences," has died, his publicist confirmed to CBS News on Thursday. He was 93.
Skerritt died Wednesday of natural causes, his family said in a statement.

"We are heartbroken by his loss," the family said. "While the world knew Tom through his remarkable acting career, we knew him for his humor, curiosity, wisdom, generosity, and the love he brought into our lives."

Skerritt was twice nominated for an Emmy — both for CBS' "Picket Fences," winning outstanding lead actor in a drama series in 1993. Other career highlights include playing the patient husband of Shirley MacLaine in "The Turning Point," Sally Field's husband in "Steel Magnolias" and a scheming opportunist who stands in the way of Jodie Foster's attempt to communicate with extraterrestrial life in "Contact."

"A writer once described me as a character actor locked in a leading man's body, and I've always loved that. It's a nice compliment. I've been able to walk the line between television and features," he told the Seattle Post-Intelligencer in 1997.

Onstage, he was the narrator in "Our Town" at Seattle's Intiman Theatre in 2004 and made his Broadway debut in 2013 in an adaptation of John Grisham's "A Time to Kill," in which The Associated Press wrote he "nicely pulls off a charming disgraced and drunken lawyer."
Skerritt's early life
Skerritt grew up in a middle-class Detroit family, his father a small businessman and his mother a housewife. He had two brothers; a sister died as a child.
He spent four years in the Air Force, attended Wayne State University and then switched to the University of California, Los Angeles, to study filmmaking, inspired by a viewing of "Citizen Kane."

His performance in a Los Angeles theater production of "The Rainmaker" led to his first film role — a supporting role as a sergeant in the 1962 scrappy, $250,000 independent Korean War film "War Hunt." The movie marked the debuts of Skerritt, Robert Redford, Sydney Pollack and Francis Ford Coppola.

Redford and Skerritt were vying for the same lead role, with the former winning out. Years later, Redford, now directing, paid Skerritt back with compound interest in "A River Runs Through It," handing him the plum role of the stern Rev. John Maclean, a minister whose governing passions are his faith and fly-fishing. The New York Times was impressed by his "halting, thoughtful manner."

Redford, who died last year, became a lifelong friend. "There was such a deep connection we made with each other that it matured into a level-headed friendship," Redford told the Seattle Times in 2007. "His values were close to mine, and he kept his integrity."
"Alien" and "Top Gun"

After "War Hunt," however, Skerritt still struggled for screen time, landing a small role in "M*A*S*H" and "Thieves Like Us" for Robert Altman, and doing a bit part as a motorcycle cop in "Harold and Maude" for Hal Ashby.

Things changed with "The Turning Point," which earned him a National Board of Review win. Then came "Alien," with Skerritt playing the beleaguered and doomed captain of the ship Nostromo, crouched in a dark, claustrophobic duct, hunting the alien with a sputtering flamethrower. He told the Seattle Times that what appealed to him in the script was that the lead actor disappeared and "the woman becomes the hero. I really like that idea."

Things shifted again after that, including a memorable role as Tom Cruise's instructor in the landmark "Top Gun": "Gentlemen, you are the top 1% of all naval aviators. The elite. The best of the best. We'll make you better," he told the students. "This school is about combat. There are no points for second place."

Skerritt achieved perhaps his best notices as the kindly sheriff in "Picket Fences," a comedy created by David E. Kelley that won 14 Emmy Awards — one for Skerritt — and a Golden Globe over its four-year run from 1992 to 1996.

Skerritt co-starred opposite Kathy Baker, playing his doctor wife in the community of Rome, Wisconsin, a place with bizarre happenings, like having a robber leaving a trail of frogs or the pope becoming the primary witness to a murder.

"It was written by the best writer on television," he told the A.V. Club in 2019. "That was the magic and brilliance of it. Because I wasn't trying to do a series, but then they said Kathy Baker was going to do it, and I thought, 'She's fabulous — what do they want me for?'"

Also on the small screen, Skerritt played William Walker on ABC's "Brothers and Sisters," Jimmy Ford on TNT's "Leverage" and he had the recurring character Evan Drake on "Cheers." He starred in the Hallmark movie "What the Deaf Man Heard," co-starring Matthew Modine, Judith Ivey and James Earl Jones. He also modeled for Guess jeans.
Directing and writing — his initial dream — had been overtaken by a career in front of the camera, though he managed to direct and star in the 1997 television movie "Divided by Hate."

"Things happen," he told The Ottawa Citizen in 1992. "You get hired for a film and the roles kept coming for me. I kept telling myself that if I stuck with acting it would be a really good training for what the problems are in directing. Then the family came along and I had to support them. The years flew by and there was a time when I said I would give up acting and really try to get into directing. But it hasn't worked out that way and I have no regrets."
He is survived by his third wife, Julie Tokashiki, and five children.

title: John Anderson, country music Hall of Famer, dies at 71
summary: John Anderson, a country music Hall of Famer with a distinctive voice, died on Wednesday, his family said. He was 71 years old.
story: John Anderson, a country music Hall of Famer with a distinctive voice, has died, his family said Wednesday. He was 71 years old.
"It is with the heaviest of hearts that we share the passing of our beloved husband, father, grandfather, and best friend," his family said in a statement on Instagram.

"To the world, he was a gifted country music singer whose voice and songs touched countless lives," they said. "To us, he was so much more. He was the heart of our family, the one who made us laugh, loved us fiercely, and made every ordinary moment feel special."
"His music will live on, but for us, his greatest legacy will always be the love he gave his family and the memories we will carry with us forever," they said.

Anderson's unmistakable voice helped make him a country music legend. And for some of Nashville's biggest names, he was required listening, with stars like Blake Shelton collaborating with him. Others, including Luke Combs and Ashley McBryde, recorded his songs for his tribute album, "Something Borrowed, Something New."
The Florida native arrived in Nashville as a teenager, playing clubs and working construction — even helping build the roof of the Grand Ole Opry.
But before long, he was the one raising it.
"Swingin'" became a no. 1 hit and the CMA Single of the Year in 1983.
A decade later, "Straight Tequila Night" and "Seminole Wind" brought Anderson's distinctive sound to another generation.
But years later, a mysterious life-threatening illness nearly silenced him, taking away his hearing and leaving him wondering whether he would ever make music again.
Anderson told CBS News in 2022 that the first part of the illness brought severe, terrible headaches, starting in 2016. Then, he said, his hair fell out and he lost his hearing "almost completely."
"They never really figured out just what it was," he said.
His return to music included the 2020 album "Years." Then, in 2024, came country music's highest honor: a place in its Hall of Fame.
"It's a long long road from Apaka, Florida, to standing right here on this stage, but I must say, behind all of that there was a lot of adventure, and I got to choose my own way," he said.
Anderson died just days after attending a Hall of Fame ceremony in Nashville on Sunday.

"I was talking with John Sunday night at the HOF ceremony," country star McGraw wrote on social media. "He was in such good spirits. We talked, we laughed, we sang his songs that I loved so much together, just goofing off. I am completely heartbroken by his passing. There will never be a stylist in music, any music, that was so defining as his."

title: Christina Applegate reveals she was misdiagnosed with MS
summary: Christina Applegate said on her MeSsy podcast that her doctor recently revealed she did not have multiple sclerosis.
story: Christina Applegate announced Tuesday that she was misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis, more than five years after announcing she had been told she had the chronic condition.

Applegate, 54, shared the news in a double episode of her podcast MeSsy, where she and co-host Jamie-Lynn Sigler discuss life with multiple sclerosis. Applegate had taken a break from the podcast in recent weeks. She said Tuesday she had taken that time to process the new information.

Applegate said that "all of a sudden, a few years ago," her doctor wanted to take her off an infusion treatment and see how her B cells reacted. The cell count didn't increase or decrease after the treatment stopped, which began "kind of a study into my diagnosis," Applegate said. Eventually, her doctor had surprising news: Applegate had never had multiple sclerosis at all.
"She came into my room and said, 'Congratulations, you don't have MS,' " Applegate said. "I was, like, not happy at all. Everybody else was so happy."

Multiple sclerosis, or MS, is a disease where the body's immune system attacks the central nervous system. Symptoms vary from person to person, according to the National Multiple Sclerosis Society, and there are multiple types of the disease. The condition has no known cause, and its progression is impossible to predict.

Dr. Marwa Kaisey, an associate professor at the Cedars-Sinai Medical Center department of neurology, said on the podcast that almost one in five people who have been told they have multiple sclerosis "didn't actually have it." Misdiagnoses with the condition are "fairly common," she said, because there is no one test for it.
Applegate said at the time of her initial diagnosis, she underwent tests including a spinal tap and MRIs. Scans showed lesions on her brain, she said.
Applegate said that she continues to have debilitating symptoms that affect her daily life and mobility.

"You don't get misdiagnosed and then all of the sudden I'm better," Applegate said. "If anything, I've gotten worse. So I'm back at square one where I don't know what's going on with me. And that's going to be an online investigation that my doctors are going to be getting into just to find out what has been going on since 2021, why did this happen?"
The investigation will begin next week, she said.

Applegate has previously described living with symptoms including numbness, an off-balance feeling, and a tingling sensation in the limbs. She said in a 2022 interview with The New York Times that she "can't walk without a cane."

In the same interview, she said she used a wheelchair during filming of the Netflix hit "Dead To Me," and the show's script was adjusted to accommodate her symptoms. In 2023, Applegate said her symptoms might lead to her giving up acting on camera. She said Tuesday that she has physical therapy three times a week.
After she was officially diagnosed with the disease, she became an outspoken advocate for MS. On Tuesday, she said the misdiagnosis made her feel "like I let everybody down."
"It's very unnerving and it's really confusing for me," Applegate said.

title: Notable Deaths in 2026
summary: A look back at the esteemed personalities who've left us this year, who'd touched us with their innovation, creativity and humanity.
story: A look back at the esteemed personalities who left us this year, who touched us with their innovation, creativity and humanity.
By CBSNews.com senior producer David Morgan. The Associated Press contributed to this gallery.

Metropolitan Opera singer Martina Arroyo (Feb. 2, 1936-Oct. 13, 2026) was a sparkling talent acclaimed as an interpreter of Verdi and Mozart, starring as the heroine in productions of "Aida," "Don Carlo," "Il Trovatore," "Macbeth," and "Don Giovanni." She was named a Kennedy Center Honoree in 2013.

Arroyo was born in Harlem to a father raised in Puerto Rico and an African-American mother who gave her a love of culture and a pioneering spirit. Her first exposure to opera came via radio. "My parents used to listen to the Metropolitan Opera on Saturday afternoon," Arroyo told "CBS This Morning" in 2013. "And I couldn't see them and I couldn't care less what they looked like. I just liked the sound and making music."

She studied the arts as a child, and took voice lessons while teaching Italian in a Bronx public school and serving as a case worker in the city's welfare department. In 1958 she won a radio competition to audition for the Metropolitan Opera's training program. The soprano would go on to sing at Carnegie Hall, and in the 1960s performed on stages in Europe.

Her big break came in New York in 1965, when Met star Birgit Nilsson fell ill; Arroyo was called in at the last minute to perform Aida. At the end, there was a standing ovation — and everything changed. She became a Metropolitan Opera contract singer, and over 20 seasons starred in a run of 199 performances, including major Verdi and Mozart roles, as well as Puccini ("Madama Butterfly"), Ponchielli ("La Gioconda"), and Wagner, becoming the first Black woman to perform Elsa in "Lohengrin." She also sang in Berlin, Chicago, Düsseldorf, Frankfurt, London, Paris, Prague, San Francisco, Vienna and Zurich.
A prolific recording artist, she also performed in recitals and oratorios, and appeared regularly on "The Tonight Show."

Arroyo gave her last opera performance in 1991, but she continued to give lectures and lead master classes around the world. She also established the Martina Arroyo Foundation in 2003 to aid artists at the beginning of their careers. In 2013 she spoke of the impact of teaching singers starting out: "Because I think that it all led to this. It's knowing that it doesn't end with you. It's going to go on, and you want it to go on even better than when you were working in that profession."

title: Theranos whistleblower calls Holmes "almost unrecognizable" in film
summary: Theranos whistleblower Tyler Shultz said he "was pretty shocked" by the version of Elizabeth Holmes he saw onscreen in the new documentary "You Can See Everything."
story: Tyler Shultz, a former Theranos employee and one of the whistleblowers credited with exposing Elizabeth Holmes' now-infamous biotech company as a fraud, said he "was pretty shocked" by the version of Holmes he saw onscreen in the new documentary "You Can See Everything."

"The Elizabeth that I knew completely commanded a room, even if that room was full of secretaries of state, secretaries of defense, generals, senators. She would own a room," Shultz said Monday on "CBS Mornings." "She had so much confidence, and the woman that I saw onscreen looked, frankly, like a, a broken woman."
"It was almost unrecognizable," he added.

Shultz also said he believes Holmes misled Nathan Fielder, who directed the documentary alongside Lance Oppenheim, when at one point in the film she pulled out what she claimed was Theranos' blood-testing device.

"She brings out the Theranos device, and she lays it across the table and all of its components, so you know you can see everything," said Shultz. "But my problem was: that was not the device that I worked with 12 hours a day. That was not the device that we hid from regulators. That was not the device that failed quality controls. That was not the device that we used to knowingly give patients incorrect medical information, and she completely misled [Fielder] down this completely different rabbit hole."

Holmes never admitted wrongdoing in the wake of the Theranos scandal, a stance on which she held firm in the documentary, which brings viewers inside Holmes' San Diego rental property in 2023 just weeks before the start of her 11-year prison sentence. At the time, she was living with her partner, Billy Evans, who is also featured prominently in the documentary, and their two children.

Holmes was convicted in 2022 of multiple counts of defrauding Theranos' investors, who, like the public, were led to believe that the company could conduct thorough clinical analyses on tiny blood samples pricked from a fingertip rather than drawn the traditional way. The technology was billed as revelatory for the field of diagnostics, increasing access to and costs of crucial, even life-saving, testing.

But Theranos turned out to be a sham — the technology couldn't do what it claimed. And Holmes, who had become a symbol of Silicon Valley's visionary potential, became the subject of widespread scrutiny as people wondered how she managed to deceive so many, and why she had gone to such great lengths to try to build a business on a false promise.

"She knows that she did something wrong," Shultz said on Monday. "She knows that she was lying, because she created this whole web of lies that you would not have needed to create if you actually believed the lies."

Shultz was hired in 2013 as an intern at Theranos, where his grandfather, former U.S. Secretary of State George Shultz, served as a board member. Tyler left the company the following year and went on to serve as an informant for investigations into its dubious practices by The Wall Street Journal and various government regulatory agencies. He later participated in the 2016 HBO documentary "The Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley," which covered Theranos' downfall.
"You Can See Everything" premiered on Friday and earned $15 million at the box office in its opening weekend, the second-most profitable opening weekend ever for a documentary.
This story published first on CBS News at 10:50 a.m. on Oct. 19, 2026.

title: Cindy Crawford and family break silence on Presley Gerber's death
summary: Cindy Crawford, Rande Gerber and their daughter, Kaia, have broken their silence for the first time since Presley Gerber's death​ last month.
story: Cindy Crawford, Rande Gerber and their daughter, Kaia, have broken their silence for the first time since Presley Gerber's death last month.

"We are beyond heartbroken to lose our beloved son and brother. We feel so blessed to have had Presley in our lives for 27 years. He is a sweet, beautiful soul who loved and is loved, now and forever," a statement from the family shared on social media said. "We are so proud of how he showed up in the world, with kindness and vulnerability. We are grateful for the outpouring of love and support from so many who know and love our family and even strangers who feel our pain. Til we meet again our sweet boy. We love you forever, Mom, Dad and Kaia."

Presley Gerber died on Sept. 20 at a Santa Monica rehab facility at the age of 27. His cause of death remains deferred, according to the Los Angeles County Medical Examiner's website. But Santa Monica police have said his death was a suspected overdose. He was often open about his battles with addiction and mental health on his social media channels.

None of Presley Gerber's family members had publicly spoken about his death until Sunday. His parents, supermodel Cindy Crawford and businessman Rande Gerber, shared the same message on their Instagram accounts, while his younger sister, actor and model Kaia Gerber, shared her own.
"I love you the bluest, to the moon and back and back again, forever big brother," the caption said.
Her post also paid tribute to Presley Gerber, recounting experiences from their childhood and how she has struggled with a feeling of emptiness since his death.

"To say loving you was the easiest thing in the world would imply that it required any effort at all. I was born loving you. I will die loving you. There was never anything else," Kaia's message said. "I am learning how to love you when I canot see you. How to tell you something without picking up my phone to call you. How to be your sister in a world that I can't reach for you in."

title: Rosalía on "Lux" and her devotion to music
summary: The Spanish singer continues to defy convention with her fourth album, "Lux," a mix of classical, opera and pop that tells the stories of female saints and mystics through history.
story: New York's Metropolitan Opera House seemed a fitting setting to chat with the Spanish pop artist Rosalía after the global tour for her latest album, "Lux" (which is Latin for light). "I really like how concentrated the energy is in spaces like this," she said.

This superstar knows about energy and performing. Her song "Berghain," inspired by the 12th-century mystic Hildegard of Bingen, featuring an orchestra and booming choir, is not the typical pop formula. Then again, there's nothing typical about Rosalía. With operatic vocals in Spanish and German, but also an appearance from Björk, the song makes clear the 34-year-old Spaniard's reverence for the classics – and desire to do something different. Opera, she said, was a big inspiration.
Watch Rosalía and Björk perform "Berghain" at the 2026 BRIT Awards:

She said her tour for "Lux" has been more demanding than any she has done – performing en pointe, for instance, and singing in Japanese, Ukrainian, Catalan and Arabic. She wrote lyrics in 14 languages. "If you find 14 languages in this album, it's not from a place of exhibition, but a search for communion," she said.

"Lux" was so anticipated that a countdown to announce it snarled traffic in Madrid. The album features the stories of female saints and mystics through history, like Olga of Kyiv. One might not think of the 10th century ruler as the source for a great song.

"I didn't know about her," Rosalía said.  "This woman, she was an assassin before becoming a saint. Some of them were poets. They were prostitutes, some were drug addicts, and sometimes you wouldn't connect sainthood to these words. It was definitely very inspiring."

Asked if she considers the commercial potential of such an album during its making, she replied, "On one side, there's the responsibility of, okay, I have an office and there's people that I care about. But at the same time, I only can do what's honest for me. It took me two years to make this album."

The self-described perfectionist kept making tweaks so close to the deadline that there are slight differences between the digital version and the vinyl. "I couldn't do this for too long, because otherwise it would be interminable," she said. "Like, I can be forever doing it."
She says she still thinks there are things that could be done differently: "Yeah, always. The mix, the violins here, they could be half a dB up. Or my voice here, I could have done another take."
Asked if she can enjoy listening to her own album, she replied, "I never listen to my albums. 'Cause it's pointless."
But it's something you created? "I create to share it, to let it go," she said. "Why would I listen it back? That would be torture!"

Her fans would disagree. Rosalía's four albums showcase vast range. Her first album, 2017's "Los Ángeles," was a modern twist on the flamenco she'd spent years studying in music school. 2022's "Motomami" fused rap and raggaeton, and topped multiple "album of the year" lists.

And now, "Lux," which hit #4 on the Billboard 200 chart, and topped the U.S. Latin chart. The album features a four-part symphonic structure. With choirs and the London Symphony Orchestra, she did not make her life easy. "Yes, it's true," she laughed. "But I don't think I ever do."
What is that inside of you? "I don't know, there's just something, some, un fuego, like, a fire. Some sort of, like, urgency and love for what, I don't know."

That curiosity was ignited in childhood. Born Rosalía Vila Tobella near Barcelona, she remembers running headlong down a hill with family trying to stop her: "I fell to the floor and then I opened my forehead. And then they had to take me to the hospital and sew it. And I have this mark here, and this is a reminder that maybe since I was a kid that's who I was. I never stay still. I never say no. If there is something like a guardian angel, mine is definitely tired. He cannot even stop for a cigarette! I stressed the poor thing out."

That stressed, tired guardian angel has been good to her, considering she was dropped from a Spanish talent show, "Tú Sí Que Vales," when she was 15. "That experience taught me that I had to prepare a lot," she said. "It really helped me grow. I'm very grateful for that."
By 2021, Pitchfork was including her on its list of the most important artists of the last 25 years.

With her sometimes-experimental sound and juxtaposition of styles, Rosalía is about as close to the avant-garde as mainstream pop gets. She's a fashionista, a staple at the Met Gala, a muse for designers and brands; and she's now acting, too, in HBO's "Euphoria." "I try to have fun while I try new things," she said, "and I try not to be in fear. I think if this is my nature, then I embrace it."

And in this latest album – inspired by saints – Rosalía reveals an almost spiritual commitment to her craft. "Being a musician is, for me, an office as noble as somebody who makes bread or shoes. So, I just go to the studio and try to put my love and my energy."
You'll just work and work and work? "Yeah, but out of devotion," she said. "I love this. I love making music, so I devoted my life to that."

title: Natural-born actor John Turturro: "I'm at a very fruitful time"
summary: He's gifted audiences with memorable appearances in more than 100 films and TV shows. Now, John Turturro, one of the great character actors, is playing a rare lead role in a charming and moving crime drama, "The Only Living Pickpocket in New York."
story: Character actors like John Turturro never fail to leave their mark on screen. He's been commanding our attention in movies and on television for 46 years, always digging deep to deliver something memorable. Called one of the great character actors in the history of movies, Turturro responded with modesty: "Oh wow, I'll take that compliment. I'm not sure of it!"

Now 69, Turturro is doing some of his best work in Apple TV's "Severance," and on the big screen in a rare leading-man part, as a thief clinging to a world passing him by, in a charming and moving crime thriller, "The Only Living Pickpocket in New York."

"Within this tense sort of crime thriller, there's all this humanity and, like, tenderness," he said. "There's like this love story, and there's this guy who basically the world has changed around him. He's obsolete in some ways. So, how does someone like that survive in such a fast-changing world? I found it very evocative and moving."
To watch a trailer for "The Only Living Pickpocket in New York," click on the video player below.
We spoke to Turturro in his Brooklyn neighborhood. He's New York through and through – and is not a recluse. "I ride the train," he said.

Growing up in Hollis, Queens, his parents were a working-class couple with a penchant for drama. "They had kind of a very intimate relationship, and volatile at certain times," Turturro said. "When we used to watch 'The Honeymooners,' when I was really a little kid, my older brother, Ralph, used to call the show 'Mommy and Daddy.' It was, you know, an expressive, sometimes explosive household. So, you learn what size is, and what, also, quiet is within that."

They also loved movies, which made a lasting impression on their son. "I didn't go to the theater that much when I was young, but I watched the 'Million Dollar Movie,' and I watched all these great movies from the '30s, '40s, '50s. Those people opened up my brains, you know, whether it was Barbara Stanwyck, or Edward G., or Cagney, or Bette Davis, and they're, like, part of me."

The idea to become an actor formed watching Dustin Hoffman in "Midnight Cowboy": "I think it was the scene in the diner when he said, he was like, 'Oh, Joey, I only got 64 cents in my pocket.' And I was like, Who is this guy?"
And it was cemented with a Broadway musical: "Bob Fosse's 'Pippin,' I saw the commercial. I felt like someone was reaching their hand out to me, like to touch me. And I was like, Wow."

After college came a scholarship to get a master's at the Yale School of Drama, but not before getting cast in his first movie, "Raging Bull." It's described as a non-speaking part, but he got a little something in there – his first line, delivered to Robert de Niro.

During his career Turturro has worked opposite Paul Newman in "The Color of Money," and been directed by Robert Redford in "Quiz Show" – always searching for ways to unlock his character, like in "Miller's Crossing," the first of four films with the Coen Brothers.

The quirky voice of his character, Bernie Bernbaum, came from his accountant; the fear from a single day in his childhood. In a list of difficult scenes, Turturro's in "Miller's Crossing," where Bernbaum faces execution in the woods, is a difficult scene.

"I had one advantage," said Turturro. "When I was younger, I was a serious basketball player. My friends and I, we were coming home from a party and we had, like, a bike with a banana seat, you know, and the handle. We pulled into a schoolyard, and this guy was shooting baskets. There was three of us. So, he thought maybe we were going to try to steal something from him. It was late … he took out a gun. He put it right to my head, on my bike, and I was like, I was frozen. But I never forgot this feeling of having this gun pointed at my head."

He's collaborated nine times with Spike Lee, starting with "Do the Right Thing." Lee sent Turturro the script, then asked him which part he wanted to play. Turturro chose Pino, the racist son of the pizza shop owner.

Asked if he thought Lee wanted him to choose Pino, Turturro replied, "I think he was happy that I did. … One thing about me is like, I don't need to be liked if I'm doing a movie. What I need to do is to hold your attention, and I can, you know, surprise you. You know, I'm not looking to soften the edges with it, or even make it, you know, worse than it is. It is what it is."
He says he has seen that guy: "Yeah, and then you see it in all different forms. I think that's one of the unspoken things in our country, which has such diversity. It's something we grapple with."
When Turturro got the script for "The Big Lebowski," he noted to the Coen Brothers that the part was very small – to which they told him, You'll make something out of it. And he did.

"And I have to say, I was really embarrassed the first time I saw it," Turturro laughed. "I was laughing, but I was really embarrassed. I was like, I can't believe you put all this stuff in there! Because it's like we were friends and we were, like, seven years old and they said 'Come on over, let's do a show together.' You want to make your friend laugh!"

He also likes discussing the craft. "Let me tell you something, my man: I like being here and talking about acting and stuff," he said, "because for me, I'm a natural-born actor. That's just how it is and stuff."

Surprisingly, this natural-born actor doesn't have an Oscar nomination. There's some buzz that might change with "The Only Living Pickpocket in New York." And though awards would be nice, it's the work that matters to John Turturro.

Asked if he can measure success without awards, he replied, "Yes, I've been able to work and do interesting things and entertain people and maybe even make them think sometimes, or laugh or cry at different times, and take them away from their lives. So, I'm very, very appreciative of where I am. I want to keep that up, and I feel like I'm at a very fruitful time."

title: The inseparable legacies of Jackson Pollock and Lee Krasner
summary: Lee Krasner has long been eclipsed by the shadow of her husband, Jackson Pollock. Now, a landmark show in New York City rewrites the story of the artists whose work and legacies were – aesthetically and personally – bound together.
story: The old farmhouse in the hamlet of Springs, N.Y., is easy to miss, if not for the sign for the Pollock-Krasner House and Study Center. Here, on the east end of Long Island, is where Jackson Pollock and Lee Krasner moved in the winter of 1945. And it was here where the Abstract Expressionists would send a seismic tremor through the art world.

It was their home and workplace. The married couple moved into a house with no plumbing or heating. "It was really a choice that they made to come out here, to go into isolation almost to really focus on the work," said the Center's director Matthew K. Ward.
Now an historical site run by Stony Brook University, the Pollock-Krasner House looks much as it did when Krasner died in 1984.
Ward showed us the custom-made speaker system that Pollack himself wired through a crawlspace. It has paint all over it. "Yeah, a lot of stuff here has paint all over it!" Ward laughed.
Krasner worked in an upstairs bedroom – small, but with a view of Accabonac   Creek. Pollock painted in the barn out back, but without an easel. "No – that's kind of Jackson's thing," Ward said.

Pollack stretched his canvases out on the floor, and would pour, drip, and splatter paint from above down onto the canvas. The floor is a work of art in itself. Ward said, "The way Pollock worked was so physical. I think we feel him through the floor."
The entire art world changed right here. In fact, Ward said, "The most modern work anybody had ever seen was made in this rustic space."
In 1949, Life magazine famously asked of Pollack, "Is he the greatest living painter in the United States?"
And yet, many people who might show up at the Pollack-Krasner House may ask, "Who's Lee Krasner?" After a new show at New York City's Metropolitan Museum of Art, no more.

In "Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous," for the first time the two artists' careers are considered together. "We hopefully prime you for this idea of creative adjacency, two careers in parallel," said co-curator Brinda Kumar.

Early in the exhibition, you see Krasner's work on the left wall, and Pollock's through a portal. "You automatically understand, hopefully, how this dialogue is happening across the studio, across the lawn," Kumar said.
Pollock was born in Cody, Wyoming. Krasner was the child of Jewish immigrants in Brooklyn. So, why did they hit it off?
"A very good question!" said co-curator David Breslin. "I think for Pollock to meet someone who had that degree of sheer intelligence, bravado, I think her connections weren't a bad thing."

As to what attracted Krasner to Pollock, Breslin said, "I don't know if she needed him. She was drawn to his work. Who the man was who could have made that work almost became a riddle that she wanted to solve."

That riddle proved confounding. Pollock drank heavily, and had affairs. "She has this great line that says something along the lines of, 'Unfortunately, I have the fortune of being married to Jackson Pollock,'" said Breslin.
But in the mid-1950s, Krasner left for Paris. Jackson moved his girlfriend, Ruth Kligman, into the house and, said Breslin, "things kind of went to hell."
In 1956, Pollock died in a car crash. Kligman, also in the car, survived, but a friend did not.
Krasner went back to the house in Springs. She would aggressively promote Pollock's legacy as a painter, but she now took over his studio.
According to Breslin, "He dies; she's unleashed."
Kumar said, "Moving into the barn after Pollock's death allowed her to work on an unprecedented scale as well."
In the Sixties, she'd paint "Through Blue," "Right Bird Left," and "Combat."
"These are painted directly on the wall," Kumar said. "There's a kind of ferocity. And today if you go to Springs, you'll see the kind of ghostly outlines [from the canvases]."

Krasner lived and worked here for another 28 years after Pollock's death. Ward said, "This home is filled with ephemera that belonged to both of them. Lee wanted Jackson's legacy to live on just as her own, and she wanted them to live on together."

In effect, the exhibition "Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous" tries to rewrite history and change the mythology about these artists. Breslin said, "Our exhibition really has been an effort to say she's an equal."

title: More people now use GLP-1s to lose weight than for other health issues
summary: Growing usage of GLP-1 drugs for weight loss is reshaping how consumers shop for food and clothes, according to consulting firm EY-Parthenon.
story: More Americans are now taking GLP-1 drugs to shed some pounds than to treat diabetes and other health conditions for which the medications were originally prescribed, new research shows.
Roughly 54% of people taking semaglutide medications such as Ozempic and Wegovy do so to lose weight, overtaking the share of people who use them for other medical reasons, according to EY-Parthenon.

Meanwhile, as usage of GLP-1 drugs for weight management surpasses other medical uses, more consumers are changing how they eat and shop, the strategy consulting firm found in a survey of nearly 15,000 people, including 3,602 current or former GLP-1 users.

For example, people taking the drugs typically consume fewer unhealthy foods and less alcohol in favor of healthier products. Sixty-three percent of GLP-1 users say they have reduced their consumption of sweet snacks, while 57% say they eat fewer salty snacks, according to EY-Parthenon's research.
Food makers, grocery chains and other retailers are adapting to those changes in consumer habits.

"We are finding that manufacturers and retailers are making more room on store shelves for GLP-1-diet-specific foods, or protein-enhanced items, and smaller portion sizes," Don Johnson, a principal in EY-Parthenon's consumer strategy practice, told CBS News. "Some consumer packaged goods makers thought this was a blip or fad. Now I don't hear that. Everyone accepts that this is a structural change that's not going away."
Smaller sizes, fitted styles

Growing use of the drugs for controlling weight is also changing how consumers shop for clothes. In the apparel department, EY-Parthenon researchers found that consumers taking GLP-1s are gravitating toward smaller clothing sizes and more fitted clothing, swimwear and athletic wear.
"You're losing a lot of weight on the drugs, so you're needing to buy differently," Johnson said.

EY-Parthenon found that 72% of GLP-1 users sized down in clothing after rapidly losing weight, requiring a wardrobe refresh. Roughly half of users increased their spending on fitness services, such as gym memberships, while 46% switched apparel brands.

GLP-1s have become accessible to a broader swath of consumers, driving increased adoption for weight loss, according to EY-Parthenon. The drugs are today available in more forms, such as a pill, and are also more affordable, leading more younger, lower-income and male consumers to use the drugs, according to the research.

Changes in public policy are also helping drive wider usage of the drugs. A Trump administration agreement last year with GLP-1 manufacturers Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk lowered the cost of Ozempic and Wegovy to between $150 and $350 per month, down from roughly $1,000 per month. The Medicare GLP-1 Bridge program also provides eligible Medicare beneficiaries with access to GLP-1 drugs for $50 a month.

GLP-1 drugs also could have clinical value in helping people deal with other issues, some researchers think. Experts at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania are embarking on a study to see if the drugs can deter risky financial decisions.

In a first-of-its-kind study, the researchers will examine how GLP-1s influence the body's reward system, a network of brain structures that reinforces certain behaviors, to see whether the drugs suppress temptations such as luxury purchases, gambling or other activities that people often find hard to control.

title: How Gen X should practice "the art of aging"
summary: NPR health and science correspondent Allison Aubrey, author of the new book, "Your Turn: How to Create a Midlife You Love," talks about facing all the possibilities of life's third chapter.
story: NPR health and science correspondent and "Sunday Morning" contributor Allison Aubrey is out with a new book. "Your Turn" is what she calls it – and here she is to explain what she means...

If you're asking what's next in life, you're not alone. For the millions of Gen Xers like me, we've been in the trenches for decades with work and parenting. Now, everything's changing – our relationships, our responsibilities – as our kids begin to launch.

So, if life is lived in three chapters of learn, earn, retire, then it's time for us to start thinking about that third chapter. But I don't like the word retire, because it doesn't describe what this next stretch of life can be

When I was a teenager, I went to the Kentucky Derby. As I watched one horse that was stuck in the back of the pack suddenly make a bold move in the third turn and surge ahead to win the race, the fans loved it. My grandfather told me, "Allison, always watch the third turn. There's something exciting and unexpected that happens here."
"Why?" I asked.
"Well, because when you can see the home stretch," he told me, "a sense of urgency arises."
Ah-ha, there's a midlife metaphor! If not now, then when?

With that in mind, I took a sabbatical from my day job – I called it a "curiosity tour" – and I set out to find people who've made bold third-turn pivots: A nurse who sings lead vocals in a band; a lawyer who opened a bookstore; a shy editor who took up improv in her 60s; a counselor who teaches Shake Your Soul dance. Their stories reframe what's possible.

Research shows the best longevity hacks are not pills or products, but rather a sense of purpose, a sense of play. Creative pursuits, such as dancing, singing, painting, gardening, a love of literature or theatre, they don't just bring us joy; they appear to slow down aging.
A recent study finds engaging with the arts is as powerful as exercise to slow aging.
Of course, exercise and diet matter. But the art of aging invites us to imagine a blank canvas and create something new, like the people I met on my curiosity tour who are revving up, not retiring.

So, if you want to surge ahead in your third turn, rip up that old script of "learn, earn, retire." The new one is "learn, earn, return" – a return to the playful kid within. Listen to your intuition. This is how to find midlife momentum.
It's your turn.
