title: Warren warns of "food insecurity crisis" from SNAP cuts and prices
summary: Sen. Elizabeth Warren is urging the U.S. Department of Agriculture to reverse cuts to the food-stamp program as consumers shoulder $22 billion in additional food costs.
story: Americans are facing a "food insecurity crisis" after shouldering an additional $22 billion in food costs due to rising inflation and billions of dollars in food-stamp cuts, according to Sen. Elizabeth Warren.

In an Oct. 21 letter to U.S. Department of Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins, the Massachusetts Democrat said that the combination of rising food prices and cuts to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program has created a "one-two punch" for millions of households.
Warren also asked the USDA to work with lawmakers to reverse food-stamp policies that have resulted in 5.2 million people losing SNAP benefits since July 2025.

SNAP enrollment, now at its lowest level since 2019, could shrink in the coming months as additional changes to the program take effect, according to anti-hunger experts. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), a tax and spending law signed into law by President Trump in 2025, expanded SNAP's work requirements and shifted more of the program's costs onto states. Those changes have created new hurdles for enrollment, according to experts.

The USDA halted its annual study on food insecurity in 2025, saying at the time that the report was "redundant, costly [and] politicized." But a May analysis from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York found "a remarkable increase in food insecurity, particularly among lower-educated and lower-income households and households with young children."

The New York Fed found earlier this year that 10% of U.S. families reported they didn't have enough food and that their children sometimes missed meals, more than double the 4% share in 2020. Almost 20% of families with annual income of less than $50,000 reported not having enough food, up from about 7% six years ago.

"My office developed a 'food misery index' to measure how much the combination of rising food prices and declining SNAP participation is costing American households," Warren said in her letter to the USDA. "The index combines the more than $17.2 billion in rising grocery prices — calculated by inflation-adjusting consumer expenditures — with the more than $5.1 billion in lost household SNAP benefits."
The USDA and White House didn't return a request for comment.

Changing SNAP policies would require lawmakers to pass new rules for the food-stamp program. Some anti-hunger advocates and state organizations are now lobbying Congress to delay some of the OBBBA's changes to SNAP, including a rule that would require states with high payment error rates to absorb billions in additional costs starting in October 2027.

The USDA serves as the primary federal regulator and rule-maker for SNAP, giving it some leeway in administering the program. For instance, the agency allowed some states to ban enrollees from using food stamps to buy soda and candy, although a federal judge earlier this year ruled that the Agriculture Department exceeded its authority in implementing the rules.

Warren also pointed to President Trump's tariffs as contributing to higher food prices. Higher import duties last year boosted U.S. inflation by about 2.9 percentage points through February, according to recent research from the New York Fed. Without those tariffs, the price of goods would have declined, the researchers said.

title: Son of Stephen Hubbard, American freed from Russian jail, speaks out
summary: In an interview with CBS News after Stephen Hubbard was released from Russian custody, his son, Fr. Joseph Coleman, said his father might have made a mistake in staying in Ukraine when the war began.
story: Washington — Fr. Joseph Coleman feared he would never again see his father, Stephen Hubbard, when they had a brief phone conversation last year while Hubbard was in a Russian prison.

"He was expressing a very extreme tiredness with life, the life that he was experiencing at that time. I don't want to say suicidal thoughts, but the conversation hinted it leaned in that direction," Coleman, a Greek Orthodox priest, told CBS News on Wednesday in his first television interview since his father's release.

Hubbard's release was announced earlier Wednesday during a meeting between U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Hubbard, a U.S. citizen, was imprisoned in Russia for more than four years after being accused of fighting for Ukraine. The U.S. government had deemed Hubbard wrongfully detained.
Hubbard touched down back in the U.S. Wednesday night, President Trump said while returning from a rally in South Carolina. He said Hubbard would visit the White House "in the next day or so."

Mr. Trump said Putin had agreed to release Hubbard at his request, with "no 'swap' necessary," though he also said that his decision to waive new sanctions against Russia played a role in Hubbard's release.

In a one-minute phone call with his father before Hubbard took off from St. Petersburg, Coleman said he sounded better than he had during their last conversation in May 2025. Witkoff was also present, leaving little opportunity for a private exchange.

"I want to embrace him as a son embraces his father. I want to personally assess his health to make sure he's well," Coleman said. He said he would also give his dad space to adjust to freedom and expected to see Hubbard later that evening.

Coleman, who lives in Cyprus, did not grow up in the same home as Hubbard, who was divorced from Coleman's mother. He said the family had lost track of Hubbard entirely for roughly three years after his detention.

Martin De Luca, Hubbard's U.S.-based attorney, told CBS News that when his legal team took on the case in February 2025, neither the family nor the U.S. Embassy knew precisely where Hubbard was being held.
Lawyers in Russia eventually located him and arranged for legal visits, money for food and basic necessities, and the brief phone call with his son.
De Luca said the isolation had taken an enormous toll.
"It's just being isolated from everybody you've ever known and just from the outside world," he said.

After Putin granted Hubbard's release, Witkoff praised the Russian president as a "humanitarian," prompting swift backlash from Republican and Democratic lawmakers.  Putin is wanted by the International Criminal Court for alleged war crimes involving the deportation of Ukrainian children, and Russian forces have been accused of widespread abuses during the war.
Asked about Witkoff's description of Putin, Coleman called his father's release "a small step toward peace in this greater conflict" and thanked Putin for signing off on the deal.
He described the decision as an act of "compassion and even mercy."

Hubbard, a 74-year-old retired schoolteacher, was captured in Ukraine shortly after Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022 and accused of manning a checkpoint for mercenaries. He was later sentenced to almost seven years in a penal colony following a closed-door trial.
His family has consistently disputed the charges.

De Luca said his legal team conducted its own investigation, interviewing people who knew Hubbard and examining his circumstances before the invasion. He said they found no evidence that Hubbard had served in the Ukrainian military or was physically capable of doing so at roughly 70 years old.

"We have not seen any evidence to support those allegations," De Luca said. He added that the Russian case file was largely sealed and that his team had repeatedly sought evidence substantiating the charges.
De Luca and Coleman both credited the Trump administration's diplomatic engagement with Moscow for securing Hubbard's freedom.

Asked whether recent U.S. decisions benefiting Russia — including sanctions relief and purchases of Russian diesel — were connected to Hubbard's release, De Luca said he did not believe there was a direct link, though he acknowledged that bilateral relationships involve multiple overlapping interests.
Mr. Trump, however, has explicitly said that allowing new sanctions to take effect would have prevented Hubbard's release.

And despite Hubbard's release, as many as 20 Americans remain imprisoned in Russia, including some whose families dispute the charges against them. The State Department continues to warn Americans against traveling to Russia because of the risk of wrongful detention.
De Luca said he was not concerned that the administration's engagement with Moscow would encourage further detentions, arguing that diplomatic dialogue had helped secure several Americans' freedom.

But Russia has not been designated a state sponsor of wrongful detention under a new Trump administration policy, despite its history of imprisoning Americans on questionable charges. Iran and Afghanistan have both received the designation.
Coleman stopped short of blaming his father for his circumstances but acknowledged he might have made a mistake by remaining in Ukraine as Russian forces advanced.

"The Russian forces told foreign nationals to leave and he did not," Coleman said. "I do not like what happened to my father. I am ecstatic that he is free. But he was living in an area that was a war zone."
"I'm not saying his detainment was justifiable. I'm not saying that," he said. "But these things happen in war."

Arden  Farhi
                  
        contributed to this report.

title: Trump rallying with Hinson in Iowa as she pledges to push back on White House
summary: President Trump is set to rally with Rep. Ashley Hinson in Iowa as he seeks to boost GOP candidates in a political environment that has dimmed for the party — prompting pushback from some candidates, including Hinson.
story: Sioux City, Iowa — President Trump is set to rally Thursday with Rep. Ashley Hinson in Iowa as he seeks to boost Republican candidates in a political environment that has dimmed for the party — prompting modest pushback from the very candidates he's supporting.

Hinson, who is running for Iowa's open Senate seat, initially pledged to be the president's "top ally" in the upper chamber. But as she faces off against Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek in a contest that, like several in the Hawkeye State, has grown more competitive than expected, she's adjusted that commitment in recent weeks.

When she and Turek went head-to-head at a debate earlier this month, the former local news anchor said she would be Mr. Trump's ally when it's "important for Iowa." But she said she would "push back on him" when it's needed — as she said she would regardless of who's in the White House.
Last week, Hinson told Fox News: "If he's going to say something that's wrong, I'm going to challenge him on it."
"I'm not afraid to say, 'hey, I disagree with you on this,'" she said. "But I'll be an ally to somebody when they're with me."

For Republicans, the Senate race in Iowa is just one of several in which Democrats appear competitive despite Mr. Trump winning the state by double digits in 2024. Iowa has been hit hard by high energy prices and last year's U.S.-China trade war, which led Beijing to boycott American soybeans. It's a picture that appeared unthinkable at the outset of the cycle — and puts Republicans' Senate majority on the line.
Hinson, who's represented the state in the House since 2021, said she would be at the rally on Thursday to welcome Mr. Trump to Iowa, "because I think this is a contrast election."
As the nation experiences challenges, she posed the question: Who do Iowans want at the helm?
"You want a mom, a minivan-driving mom who's common sense, who's driving that common sense back into Washington, D.C.," she said. "I think that's what Iowans want as their U.S. senator."
Hinson has made the minivan motif central to her campaign. She connected the image to her emphasis on working with Mr. Trump for Iowans earlier this week, describing a recent call with the president.

"I had just finished dropping off the boys, I was ready to run an errand," Hinson said at an event in Des Moines geared toward moms, alongside Sen. Katie Britt. "And I see pop up on my caller ID in my minivan, 'DJT.'"
She continued, "'Ashley, it's your favorite president,' that's how he introduced himself."

Hinson said the call lasted five minutes and that Mr. Trump was "just checking in on us here in Iowa." She said she thanked the president for his efforts to move forward on trade with China and asked about a deal for China to buy more soybeans.

At the event, Hinson also delivered her latest break with the president, according to Semafor, telling reporters, "I don't think we need to be making any more deals with Russia," regarding Mr. Trump's waiver of sanctions against Moscow.

The criticism follows Hinson's move to separate herself from the president's handling of the war with Iran late last month. Tucked within a post expressing support for methods to combat high prices, such as a pause on diesel exports, Hinson made one of the first splits by a GOP Senate candidate with the president over the war, writing: "The war needs to be brought to a successful and immediate end."

The statement appeared in contrast to Hinson's vote earlier in September, when the House considered a resolution aimed at reining in the president in Iran. While two other Iowa Republicans locked in tight races supported the resolution, Hinson opposed it.

At the debate a couple weeks later, Turek pressed Hinson over those votes, saying during a discussion on energy costs: "We are in this situation because of this unnecessary war in Iran that Ashley Hinson voted in favor of continuing."

Hinson clarified during the debate that she believes the war must be brought to an "immediate and successful end" by not allowing Iran to have a nuclear weapon and by making sure that U.S. allies in the region are protected. Asked why she doesn't support the efforts to pass war powers resolutions in Congress, Hinson said, "I don't think we need another resolution."
"And I certainly don't want to see the president not be able to do a orderly end to this war," she added.

Thursday's rally marks the president's second visit to Iowa this year, after he kicked off campaigning in the midterms with a trip to the Des Moines area in January. Mr. Trump also announced plans last month for the largest steel plant in U.S. history to be built in Iowa, in an Oval Office event with Hinson in attendance. During the announcement, the president pledged to visit the state for a "great rally" to help get the Republican candidates elected.
"We'll save you a good Iowa pork chop, sir," Hinson replied.

title: Candidates clash over Trump policies, Senate control in debate
summary: GOP Sen. Roger Marshall and Pastor Adam Hamilton debated tariffs, war and high fuel prices, and also addressed the most controversial issues in each of their campaigns.
story: The candidates in Kansas' surprisingly competitive Senate race faced off in a debate Wednesday evening, as Republicans fight to head off the possibility of their first loss in a Kansas Senate contest in nearly a century.

Incumbent GOP Sen. Roger Marshall hammered away at what it would mean if he were to lose — that it could help hand control of the Senate to Democrats: "My opponent's going to say anything he can to lie to get into that office and give control to Chuck Schumer."

Marshall's Democratic challenger, megachurch pastor Adam Hamilton, tried to convince voters that he's not too progressive for Kansans and went on the offensive against Marshall over the impact of tariffs, the Iran war and other Trump administration policies on the state.
Marshall hewed closely to many of President Trump's views, and like him, blamed rising diesel costs on the war in Ukraine, rather than the Iran war.

"The real problem with the cost of diesel, in particular, is No. 1, is the Ukraine war, and because of that, diesel production has gone down," Marshall said. But at the same time, he said of Mr. Trump's recent announcement that the U.S. would purchase Russian diesel, "it doesn't sound like a great idea to me." He added, "If this brings Russia to the bargaining table and it ends the war, then I'm all for it right now."

While Marshall implored Trump voters to come out and vote for him, he said he does not always align with the president and has "objected" to him multiple times before, specifically citing the ICE raids in Kansas and Mr. Trump's short-term waiver on beef imports, both of which have hurt Kansas farmers.
Hamilton described himself as a "moderate or independent-minded Democrat" and vowed to "work across the aisle to try to bring people together to solve problems."

Hamilton largely sought to distance himself from mainstream Democrats. He promised not to vote for Schumer to be majority leader if Democrats win the Senate, called the Biden administration's border policies a "disaster" and said during a discussion on transgender participation in sports: "I have a 12-year-old granddaughter. I don't want biological men or boys competing against her that could harm her."
Marshall argued Hamilton leans further to the left than he has let on. The Republican senator also questioned how independent Hamilton would be.

"He's going to say he's going to vote against these things, but every Democrat stands up, and when Schumer tells them to jump, they say, 'how high?'" Marshall said during the sports discussion. "So why is he going to be any different once he gets to Washington? He can tell us one thing, but let's see what his actions would be like."

Hamilton said he would try to "force" Mr. Trump to end the Iran war. High gas prices and tariffs are putting many farms in the state in dire economic straits, with many voters telling CBS News that they aren't sure if they will survive past next year if conditions continue.
"It was not a good decision to go to war in Iran, and we need to get out," said Hamilton.

Marshall said he "want[s] this war to be over … as soon as possible, but we cannot let Iran have a nuclear weapon." He described Hamilton's views as "war through weakness, as opposed to peace through strength."
Hamilton slammed Mr. Trump's tariffs, arguing they have led to chaos and uncertainty. Marshall said the president's tariffs have led to a "manufacturing renaissance."

Mr. Trump's immigration policies have also drawn scrutiny in Kansas, including a string of Immigration and Customs Enforcement raids that agricultural leaders warned could cause workforce disruptions. Marshall pushed back last month, saying in a post on social media that ICE "needs to coordinate with our local law enforcement."

During Wednesday's debate, Hamilton called ICE's practices "militarized" and "politicized." Marshall said "all this discussion starts with a secure border," arguing Democrats could loosen border enforcement.
Polling suggests a tight race, and millions of dollars have gushed into Kansas, flooding the state's airwaves with anti-Marshall and anti-Hamilton ads.

The debate's moderator wasted no time in asking both candidates about their biggest controversies. For Marshall, that's the New York Times report about how the OB/GYN aggressively pursued his former patients — many of whom struggled economically — for medical debts and in some cases had them arrested.
Hamilton faced questions regarding his church's response to an incident of child sex abuse at a youth summer camp in 2005.

Marshall said "we did everything possible to take good care of people" and that many of his patients got free care. He conceded that some patients were turned over to collections agencies, which he called a fairly rare occurrence that is standard in the medical industry.

At his rally in Wichita on Monday, Mr. Trump defended Marshall against these allegations, saying he was required by law to report the debt, and that he's been unfairly "made out to be some kind of Shylock character." (The Anti-Defamation League later said the term "Shylock," a reference to a Jewish moneylender in William Shakespeare's "The Merchant of Venice," is "rooted in a longstanding antisemitic stereotype.")

On the abuse scandal, Hamilton said his church subsequently changed its policy on handling allegations of abuse, and "ultimately, we helped get this man put behind bars." Still, Hamilton admitted, "I should have checked to make sure that he wasn't going back (to the youth camp). That was a mistake on my part."
Cathy Bien, a spokesperson for Hamilton's United Methodist Church, told CBS News on Wednesday that the incident was "handled the best way [they] knew how 20 years ago."

Kansas could decide which party controls the Senate, and even before the debate, early voting numbers were skyrocketing in the state. Election officials say that they are fielding numbers that rival the 2024 presidential election.

The race could hinge on how many Republicans cross party lines to vote for Hamilton. At least 100 Kansas Republican leaders have endorsed Hamilton, including former governors, state officials and Mr. Trump's own former White House press secretary, Stephanie Grisham.

But many are voting early to ensure Republicans maintain control of the Senate. One early voter in Wichita, Tim Higgins, told CBS News that he's backing Marshall because "it's important to keep the progress that the nation is currently on since the presidential election."
However, for many, the race is about state issues.
"Rural Kansas is struggling, urban Kansas is struggling," said former Republican state Rep. Terrie Huntington, who is voting for Hamilton. "I think people are looking for change."

title: Abdul El-Sayed and Mike Rogers clash in final Michigan Senate debate
summary: Republican Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed clashed onstage Wednesday during the second debate in the increasingly bitter Michigan Senate race.
story: Republican Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed clashed onstage Wednesday during the second, and final, debate in the increasingly bitter Michigan Senate race. El-Sayed repeatedly argued his opponent is and would be a "sock puppet" for President Trump in the Senate, while Rogers cast his opponent as untrustworthy and trying to run from past, further-left positions.

The neck-and-neck race is one of the nation's most closely watched contests in the November midterms and could help determine which party wins control of the Senate. Democrats hope to take advantage of Mr. Trump's unpopularity and voters' frustration with inflation and the Iran War. Republicans have sought to capitalize on divisions between progressives like El-Sayed and more moderate Democrats on Middle East policy and Medicare for All.

El-Sayed called Rogers' platform a "MAGA vision" and argued the former congressman "stand[s] hip-to-hip with Donald Trump on all of his worst policies, the policies that are raising the price of your gas, making it impossible to afford your groceries." The Democratic former health official responded to attack lines by inviting the audience to play "MAGA bingo."
"He's going to bend to Donald Trump because he is a sock puppet for the man," said El-Sayed.
Rogers pushed back at one point, saying: "He wants to make this about Donald Trump. The bingo game ought to be: 'How many times can he put Trump in any answer?'"
Asked by reporters after the debate if he's planning to attend Mr. Trump's Michigan rally on Sunday, which El-Sayed brought up, Rogers said he'd go but didn't know all the final details yet.
During the debate, Rogers argued El-Sayed has not been honest about his platform, accusing him of engaging in a "pattern of deception."

"Think about this: there are so many Democrats who are coming out today and saying they can't vote for Abdul El-Sayed because he's too extreme," Rogers said. He also claimed he's "doing exceptionally well with Jewish Democrats who are literally afraid," alluding to some community members' reluctance to support El-Sayed, a frequent critic of the Israeli government.
The debate was somewhat tamer than the two candidates' first faceoff earlier this month, which featured insults and interruptions in virtually every answer. But it was still testy.

One of the more contentious moments came after Rogers tried to link El-Sayed to the Muslim Brotherhood and suggested he had the same supporters as terror groups like Hamas — allegations El-Sayed has vehemently pushed back against.

Earlier this month, several news outlets reported on social media posts by El-Sayed's half sister suggesting the Democratic candidate's mother had supported the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamist group and political movement founded in her home country of Egypt.

El-Sayed has disavowed any connection to the organization, and has noted that he wasn't raised by his birthmother since his parents divorced when he was young. Rogers said El-Sayed was trying to make himself look like "a victim."

"You can grin and you can smile and you can talk real pretty, but I'm going to tell you what, that is a risk to our national security," Rogers said. He told reporters after the debate that he questions whether El-Sayed can get a security clearance if elected.
El-Sayed called the allegations "shameful."

"He keeps raising this question about this association with an organization I've never been a part of, because [of] my mom, who's a nurse in Missouri?" the Democrat said. "It doesn't make any sense, and it's actually really quite beneath you, Mike."
El-Sayed pressed Rogers on the Iran war, pointing to the conflict as the cause of high consumer prices and casting the Republican as a hawk who has "a war for everything."

"We need a War Powers Resolution, rather than a senator who is going to stand hip-to-hip with Donald Trump on this war that made no sense when it started and certainly makes no sense now," El-Sayed said when asked how he would bring costs down.
Rogers has called on the war to end, but also said on the debate stage that if Iran is allowed to control the Strait of Hormuz or build a nuclear weapon that gas could rise even higher.

The moderators asked El-Sayed whether he views Iran as a significant threat to U.S. national security. It was a variation on a question during the first debate, when El-Sayed was asked whether Iran or Israel is a bigger threat, which he called a "ridiculous hypothetical."

El-Sayed said Wednesday that "there's no doubt that Iran has posed a threat," but he argued "that threat had been contained" by the Obama-era deal that limited Iran's nuclear program. Mr. Trump ended that deal during his first term in office.
Rogers said Iran is "absolutely" a threat and argued El-Sayed's previous answers on Iran were "an absolute nonstarter if you're going to send somebody … to the United States Senate."
Meanwhile, Rogers pushed El-Sayed on some of his progressive policy views, including his support for Medicare for All, a single-payer healthcare plan.
"Money in your pocket? You'll be lucky to have a damn pair of pants when you're done," said Rogers, arguing El-Sayed's policies would require significant tax hikes.

El-Sayed responded by saying: "Right now, the folks pulling the money out of your pocket are the big corporations who are buying his campaign." Asked by CBS News after the debate about how much the plan would cost, El-Sayed argued if implemented it'd be less expensive than the costs of healthcare currently, and said the platform has bipartisan support.
On tariffs, El-Sayed criticized Mr. Trump's tariffs but said he is open to some import duties. He said, "You don't give all the chemo all at once, all at the same time."
Rogers called the president's tariffs a "mixed bag," questioning the trade war with Canada but saying the "reshoring of manufacturing is underway."

title: U.S. ordering some government staff to depart Saudi Arabia
summary: The U.S. military has also been quietly reducing its footprint at posts in the Middle East due to regional threats from the Houthis and direct threats from Iran, CBS News has learned.
story: The U.S. State Department has ordered non-essential U.S. embassy personnel to depart Saudi Arabia, following an uptick in attacks on the kingdom by Iran-backed Houthi militants.

The U.S. military has also been quietly reducing its footprint at posts in the Middle East due to ongoing regional threats from the Houthis and direct threats from Iran, a U.S. official and a senior U.S. military official told CBS News on Wednesday.

The State Department "issued an ordered departure for non-emergency U.S. government employees and their family members in Saudi Arabia only," spokesperson Tommy Pigott wrote in a Wednesday X post, pushing back on a report that orders could apply to other Gulf states.

CBS News has learned several other embassies adjusted their staffing under "restricted operations" status, but have not gone on ordered departure, which involves the mandatory evacuation of designated diplomatic staff and accompanying family due to security risks.
The restricted operations status, which the department introduced in August amid flare-ups in the war with Iran, allows embassies to reduce staffing and services without fully suspending operations.

The decision to draw down personnel in Saudi Arabia comes after U.S. embassies in the kingdom, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and other countries issued warnings over the weekend, urging Americans in the region to exercise caution and prepare for travel disruptions due to Houthi attacks.
Why can't Saudi Arabia stop the Houthis' deadly attacks?
Why can't Saudi Arabia stop the Houthis' deadly attacks?

"Iranian-supported Houthis have increasingly engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions," Pigott said Wednesday.

The Houthis have launched drones and missiles at airports and oil facilities in Saudi Arabia in recent weeks, including a strike on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport earlier this month that killed 12 people and injured more than 300 others. One American was among those killed.
The attacks have continued, with a Saudi-led military coalition reporting that it intercepted multiple Houthi drones on Monday and Tuesday.

Saudi Arabia's energy ministry said Tuesday that air defenses blocked a drone attack on the country's Shaybah oil field. Two people were killed and two were injured by falling debris, according to the agency, which did not specify who launched the drone.
Meanwhile, the Houthis have sought to expand their territorial control in Yemen. The group has controlled a large swath of the country for more than a decade, including the capital of Sanaa.
Some Saudi officials have blamed Iran for the conduct of the Houthis, which are aligned with the Islamic Republic. Iran has denied any role in the escalation.

The conflict could cause problems beyond Saudi Arabia due to the Houthis' proximity to the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a key maritime chokepoint that a large share of the world's oil flows through. The strait has become more important in recent months due to disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz wrought by the U.S.-Iran war.
Ambassador Marwan Ali Noman, political adviser to the Foreign Minister of Yemen, warned in an interview with CBS News on Tuesday that the Houthis could continue their attacks unless confronted.
"We are fighting on behalf of everyone, because the threat and risk of the Houthis will expand," Noman said, adding that the Yemeni government is seeking international assistance.
The United Kingdom has offered support to Saudi Arabia, including defensive air operations.

It's not clear whether the Trump administration is also planning to assist Saudi Arabia. President Trump did not rule out strikes on the Houthis after the group's deadly Oct. 10 attack on the Riyadh airport, telling reporters: "We may."
Mr. Trump said earlier this month: "We have communication with the Houthis, and we'll see what happens. But what they did was very bad."

title: Collins enlists Manchin to woo moderates as she distances herself from Trump
summary: Republican Sen. Susan Collins campaigned Wednesday with an unusual ally: Democrat-turned-independent Joe Manchin.
story: Lewiston, Maine — Republican Sen. Susan Collins is campaigning on a simple idea: She can sit across the table from anyone. On Wednesday, she did it literally, sharing breakfast sandwiches with Democrat-turned-independent Joe Manchin and a roomful of Maine voters as she makes her case to people of every political stripe.

"She's not a Trump senator. She's not a Republican senator or a Democrat senator," Manchin told reporters after dining with Collins in the morning. "She's an American senator that represents her state of Maine."

Collins is the only Republican senator up for reelection in a state that President Trump lost. CBS News rates the race a toss-up. But Collins, who is running for a sixth term, has a history of surviving tough reelection battles and outrunning other Republicans. In 2020, she won by more than 8 points, even as Mr. Trump lost Maine by 9 points.
Both Collins and Manchin — who represented deep-red West Virginia in the Senate before leaving the Democratic Party and retiring in 2024 — have a history of clashing with their respective parties.

Collins worked to distance herself when pressed on Mr. Trump on Wednesday. While touring a local New Balance factory, she was asked about Trump envoy Steve Witkoff calling Russian President Vladimir Putin a "humanitarian" for releasing a jailed U.S. citizen. The question drew a visible reaction from Manchin, who shook his head. Collins responded with a flat "no."

"I would describe Putin as a warmonger, a thug. He's certainly not a humanitarian. He is the aggressor in the war against Ukraine," she said. She also said she does not support Mr. Trump's decision to waive new sanctions on Russia and strike a diesel deal with Moscow to import Russian diesel, arguing it will give Russia more funding to attack Ukraine.

Collins, who has long defected from parts of Mr. Trump's agenda, has also criticized the president's handling of the Iran war. In debates, she has said the president did not have a good plan and that the conflict should end. Her Democratic opponent, Troy Jackson, doesn't believe she's sincere in her rebukes.

"She's the chair of appropriations. If she wants to stop the war, she can cut the funding off for the war," Jackson said at a debate last week. "But she's not willing to do that because Donald Trump wants this and that's what is going to happen."

Similar skepticism popped up outside of Collins' breakfast stop. A group of protesters shouted for the incumbent to retire and held signs and cutouts of Brett Kavanaugh's face, a reference to her vote to confirm the Supreme Court justice. Collins' supporters, dressed in bright red, drowned them out with chants of "six more years," when she stepped outside to talk to the press and her tour bus blocked the demonstrators from view.

Elaine Makas, a Lewiston Democrat who served in the state legislature from 2002 to 2008, joined the protest. She said she's grateful for Collins' service and calls her "genuinely a nice person," but argued that is not enough.
"She's just voting wrong," Makas told CBS News. "She's fallen completely in line with the president."
Collins has argued that she frequently votes against Mr. Trump's wishes.

Makas echoed Jackson's line of attack. "She only disagrees with him when her vote doesn't matter," she said. She said she personally knows Jackson, a former state Senate president,  from their time in the legislature and believes he'll "listen" to Mainers.

title: Witkoff blasted for calling Putin a "humanitarian"
summary: After special envoy Steve Witkoff told Putin he was a "humanitarian" for releasing a U.S. citizen deemed to have been wrongfully detained, GOP Sen. John Cornyn responded, "No. Putin is a stone cold killer."
story: Washington — U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff faced immediate backlash Wednesday for praising Russian President Vladimir Putin as a "humanitarian" after he released 74-year-old Stephen Hubbard, an American who had been imprisoned in Russia for four years and who had been determined to be wrongfully detained.

"You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian," Witkoff told Putin Wednesday in response to Hubbard's release. "You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that, I commend you, and I thank you again."

Witkoff made the comment in St. Petersburg during a visit with the Russian president that was aimed at moving toward a resolution of the Ukraine war that Putin started four and a half years ago. Over the past month, Russia has been intensifying its strikes against civilian and energy infrastructure to try to cripple the power grid before the brutal Ukrainian winter.

Mr. Trump was asked later in the day if he would describe Putin the same way Witkoff did. "Well, I guess you have to say for that particular purpose, for the purpose of allowing a man who was thinking he was going to be in prison for life out," Mr. Trump said during a White House roundtable on cyber crime. "But I wouldn't say anything one way or the other."
Witkoff's "humanitarian" comment sparked pushback from Republicans, some of whom have openly criticized the president and his administration in recent months.

"WTF, Steve?" wrote North Carolina Republican Sen. Thom Tillis. "Look up the definition of 'humanitarian.' What an embarrassing and outrageous thing to say. You should go back to Ukraine and ask the families of the children Putin has kidnapped and murdered whether they agree your friend Putin is a 'humanitarian.'"
Republican Sen. John Cornyn of Texas responded to a video of Witkoff's comments: "No. Putin is a stone cold killer," he wrote on X.
"Another embarrassment," said Republican Rep. Don Bacon of Nebraska, who has been critical of the Trump administration's handling of Russia and Ukraine.

Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine, who has also been critical of the administration, was asked about the comment on the campaign trail and replied, "I would describe Putin as a warmonger, a thug. He's certainly not a humanitarian. He is the aggressor in the war against Ukraine."

Former U.S. Ambassador to Ukraine William Taylor, who served during the Bush and Obama administrations, said in an interview with CBS News that it's "absolutely a good thing" Hubbard is coming home, "but he should never have been there in the first place."
"We should not give the Russians any credit for releasing someone who should not have been in jail," Taylor said. "And to call Putin a humanitarian, that's cringeworthy."
Republican Sen. Joni Ernst of Iowa said Putin is "not our friend."

"Vladimir Putin is not our friend, and he is certainly no humanitarian," she posted on X. "His relentless attacks on innocent civilians in Ukraine show his total disregard for human life.   Appeasement won't end this war. Pressure will."

Witkoff's praise of Putin also comes as Mr. Trump made the surprise move last week to waive new U.S. sanctions on Russia two days before they were supposed to go into effect, defying Congress and his late friend, Sen. Lindsey Graham. The waivers came one week after Mr. Trump had eased sanctions on Russian diesel and announced a deal with Putin to import diesel to the U.S. market.
Mr. Trump has expressed increasing frustration with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and on Tuesday, said "Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine. They haven't been doing much."
Before heading to Russia, Witkoff was in Oslo, Norway, where he met with and embraced Zelenskyy. Secretary of State Marco Rubio described that meeting as "positive."

title: Musk chose to restrict Ukraine's access to SpaceX network, sources say
summary: A decision by Elon Musk led to restrictions on Ukraine's use of SpaceX's satellite communications network, people familiar with the matter told CBS News.
story: A decision by Elon Musk led to restrictions on Ukraine's use of SpaceX's satellite communications network, people familiar with the matter told CBS News.
The satellite service, which is used for drone operations, hitting certain targets and protecting sites in Ukraine, was slowed significantly last week.

Musk held multiple conversations with administration officials leading up to the order, the sources said. He wanted clarity on the president's thinking on the matter. Musk has expressed distaste with his company being seen as profiting from the continued war between Russia and Ukraine.
It's not clear how Musk's order to curtail service was executed.
Musk licenses SpaceX's Starshield technology to the U.S. government. He said last week the U.S. controls who can access the technology and what level of service those users receive.
"Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," Musk, the world's richest person, wrote on X.
Musk did not reply to a request for comment. CBS News has reached out to the White House and the Pentagon for comment.
The Wall Street Journal was first to report on Musk's order.

The temporary restrictions came as a surprise to some officials inside the administration, who said neither Mr. Trump nor the Pentagon specifically ordered any limits meant to deliberately disrupt drone operations and battlefield communications.
Mr. Trump said Monday he was seeking details on who ordered the slowdown.
"I don't know who it was, but I'd like to find out," he said.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Tuesday the Pentagon has not manipulated the service.

"We haven't pulled anything back. There are terms of service that ultimately need to be complied to. And that's where Starlink has the option to make those decisions, but nothing's changed from our view. We haven't made any directives or anything like that," Hegseth told reporters, adding that "we wish the Ukrainians, obviously, success."
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's office told CBS News on Wednesday that Ukraine's use of the system was still throttled.
What is Starshield?
Starshield is a military-grade satellite network made by SpaceX for the U.S. government and its partners. It runs on similar technology to its civilian sister, Starlink.
The U.S. government pays to use Starshield and controls who can access the technology. Its use has been limited to Ukraine and occupied territories. It is not available in Russia.
Starshield is essential to Ukraine's armed forces as it allows personnel to communicate and carry out strikes, including by maintaining contact with drones across long distances.
There is no working alternative to Starlink, which has put a massive constellation of low-earth satellites into orbit, and no direct competitor comes close.
What happened in Ukraine?

Ukrainian officials and soldiers told CBS News the country's military began experiencing sudden difficulties with Starshield equipment late Tuesday, including a throttling effect that made it more difficult to carry out missions with fast-moving drones. Sources in Ukraine's Ministry of Defense said SpaceX had unilaterally imposed the Starshield restrictions.

Regular Starlink terminals have a 70 km/hr speed cap, that is, the speed at which internet can be used in a vehicle in motion. At rates faster than the cap, the internet degrades and is no longer usable.

Starshield has no artificial speed cap and is known to work at speeds of at least 160 km/hr. Strike drones equipped with Starshield cruise at 160 km/h or higher, and they're the backbone of Ukrainian mid-range strikes.

Ukrainian units reported link drops at speeds as low as 90 km/hr, making those drones inoperable. The degradation of Starshield is estimated to have cost Ukraine tens of millions of dollars in losses, according to an analysis by Dimko Zhluktenko, a drone pilot and analyst in the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
Zelensky said Saturday the speed limits had prevented Ukraine from using Starshield to shoot down Shahed attack drones.

The Ukrainian leader wrote on X last week that "the Russians are trying to take advantage of the problems with Starlink in Ukraine, as our interceptor drones depend on this connection among other things."

Zelenskyy has suggested there are still some restrictions. He told NBC News over the weekend the maximum speed was 161 km/hr, and he said Tuesday that he'd spoken with Secretary of State Marco Rubio about "the situation with Starlink/Starshield, which needs to be restored."
The apparent restrictions drew swift pushback from U.S. lawmakers, with a bipartisan group of senators asking the Defense Department's internal watchdog to investigate last week.

"There needs to be an investigation, we need to find out who these people are because lives are at risk and lives are lost over these things," Republican Rep. Mike Turner of Ohio said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" over the weekend.
Why have Trump and Zelenskyy clashed?
Beyond the Starshield disruptions, Zelenskyy has said in recent days that Russia struck Ukraine without warning from the U.S., and deliveries of key interceptor missiles to Ukraine have slowed down.

A senior Pentagon official told CBS News on Monday there had been "no change to Department of War policy regarding intelligence sharing or any capabilities we are enabling Europeans to provide to Ukraine."
Mr. Trump has grown increasingly frustrated with Zelenskyy in recent weeks, accusing him of not doing enough to seek an end to the Russia-Ukraine war.

The U.S. president argues the war is responsible for high energy prices. His administration waived restrictions on buying Russian diesel earlier this month in an effort to ease pressure on the price of the commodity, a move Zelenskyy argued could embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin. Mr. Trump also waived sanctions on Russia last week.

Mr. Trump said earlier this month that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to stop striking each other's energy infrastructure — announcing an "energy ceasefire." Zelenskyy initially said Ukraine was willing to abide by such an agreement, but that Russia's strikes never ceased, and several days later he told the Financial Times his country would no longer hold off on striking Russian refineries because Russia was still attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
The Russian government never confirmed that it had agreed to a ceasefire.

In a Newsmax interview late Thursday, Mr. Trump called Zelenskyy "not a good guy for us to deal with," and argued Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries would be a "disgrace," as he urged both sides to make a deal while adding that the Ukrainian leader is harder to deal with than Putin.
"I'm not a big fan of Zelenskyy," Mr. Trump said.

title: Trump spurs states to dump laws regulating new hospitals
summary: The Trump administration has tied billions in rural health funding for states partly to the policy commitments they make, including ending their certificate of need, or CON, laws governing the construction of new hospitals.
story: The Trump administration has hinged federal funding for states on whether they end or loosen powerful but controversial laws that regulate the construction of new hospitals — with a handful of states poised to comply.

A chunk of the $50 billion available to states through the five-year Rural Health Transformation Program is partly contingent on policy commitments. The administration told states it would score their applications higher if they walked back their certificate of need, or CON, laws, which give a state approval authority over the expansion or construction of any healthcare facility. Six states indicated plans to revisit their laws in their applications.

Certificate of need laws, which require that a healthcare provider prove a community need for a new service, were intended to curb monopolies and rising costs. But critics of the laws say they've instead raised healthcare prices, stalled needed facilities, and barred rural patients from new technology. More than 30 states, plus Washington, D.C., enforce some sort of certificate of need law, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures.

Legislators in several states have been pushing to end the laws, which have faced scrutiny for decades — under Republican and Democratic administrations. But the Trump administration's aggressive approach to tie the policies to funding has forced states to reckon with their laws quickly.

The Rural Health Transformation Program was added to President Trump's signature One Big Beautiful Bill Act as an initiative to modernize healthcare in remote areas. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, in its notice to states applying to the program, called certificate of need laws "an additional expense and burden on rural facilities" and explained how states with fewer certificate of need rules would get higher scores.

"It's not the first time the federal government used funding as a state carrot (versus using a stick) to encourage alignment on an administration's policy goal," Maureen Hensley-Quinn, a researcher at the National Academy for State Health Policy, said in an email. She noted that President Barack Obama's administration included millions of dollars in performance bonuses for states that made it easier for children to enroll in federally funded health insurance.
Hensley-Quinn said the funding "carrot" was an opportunity to take a hard look at whether policies like certificates of need were truly worth it.

"States need to carefully weigh the trade-offs of supporting a 'voluntary' federal policy no matter what," she said, "and additional federal financing, especially in tight state budget years, can tip the scale."
Obama, Trump on same page

Since the Rural Health Transformation Program became law last year, Tennessee has taken the most concrete action. In a bipartisan vote in April, state lawmakers passed a bill that will unravel most of its remaining certificate of need rules over the next four years. Alaska, Connecticut, Delaware, Iowa, and Mississippi have also said they would consider ending or loosening their laws.

"If there's an issue where you can have President Obama and President Trump in agreement on something, that tells you the idea probably has some merit," Wes Climer, a Republican state senator in South Carolina, said in 2021, supporting the repeal of that state's certificate of need law. The legislature voted in 2023 to end most rules in the law, and in January it will stop requiring certificate of need applications for new hospital construction or expansion, leaving them only for nursing homes.

Some certificate of need laws require approval for changes as minor as a new piece of expensive equipment. In North Carolina, a hospital that won a certificate of need to build a much-needed facility was mired in a court battle for three years before breaking ground in 2026.
As more states consider removing their certificate of need laws, Hensley-Quinn warns of unintended consequences: Fewer records will exist that help states track hospital ownership.

Hensley-Quinn said frustrated state officials have come to her years after their states repealed certificate of need laws, saying that even with a licensure process, they don't have insight into the financial state of their health systems or facilities, or how they're managed. Certificate of need laws force companies seeking a new foothold in the state to submit voluminous applications. Once the laws are gone, few regulations force transparency. That leaves states unaware when a health system contracts with private equity to provide hospital services, for example.
"Without CON, without ownership reporting, and without an entity that monitors transactions or providers in that way, there's no way for you to know," Hensley-Quinn said.
Tennessee's certificate of need law

Tennessee lawmakers had pushed to change the state's certificate of need law for years but didn't pass sweeping legislation until it faced losing out on federal funding. Like all states, Tennessee is set to receive an equal share of half of the Rural Health Transformation Program's grants, while the other $25 billion in funding is contingent on other factors, including states' policy commitments.

In 2024, the state's hospital association opposed a repeal effort in a letter penned by 12 hospital and health system leaders, many serving rural areas, though that more limited legislation passed anyway.

A repeal would harm vulnerable patients by driving up costs and thinning existing hospital staff, said Martin Chaney, CEO of Maury Regional Health, a system in rural Middle Tennessee south of Nashville. Ending the law would create rural healthcare deserts, Chaney wrote in the letter, because hospitals would choose to expand in areas that were already the most profitable, where residents had a range of health insurance providers.

"The premise that eliminating CON regulations will expand health care opportunities by increasing competition is not true for ALL Tennesseans," Chaney wrote. "Instead, it would result in cherry-picking and increasing the gap in access to medical care in rural areas."

A month later, TriStar Health — owned by the largest hospital company in the U.S., for-profit HCA Healthcare — applied for a certificate of need to build a hospital just 20 minutes north of Maury Regional Medical Center. Nashville-based HCA received approval despite brief opposition from Maury Regional Health, the system led by Chaney.
HCA did not respond to requests for comment.

Local leaders are divided on what the new hospital would do to healthcare in the region. "Competition is good," Maury County Commissioner Kevin Markham told KFF Health News. Markham, like many in favor of the new hospital, said that patients should have options when it comes to choosing where they get hospital care.

But leaders of smaller hospital systems in Tennessee are worried. Judy Herbert, a Williamson County commissioner and board member at Williamson Health, another health system in the area, said ending certificate of need laws will prompt hospital closures. Big hospital systems will become the default for expensive procedures and dominate rural markets, while smaller hospitals that provided those procedures before will lose so much money, they'll be forced to shutter or sell, Herbert reasoned, echoing the concerns of other advocates of the laws.

"Many challenges have emerged that place increasing pressure on healthcare organizations, especially independent nonprofits like Williamson Health," that health system's leadership said in an open letter in July 2025, citing Tennessee's intentions around certificates of need.

In July of this year, Williamson Health's board voted to sell its network of clinics, diagnostic centers, and a more than 330-bed hospital in a $900 million deal with Ascension St. Thomas, part of one of the largest healthcare systems in the nation.

KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

title: Japan launches ambitious robotic mission to Martian moon Phobos
summary: Soil samples collected by the MMX probe will shed light on the mysterious origin of the red planet's two moons, Phobos and Deimos.
story: Japan launched an ambitious $350 million mission to Mars on Monday to study the red planet's two moons in unprecedented detail, dropping a small rover on the largest — Phobos — before the mothership touches down to robotically collect soil samples for return to Earth.

The primary goal of the Martian Moons Exploration mission, or MMX, is to determine whether Phobos and the smaller moon Deimos were created by the impact of a large body early in the solar system's history or whether the two are asteroids that once passed close enough to Mars to be captured by the red planet's gravity.

The Martian moons are much smaller than Earth's, with Phobos measuring just 17 miles across at its widest while Deimos is less than half that size. Both are irregularly shaped and similar in appearance to asteroids. But size and shape alone are not enough to answer the question of their origin.

"One of the most intriguing questions about Phobos and Deimos is simply why these two little moons are there in the first place," said Thomas Statler, who helped oversee development of two NASA instruments aboard the MMX spacecraft.

"In some ways, they resemble asteroids from the outer part of the asteroid belt ... but there (are) other lines of evidence pointing to these moons being remnants of a giant impact early in Mars' history."
The collected samples, expected to be returned to Earth in 2031, should answer that question one way or the other.

"By going to the Martian moons, studying them up close and bringing samples back to Earth, we'll be able to determine whether Phobos material is more consistent with an asteroid composition or with debris created by a collision involving Mars," Statler said.

The mission got underway at 3:41 p.m. EDT (4:41 a.m. Japan time) with the sky-lighting launch of a Japanese H3 rocket from the picturesque Tanegashima Space Center operated by the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency, or JAXA.

Four solid-propellant strap-on boosters and two hydrogen-fueled first stage engines powered the rocket out of the dense lower atmosphere before the H3's second stage took over to continue the climb to space.
One hour and 11 minutes after liftoff, following two firings of the upper stage engine, the 9,900-pound MMX probe was released to fly on its own.
If all goes well, the spacecraft will brake into orbit around the red planet in September 2027 on a trajectory that will allow it to circle the planet in lockstep with Phobos.

MMX will spend three years in that orbit, training a battery of instruments on Phobos and its surrounding environment, studying its chemical and mineral composition, assessing its possible use as a staging base for future astronauts and dropping a small rover, supplied by the German and French space agencies, onto the moon's surface in early 2029.

The 55-pound rover is not equipped with braking rockets or anything else to slow its descent. Given the gravity of Phobos is just 1/1,000th as strong as Earth's, the rover is expected to bounce down on the surface, tumbling gently to a stop.

It is designed to right itself regardless of how it ends up after coming to rest and then to begin its surface exploration. It is equipped with cameras for navigation and to study the soil as it rolls about, an instrument to fire laser beams into the ground to determine what minerals might be present and another that will monitor soil temperatures.

About a year after the rover's landing, in the 2030 timeframe, the MMX spacecraft itself will touch down on Phobos once and possibly twice to collect a tiny amount of soil using two devices, one built by JAXA and the other supplied by NASA.
The official mission requirement is to capture at least 10 grams, or less than half an ounce, of material. Depending on the nature of the soil, however, the sample size could be larger.

The MMX then will lift off and, after wrapping up remote observations of Deimos, head back to Earth, putting the Phobos samples into an aerodynamic, heat-resistant capsule that will re-enter the atmosphere over Australia, where a recovery team will be standing by.
The samples will be studied by an international team of researchers.
"There's a lot of adrenaline, a lot of excitement, and a lot of wow," said Statler. "MMX will be the first spacecraft ever to return to Earth from the Mars system. That says a lot."

But "the most exciting thing of all," he said, "will be watching the sample return capsule re-enter Earth's atmosphere and opening that capsule and seeing those materials for the first time. There is absolutely no lack of excitement and adrenaline on this mission."

title: What to know about the PHP bug affecting 70% of world's websites
summary: AI was used to uncover a security weakness that affects most of the world's websites, researchers said. Here's what internet users should know.
story: Hackers could exploit weaknesses in a widely used programming language for websites, online platforms and other technology services to steal users' information and cause other problems, cybersecurity researchers warn.

The programming language PHP, short for "Personal Home Page," powers up to 70% of the world's websites and web applications, including those used by government agencies, social media platforms such as Facebook and sites including Wikipedia.

The bug, dubbed PHP2Shell, can target two security flaws in PHP,  according to Voldemaras Kadys, head of security at Mediatech. Those weaknesses could enable cybercriminals to seize control of unprotected website servers, install malware, pilfer customer data and even take sites down completely.
"The potential impact of these vulnerabilities may be huge, as most websites run on PHP," he said in an email.

The flaws in PHP were discovered when security researchers used an OpenAI artificial intelligence model to identify the problem, Wall Street Journal reporter Robert McMillan, who first reported on the PHP security issue, told CBS News.
"There are a lot of sites that I don't think even know that they have a problem, and they may find out the hard way."
What should consumers know?
Consumers' personal information could be vulnerable if they have an account with an online store or booking platform whose site uses PHP and is exposed to the bug.

"For regular internet users, simply visiting a PHP website doesn't necessarily mean their device will be compromised," Kadys explained. "The risk is that attackers may exploit a website that holds their personal information. For example, if a user has an account with an online shop, attackers may be able to hack that website through this PHP vulnerability and extract the information the user has stored there, such as their email address, physical address, name and date of birth."
But just because a site is vulnerable doesn't guarantee that a breach has occurred or will occur.

"There's no reason to stop browsing or shopping online, but users should still be extra cautious about suspicious messages because we don't know what kind of data hackers may have stolen through this vulnerability, and from which websites," he added.
Racing hackers

Andrés Guerrero-Saade, vice president of intelligence and security research at SentinelOne, told CBS News that the incident illustrates "how AI is accelerating the ability of vulnerability researchers" while also boosting bad actors' capacity to exploit security flaws.

The time between a vulnerability being detected and a fix being released is crucial for cybersecurity experts, he added. Yet that vital window of time has been shortened by AI, allowing cybercriminals to move much faster today than in the past.
"That whole gap between the patch being available and attackers getting to exploit that before anybody patches, that's the whole game essentially," Guerrero-Saade said.
In a post on X, the FBI's cyber threat division encouraged any organization that can't immediately patch its sites to temporarily take them offline.

The PHP Foundation, which includes tech developers who work on securing the programming language, said on Wednesday that it had released fixes for the vulnerabilities, along with instructions on how to update systems.

"If you run PHP, it is imperative that you update now. The announcement on php.net contains and references technical details on the vulnerabilities, attack vectors, and instructions on how to update on which systems," the group said.

The discovery of the flaws highlights the battle between security professionals and hackers in using AI to spot potential holes in organizations' technology systems. In this case, security researchers were the first to uncover the bug, which had existed for at least a decade, McMillan noted.

"People knew something weird was going on. But no one could really find a way to write an exploit — of turning a bug that might cause a computer to crash into something really bad that would allow somebody to run software that they weren't supposed to be able to run on a computer," he said.

title: Memphis fails to pass 1-year data center moratorium, opts for shorter-term ban
summary: Memphis has become a hotspot for data centers driven by Elon Musk's SpaceXAI.
story: In a heated city council meeting on Tuesday, leaders in Memphis, Tennessee, failed to pass a moratorium that would have paused data center development for a year in the city,  which has become a hotspot for the facilities driven by Elon Musk's SpaceXAI.

Instead, city council members passed a substitute ordinance — which some said they received on short notice and did not have time to review — that would halt construction of data centers for 135 days.

Residents and activists have pushed back against data center development in the region for years, starting with the construction of SpaceXAI's Colossus 1 data center in 2024. The company has also built two other data centers and has two under construction in Memphis and the surrounding region, including across the state border in Southaven, Mississippi.
Also in Southaven, a plant powering the company's data centers is using methane gas turbines, which prompted a lawsuit from the NAACP and other organizations over alleged pollution.
SpaceXAI did not reply to a request for comment. The Trump administration moved to dismiss the case, but on Monday, a Mississippi federal judge rejected that bid.

Supporters of data centers argue they are needed to support the growth of artificial intelligence technology. Advocates also say they will create much-needed jobs, although experts counter many of those jobs are in the construction industry and therefore temporary.

The moratorium would have paused the construction of new data centers for a year, allowing the city to adopt permanent zoning and development regulations as well as establish disclosure requirements for data center applicants. It also would have provided the opportunity to study impacts on air quality, electrical infrastructure, water protection and noise. The moratorium would not have halted existing data center operations.

The language of the ordinance that was passed Tuesday states that it is intended to complement Memphis Mayor Paul Young's executive order to establish a 90-day period to study the impacts of data center development.

Many attendees in the chambers appeared shocked and confused at the proposal for the new ordinance. A few members of the crowd remained in the chambers following the vote where they sang, chanted and vocalized their frustrations.
The city council's move comes after a postponement of the vote earlier this month spurred protests in the chambers and resulted in an early end to an Oct. 6 meeting.

Community members' opposition to data center development in Memphis is reflective of the broader attitude across America in recent months. According to a recent Pew Research Center survey, over half of Americans say they're not comfortable with a new data center operating in their area — a sentiment that's spilling over into city council meetings and town halls across the country.

Ahead of the vote, KeShaun Pearson, the executive director of the Memphis Community Against Pollution, said that community members were concerned about what they feel has been a lack of transparency from local government officials and data centers' environmental impact.

"It's as if the people who have been elected to protect us and to stand up to corporations and be that representative have just completely abdicated that responsibility, and left us to fend for ourselves," he said.
Pearson and his brother, Tennessee Rep. Justin Pearson, were among a handful of people barred from city council meetings following the protests at city hall earlier this month.
A federal judge lifted the ban and the two were present during the vote. Pearson and the group have sued the city council over the ban.

title: iPhone Duo already backordered until 2027 as pre-order sales soar
summary: Consumer demand for Apple's first foldable phone is strong despite the device's hefty $1,999 price tag.
story: Apple is seeing strong demand for its new foldable iPhone, with supplies quickly selling out after pre-order sales opened on Friday.

"Apple opened iPhone Duo pre-orders this morning, and the early read looks robust in our view, with demand for Cupertino's first foldable running well ahead of supply out of the gates," Wall Street analyst Dan Ives, a partner at Yorkville Ives, said in a research note.

The pre-order window for the Duo opened on Friday at 8 a.m. ET on apple.com and in the Apple Store app. Within minutes, the estimated delivery of the phone was pushed back past Oct. 23, the device's official launch date, and into next year. As of Friday afternoon, the Apple phone was backordered until late January.
"It's been 3 minutes, and it's sold out at every store around the NYC/CT area," Max Weinbach, an analyst for the market research firm Creativestrat, said on X.
Apple did not immediately respond to a request for comment on how many pre-order requests it received.
When the Duo officially launches on Oct. 23, Apple said it will have some inventory at its stores, but noted that supply could sell out quickly.

"On Friday morning, our teams look forward to welcoming customers at Apple Stores to experience iPhone Duo and the incredible iPhone line-up for themselves," an Apple spokesperson said in an email. "Apple Stores will have limited iPhone Duo available for walk-in customers, and we're working hard to get this revolutionary new product into customers' hands as quickly as possible."

Apple's new CEO, John Ternus, announced the iPhone Duo last month. The Duo lets users split the screen to use two different apps on the device, or two windows of the same website for uses such as comparison shopping.

Prices start at $1,999 for a device with 256 GB of storage. When folded, it's about the size of a passport. The full display is the largest of any Apple phone, resembling more of an iPad than an iPhone.
Ternus also announced the iPhone 18 at Apple's annual fall showcase, which went on sale last month.

Ives thinks demand for the Duo will remain strong into 2027, with many iPhone users planning to upgrade. He projects Apple will sell around 10 million Duos in the next few quarters and up to 25 million in 2027.

title: On dating apps, men use AI to put their best face forward
summary: How much AI is too much when it comes to finding love on the apps? "It's very subtle," one dating app user said of his AI-enhanced photos.
story: Marissa, a 31-year-old Boston resident, downloaded dating apps because she is looking for love. But more and more, she finds herself looking for something else: AI-free photos.

The marketing professional said she routinely comes across dating app profiles that appear to be digitally altered. Usually, the changes are minor and can be easily made using tools like Photoshop, such as editing someone out of a photo. Sometimes, however, the photo appears to be completely AI-generated, she told CBS News, citing a photo she came across on Bumble of a man dressed in a suit tiling a bathroom wall.
"AI aside, I'm not sure what the appeal is there," she said (Marissa asked to withhold her surname for privacy reasons).

Numerous women on TikTok also report spotting photos of men on dating apps that appear to be AI-generated. Their accounts demonstrate how AI is blurring the line between what's real and what's fake in the already fraught arena of online dating. They also raise ethical questions about how far is too far when it comes to manipulating your online persona.

"People want authentic connections and conversations," Kathryn Coduto, an assistant professor at Boston University who studies dating apps, told CBS News in an email. "I think AI has made people more wary and skeptical of others, especially people they don't know."

Of course, dating app users have long relied on filters and other editing tools to polish their photos. But AI tools are upping the ante, allowing people to create high-quality images within seconds, and in some cases, fabricate fake scenes.

"A dater has to think about how they're going to capture someone's attention in a few seconds or less," Coduto told CBS News. "This might mean making your photo look a little better than it might have before."
To be sure, this practice isn't exclusive to men. However, they appear more likely to use AI to spruce up their dating profiles than women, Coduto added.
"So far, men are more interested in AI in the dating space, which isn't surprising," Coduto said. "Women tend to receive more matches and messages, so men have a harder time standing out."
The "digital stylist" who helps men AI their photos

AI can create obvious distortions when it generates photos, such as omitting a finger from someone's hand. For Marissa, a telltale sign is the person's face, which sometimes looks "waxy" in AI-generated photos, she said.
Still, as technology improves, it's becoming harder to distinguish a real photo from one created by AI models.

Lana Li, a Brooklyn, New York, dating consultant who runs the Substack "Love Me Like a Robot," calls herself a "digital stylist." She uses AI to help men level up their dating app photos, and defends using the technology as long as the photos still genuinely represent who they are.

"I can take a picture of somebody and then put them in a different outfit or change their hairstyle a little bit, or put different shoes on them," she told CBS News. "Or if I think their body language doesn't look confident in the picture, I will have [ChatGPT] change that."
The 37-year-old also uses FaceApp to change men's facial expressions. She said the edits are subtle, such as slightly lifting the corner of someone's mouth to make them look "friendlier."

Despite her liberal approach to using AI, there are lines Li is unwilling to cross. For example, one client asked her to digitally alter a photo so that his head was on a marathon runner's body — a request she declined.
"I told him, 'I can't work with you if you want to not represent yourself accurately,'" she said.

Two men who spoke to CBS News on the condition of anonymity to maintain their privacy told CBS News they've used AI in their online dating photos, but in ways they feel stop short of being misleading and remain true to who they are.
A ban on Hinge
One man, a 30-year-old tech employee and client of Li's, said she used ChatGPT to digitally clothe him in more professional garb and to tame his frizzy hair.

"It's very subtle," the New York City resident said, saying he still looked like himself, even with the edits. He emphasized that he doesn't want to "catfish" anyone — a concern for singles even in the absence of AI.

Another man is pulling back after one of his AI photos backfired. The 50-something-year-old New York City resident said he fed photos of himself into Aragon.ai, an AI headshot generator, which produced a picture of him standing on a Manhattan roof with a sunset in the background. It immediately drew hits on his Hinge profile.

"This picture generally got the most likes," he told CBS News. "Now that could just be because it was the first thing they saw. But regardless, it was proving to be effective, and women seemed to like it."
That was, until Hinge banned him. He managed to get his account back but ultimately decided to delete the sunset photo, suspecting it was the reason for his removal from the app.
"How much AI am I OK with?"

Most popular dating apps have policies that limit the use of AI-generated images in people's profiles. Hinge emphasizes the importance of authenticity on its website, noting that people should be able to discern "fact from fiction."
"If you decide to include generative AI images, audio, or video in your profile, it should not be used to misrepresent yourself or your intentions," the company says on its AI policy page.

Hinge also uses automated tools and human reviewers to detect and remove "prohibited material," according to the company's terms of service. If users see suspicious AI material, they can confidentially report it through the app or online.

A spokesperson for Match Group, which owns Hinge, Tinder and a handful of other dating apps, told CBS that as generative AI evolves, the company is "watching closely and listening to daters, who tell us they want more transparency, more authenticity, and more confidence that a real person is on the other end."

Bumble also uses tools to detect and weed out AI-generated content, and lets users report profiles that feature such images. A spokesperson said the company prohibits inauthentic profiles, and Bumble's community guidelines bar the use of "artificially generated photos or enhanced photos to deceive others."

"We enforce this through a combination of AI-powered tools, human moderation, verification features and member reporting, and we take action based on the severity of a violation, up to and including permanently banning accounts," the spokesperson said.
Marissa, the 31-year-old who lives in Boston, said that when she sees a person's profile whose photos bear the hallmarks of AI, she chooses to move along.
"The dating pool is already challenging, and this is just another thing we have to grapple with," she said. "How much AI am I OK with?"
