title: Memphis fails to pass 1-year data center moratorium, opts for shorter-term ban
summary: Memphis has become a hotspot for data centers driven by Elon Musk's SpaceXAI.
story: In a heated city council meeting on Tuesday, leaders in Memphis, Tennessee, failed to pass a moratorium that would have paused data center development for a year in the city,  which has become a hotspot for the facilities driven by Elon Musk's SpaceXAI.

Instead, city council members passed a substitute ordinance — which some said they received on short notice and did not have time to review — that would halt construction of data centers for 135 days.

Residents and activists have pushed back against data center development in the region for years, starting with the construction of SpaceXAI's Colossus 1 data center in 2024. The company has also built two other data centers and has two under construction in Memphis and the surrounding region, including across the state border in Southaven, Mississippi.
Also in Southaven, a plant powering the company's data centers is using methane gas turbines, which prompted a lawsuit from the NAACP and other organizations over alleged pollution.
SpaceXAI did not reply to a request for comment. The Trump administration moved to dismiss the case, but on Monday, a Mississippi federal judge rejected that bid.

Supporters of data centers argue they are needed to support the growth of artificial intelligence technology. Advocates also say they will create much-needed jobs, although experts counter many of those jobs are in the construction industry and therefore temporary.

The moratorium would have paused the construction of new data centers for a year, allowing the city to adopt permanent zoning and development regulations as well as establish disclosure requirements for data center applicants. It also would have provided the opportunity to study impacts on air quality, electrical infrastructure, water protection and noise. The moratorium would not have halted existing data center operations.

The language of the ordinance that was passed Tuesday states that it is intended to complement Memphis Mayor Paul Young's executive order to establish a 90-day period to study the impacts of data center development.

Many attendees in the chambers appeared shocked and confused at the proposal for the new ordinance. A few members of the crowd remained in the chambers following the vote where they sang, chanted and vocalized their frustrations.
The city council's move comes after a postponement of the vote earlier this month spurred protests in the chambers and resulted in an early end to an Oct. 6 meeting.

Community members' opposition to data center development in Memphis is reflective of the broader attitude across America in recent months. According to a recent Pew Research Center survey, over half of Americans say they're not comfortable with a new data center operating in their area — a sentiment that's spilling over into city council meetings and town halls across the country.

Ahead of the vote, KeShaun Pearson, the executive director of the Memphis Community Against Pollution, said that community members were concerned about what they feel has been a lack of transparency from local government officials and data centers' environmental impact.

"It's as if the people who have been elected to protect us and to stand up to corporations and be that representative have just completely abdicated that responsibility, and left us to fend for ourselves," he said.
Pearson and his brother, Tennessee Rep. Justin Pearson, were among a handful of people barred from city council meetings following the protests at city hall earlier this month.
A federal judge lifted the ban and the two were present during the vote. Pearson and the group have sued the city council over the ban.

title: Feds charge powerful Virginia Democrat in alleged drug scheme
summary: L. Louise Lucas, a longtime state senator from Virginia, has been arrested in connection with an alleged bribery and racketeering scheme.
story: Norfolk, Virginia — L. Louise Lucas, a powerful Virginia state senator and vocal Trump critic who played a central role in the state's redistricting effort last year, was taken into federal custody Thursday and charged in connection with an alleged bribery and racketeering scheme, the Justice Department said.

According to a 45-page indictment filed in the Eastern District of Virginia, Lucas and six other co-defendants are charged with conspiring to distribute and possess marijuana, conspiring to launder money, laundering money and committing bribery by distributing large quantities of illegal marijuana under the auspices of her legal medical cannabis business.

A federal grand jury returned the indictment last week. Lucas, 82, surrendered to law enforcement on Thursday morning. She faces five of the eight charges included in the indictment and is set to make her initial appearance before a federal magistrate judge Thursday afternoon.
Lucas vowed to fight the charges in a statement on X.

"Today, the FBI, the Department of Justice, and the full weight of the federal government have been wielded against an 82-year-old great-grandmother," she said. "I grew up under Jim Crow. I've seen what happens when people in power try to silence those who stand up to them. I spent my life fighting back, and I'm not stopping now."

At a press conference to discuss the charges in Norfolk, Virginia, Attorney General Todd Blanche dismissed concerns about bringing the charges so close to the midterm elections, noting that Lucas is not on the ballot. He said there was "nothing improper" about the timing of the indictment.

The case comes nearly six months after federal law enforcement searched Lucas' office and a shop called The Cannabis Outlet that she co-owns in Portsmouth, Virginia. One source familiar with the investigation told CBS News at the time of the search that the investigation started during the Biden administration.
Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger criticized the timing of the indictment just before the elections and said it erodes Americans' trust in the Justice Department.

"I have read the charging document alleging a series of criminal acts by a member of the Virginia Senate. In our American system of justice, people are presumed innocent until proven guilty, and that is true for Senator L. Louise Lucas," Spanberger said on X. "She and her family deserve the opportunity to present their defense and speak to the allegations presented."
The charges

Federal prosecutors in the Eastern District of Virginia alleged that since at least 2019, Lucas has been the leader of the scheme and used her political influence in Virginia to enact legislation and regulations to financially benefit herself and co-defendants, as well as insulate the alleged criminal enterprise she was running from state law enforcement.

Lucas allegedly directed the enterprise to buy and sell over 100 kilograms of illegal marijuana. She was indicted alongside her daughters, Lisa Lucas-Burke and Theresa Lucas-Lamb, and grandson, Ryan Eichelberger, in addition to other co-defendants.
Blanche said that Lucas and her co-defendants allegedly engaged in a "large-scale RICO drug trafficking and money laundering conspiracy."
Prosecutors will prove that Lucas "violated the trust of the people of Portsmouth and Chesapeake, Virginia, and of her state Senate colleagues," Blanche said.

"Through her elected office, Sen. Lucas has been a public servant of the people of Virginia. Her first duty should have been looking out for her constituents before herself," the attorney general said. "But the charges listed in the indictment reflect the alleged behavior of a public servant who put her own financial interests before the people she was elected to serve. Whether you are a Democrat or a Republican, an elected official or an everyday citizen, nobody is above the law."
Blanche said the investigation that led to the charges began "many years ago" and was not started by the Trump administration.
FBI Director Kash Patel also spoke at the press conference and said Lucas "has many things to answer for." He characterized her actions as "truly the epitome of hypocrisy for a public official."
As a result of the alleged scheme, Lucas accumulated nearly $5 million in "ill-gotten gains," according to the FBI director.

Medical marijuana can be sold by licensed dispensaries in Virginia and people can possess a certain amount for personal use. The state is set to launch regulated retail marijuana sales next year after the Virginia legislature legalized the sale of recreational cannabis in July.
Lucas sponsored a legalization bill in the state Senate in 2021 and has supported other measures decriminalizing marijuana, according to the National Organization for the Reform of Marijuana Laws.

Prosecutors claimed that in 2023 and 2024, Lucas was issued violation notices from the state's Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services related to The Cannabis Outlet for selling cannabis products that did not comply with state law.

According to the indictment, Lucas allegedly told an unindicted co-conspirator that she wanted a recreational license in the state to create "generational wealth" for her and her family, adding "this is my last chance."

In a phone call with a Virginia state lawmaker in March, Lucas allegedly said she needed the recreational industry to get off the ground, because "when I did it, it was obviously illegal." The indictment also alleges that Lucas was warned by a senior law enforcement official in multiple meetings that selling marijuana was illegal.

Prosecutors unveiled the indictment just weeks before the November elections. Lucas is not up for reelection, but her daughter, Lucas-Burke, is running for the Portsmouth City Council. As a general practice, the Justice Department has historically avoided overt law enforcement or prosecutorial activities involving political figures within 60 days of an election.

Blanche said the unwritten so-called "60-day rule" is not part of the Justice Manual, which lays out internal department policies and procedures. He defended the decision to charge Lucas and her daughter.
"We don't do political paybacks," he said.

Lucas was a key figure in pushing for a new congressional map through Virginia's Legislature that had added four Democratic-leaning seats. The map was approved in a ballot referendum in April but in May the Virginia Supreme Court tossed out the new map, dealing a blow to state Democrats. The U.S. Supreme Court then rejected an effort by Virginia Democrats to revive the new House lines.

Lucas was first elected to the Virginia General Assembly in 1991 and is currently the Senate president pro tempore. As she helped lead the Democratic redistricting plan earlier this year, Lucas used social media to taunt Republicans, President Trump and even the Democratic U.S. senators from her state. She was reelected in 2023 to a four-year term and is not up for reelection until 2027.

"You all started it and we f***ing finished it," she posted on social media after the measure passed, referring to Mr. Trump's push to redraw Texas' congressional map that kicked off the redistricting battle between the two parties.

title: Judge says Trump must sit for deposition in BBC defamation lawsuit
summary: A federal judge said President Trump must sit for a deposition with lawyers for the BBC by Dec. 11 as part of his ongoing defamation lawsuit.
story: Washington — A federal judge said President Trump must sit for a deposition with lawyers for the BBC by Dec. 11 as part of his ongoing defamation lawsuit against the British broadcaster.

U.S. Magistrate Judge Enjolique Lett set the deadline during a hearing in Miami on Thursday morning, according to the Associated Press. The judge ordered Mr. Trump to answer questions by Dec. 11 or face penalties, which could include dismissal of his lawsuit against the BBC, unless the period for the president and the network to collect information in the case is extended, the AP reported.

Mr. Trump was supposed to sit for a deposition Friday, but his lawyers told the BBC late last month that he would no longer be available to answer questions "due to other matters of national importance." The BBC told the court that on the day of the scheduled deposition, Oct. 16, the president spoke at a rally in Georgia alongside GOP candidates for the Senate and governor. He then traveled to his South Florida resort, Mar-a-Lago, where he attended an event for the Republican National Committee.
The president said he would be available for the deposition in the second or third week of January, according to the BBC.
Lawyers for the broadcaster had asked the judge to compel Mr. Trump to confirm a date for the deposition and answer their questions.

In a statement, a spokesman for the president's legal team did not address the judge's demand for a deposition, but said his "powerhouse lawsuit is holding the BBC accountable for its defamation and reckless election interference just as he has held other fake news mainstream media responsible for their wrongdoing."

Mr. Trump filed his $10 billion lawsuit against the BBC in December over a documentary that featured spliced-together portions of a speech he gave outside the White House on Jan. 6, 2021. Mr. Trump alleged that the documentary, which aired in October 2024, just weeks before the presidential election, misled viewers and falsely depicted his remarks to supporters.

Following the president's speech, a crowd of his backers marched to the U.S. Capitol and breached the building, where lawmakers and then-Vice President Mike Pence were gathered to reaffirm the results of the 2020 election.

The BBC said in November 2025 that it "sincerely regrets" how the clip of Mr. Trump's speech was edited but disagreed that there was a basis for a defamation claim. The network apologized to the president.

At the hearing Thursday, lawyers for the BBC and the president were set to discuss the network's subpoena for deposition testimony from Jack Smith, the former special counsel who brought criminal charges against Mr. Trump in 2023. The case involved Mr. Trump's alleged efforts to subvert the transfer of presidential power after the 2020 election. The charges were dismissed after the president was elected to a second term in 2024.

In defending the subpoena for Smith's testimony, the BBC said in a court filing that the former special counsel could shed light on matters involving Mr. Trump's speech on Jan. 6, including whether the president knew his remarks could lead to violence. The network said Smith does not object to the subpoena.

But Mr. Trump's lawyers refuted the notion that Smith has personal knowledge about the president's speech or state of mind when he delivered it. They also said Smith's testimony would be "duplicative," since he authored a final report on his investigation and testified twice to Congress about his case against Mr. Trump.
The BBC is also seeking documents from Mar-a-Lago about its membership and initiation fees, which the president's lawyers argue does not serve a legitimate purpose.

The discovery process began in February and is set to end Dec. 18. BBC lawyers said in a filing that nearly eight months into discovery, they still have not spoken with Mr. Trump and do not have a schedule to question him. They called the president "the most central figure in this case."

"There is hardly a more crucial and relevant piece of discovery in a defamation lawsuit than the deposition of the Plaintiff. For that reason, a plaintiff's unwillingness to sit for a deposition can be perilous to his claim," they wrote in a motion earlier this month.

title: DOJ asks Supreme Court to allow border wall construction in Big Bend region
summary: The Justice Department asked the Supreme Court to lift a lower court injunction that temporarily blocked the Trump administration from building a border wall and related infrastructure in the Big Bend Sector.
story: Washington — The Trump administration on Wednesday asked the Supreme Court to allow it to resume for now construction of a border wall and other infrastructure through a remote area of West Texas that includes Big Bend National Park.

The Justice Department urged the high court to lift a lower court injunction that temporarily bars the Department of Homeland Security from building the barrier or related infrastructure in the Big Bend Sector, which covers more than 500 miles of the U.S.-Mexico border and 77 counties in Texas.

"The district court's injunction significantly frustrates the government's ability to stop the flow of illegal aliens and drugs across the southern border," Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote in the request for emergency relief. "The Secretary identified the Big Bend project areas at issue because of the high rates of illegal-alien crossings and drug smuggling in the region over the past several years."

In response to the Justice Department's emergency appeal, the Center for Biological Diversity, which is challenging the Trump administration's effort to build the wall in the Big Bend area, pledged to fight to ensure the park is protected forever.

"We're deeply disappointed that the Trump administration is asking the Supreme Court for a green light to bulldoze one of America's wildest, most extraordinary landscapes," said Zeynep Graves, a senior attorney at the center, in a statement. "Once Big Bend's canyons, cultural treasures and wild ecosystems are destroyed, they'll be lost forever. We're confident the law is on our side and that only Congress can authorize something as consequential as walling off the entire U.S.-Mexico border."

President Trump's promise to build a wall along the southern border has been a hallmark of his immigration agenda for the last decade. But earlier this year, the president's plans were met with significant pushback from lawmakers in both parties, cattle ranchers and local law enforcement officials in Texas when photos and videos shared to social media showed bulldozers arriving at Big Bend National Park.

In response to the backlash, Customs and Border Protection Commissioner Rodney Scott paused construction inside the park until the end of September. The agency has said that the proposed border wall will not cut through Big Bend National Park, but other infrastructure would, including patrol roads, detection technology and roughly 17 miles of vehicle barriers.

Construction of a 47-mile-long stretch of wall in the Big Bend region began last month, according to CBP. The government has awarded contracts for five border-barrier projects in that area along the U.S.-Mexico border, the Justice Department said.

The Trump administration announced in February that the Department of Homeland Security would build barriers and roads in the Big Bend Sector. The project includes the construction of 30-foot-tall bollard walls stretching from Fort Quitman, Texas, to Closed Canyon, which is located in Big Bend Ranch State Park. Border walls and roads would span more than 300 miles, according to the government.

Because of the project's impact on cultural, recreational, wildlife and environmental resources, the federal government would typically have to ensure compliance with federal environmental protection and historical preservation laws before moving forward.

But when then-Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem announced the project earlier this year, she invoked a 1996 federal immigration law that gives the secretary the authority to waive all legal requirements deemed necessary to ensure quick construction of physical barriers and roads in the vicinity of the southern border to "deter illegal crossings in areas of high illegal entry." Secretary Markwayne Mullin, who succeeded Noem after her firing, issued two more waivers allowing CBP to construct barrier systems.

In response to the move, an environmental nonprofit, a professional riverboat guide and a religious organization dedicated to preserving the Sacred Heart of the Church of Jesus along the Rio Grande filed a lawsuit in April seeking to stop the Trump administration from implementing the project.

The Trump administration argued that the stretch of land at issue in the case is an area of "high illegal entry" given the rates of illegal crossings and drug smuggling. The government said more than 89,000 people were apprehended trying to cross into the U.S. illegally in the Big Bend Sector between 2021 and 2025.

But the plaintiffs said that the Big Bend Sector ranks last for apprehensions compared to the other six sectors along the southern border. While the area covers more than 25% of the U.S.-Mexico border, annual apprehensions in the Big Bend Sector ranged between 0.3% and 2.2% of total border-wide apprehensions, according to court filings.

Earlier this month, U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone granted the challengers' request for a preliminary injunction and barred the Department of Homeland Security from building border barriers or related infrastructure, or engaging in "any construction or ground disturbing activities" in the Big Bend Sector.
Cardone found that Noem and Mullin exceeded their authorities when issuing the waivers between February and July that allowed construction to proceed.
Just before the Justice Department sought the Supreme Court's intervention, Cardone rejected the Trump administration's request to pause her decision.

title: Judge curbs DHS efforts to conduct sweeps for possible noncitizen voters
summary: A federal judge ruled DHS's practice of knocking on doors and asking people about their immigration status — and whether they have voted in recent elections — likely violates the Voting Rights Act.
story: A federal judge ruled late Wednesday that the U.S. Department of Homeland Security's practice of knocking on doors and asking people about their immigration status — and whether they have voted in recent elections — likely violates the Voting Rights Act.

The ruling took aim at an operation that was documented by a CBS News investigation earlier Wednesday. Homeland Security Investigations has posted photos and videos of agents approaching homes in multiple states. The Trump administration says the practice is part of an effort to crack down on voting by noncitizens, but critics say it could intimidate legal voters.

In her ruling, U.S. District Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin ordered federal immigration authorities to stop carrying out "elections-related field operations and field interviews" in nine states, including California and New York, if the operations are likely to involve people who government officials "know, suspect, or should reasonably know or suspect are U.S. citizens."
Her order will remain in effect until polls close on Election Day. She stayed the ruling until 5 p.m. on Friday, which will give the government a chance to seek appeal.

Martinez-Olguin sided with groups that sued over the noncitizen voting investigation surge, including the California Nurses Association and National Nurses United. She found the policy likely ran afoul of a section of the Voting Rights Act that makes it illegal to "intimidate, threaten, or coerce" those who assist people with voting or engage in voter mobilization efforts.

"Plaintiffs do not claim, nor does the Court find, that it is unlawful for federal officials to undertake investigations into unlawful voting in federal elections," the judge wrote. "Rather, Plaintiffs seek to stop DHS from continuing to investigate U.S. citizens, who have a legal right to vote, in a way that intimidates and threatens the participation of CNA/NNU members from urging or aiding others to vote."

Martinez-Olguin also pointed to the "high likelihood of error" in the government's process for assembling a list of potential targets, which includes data from government agencies and commercially available data.

Homeland Security said in a statement on Thursday that the department is "laser focused on identifying, prosecuting, and removing aliens who vote and dilute the votes of U.S. citizens." The department added that they have "no plans to question or investigate people we believe to be U.S. citizens."
Protect Democracy, one of the groups that sued over the policy, celebrated the ruling.

"It was clear from the start that DHS built its lists on bad data, never checked how often it was wrong, and recklessly sent agents to people's homes weeks before an election," Beau Tremitiere, counsel at Protect Democracy, said in a statement to CBS News. "Today's ruling should remind us that American citizens hold the ultimate power in our democracy, not the government–no matter what the administration says otherwise."
CBS News has reached out to DHS for comment.

President Trump has prioritized cracking down on voter fraud during his second term, although there has been little evidence to back up his claims of widespread voting by noncitizens. Just 156 people have been charged with voting-fraud related offenses since the beginning of the Trump administration, according to the Justice Department.
The Justice Department reported earlier this week that it arrested several dozen green card holders in California on allegations they illegally registered to vote in U.S. federal elections.

title: Airbnb limits guest chores like laundry, drawing host backlash
summary: The new policy prevents hosts from asking guests to strip beds, start a load of laundry and other tasks that "require significant effort or time."
story: Airbnb is updating its rules to shield visitors from onerous cleaning tasks it says could negatively impact their stay.

The new policy, announced this week, prevents hosts from asking guests to strip beds, start a load of laundry and other household chores Airbnb says "require significant effort or time" and would typically be performed by a cleaner.
These tasks could lead guests to write negative reviews, Airbnb said, which ultimately hurt the property owner.

The new policy sparked backlash among some hosts, with more than 5,000 people signing a Change.org petition calling on Airbnb to reverse the rules. The signatories argued that the policy goes too far and is "unreasonable."
Requiring a cleaner to pick up the slack could hike expenses for hosts, which could ultimately be passed on to guests in the form of higher accommodation prices, the petition says.
"These are not professional cleaning duties," the petition says. "They are ordinary aspects of living responsibly in somebody else's property."
What are the new rules?

The online booking platform clarified which requests are "reasonable" as part of a new policy it unveiled on its website. The new rules apply to reservations booked on or after Nov. 20, according to Airbnb.

In some cases, it's a fine line: hosts can ask guests to put used dishes in the sink, but they can't ask them to wash or put away dishes. They can request that guests separate trash and recycling, but can't ask guests to deposit garbage at an off-site facility.
"When adding a request, remember that most guests want to avoid unexpected chores," Airbnb said on its website.

Airbnb said that if hosts repeatedly violate the rules, the rental company could reduce the visibility of their listing page or issue a notice to guests on the listing page about the host's violation.

title: Roller coaster safety experts weigh in on Six Flags investigation
summary: The Goliath roller coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia has been closed since a man died after witnesses say he was ejected from the ride.
story: Ride inspection experts expect the investigation into the death of a man who fell from a Georgia roller coaster this month to examine if maintenance issues, design flaws or human error led to the incident at Six Flags Over Georgia.
The Goliath has been closed since 42-year-old Hassan Kariem died after witnesses say he was ejected from the ride.

John F. King, Georgia's Insurance and Safety Fire Commissioner, who is leading the investigation, said investigators will not "cut corners, rush to conclusions, or leave questions unanswered without making every effort to resolve them."
"Our team has been on the ground working day and night to ensure that every relevant detail receives the attention it deserves," he said in a statement last week.
A spokesperson for the park said in a statement to CBS News that "our thoughts remain with the family and loved ones affected by the tragic incident in Georgia."

"Nothing is more important to Six Flags than the safety of our guests and team members, and we remain focused on supporting ongoing investigations alongside state authorities and the ride manufacturer," the spokesperson said.

A March inspection of the Goliath roller coaster found no violations or deficiencies, King said. The inspection report did include a note indicating that staff "need to replace bushings" — a piece of the puzzle inspectors are sure to home in on, experts said.
Bushings are parts designed to reduce friction and absorb shock in various mechanical assemblies.
Maintenance issues or a design flaw?

Six Flags has opened five Goliath roller coasters at parks across North America in the last 25 years. The coaster, which opened in 2006 in Georgia, can reach speeds of up to 70 miles per hour on towering tracks that rise 200 feet. It was designed by Bolliger & Mabillard, a Swiss-based roller coaster manufacturer.

For Kariem to have been ejected from the ride, ride operators and roller coaster engineers suggested either a mechanical malfunction, operator error — for instance, failing to properly check and secure the restraint — or a combination of both, could have played a part. Rides and their restraints are supposed to be inspected by park maintenance each morning, they said.
The park spokesperson said, "Safety is our ethos and is at the heart of everything we do at Six Flags."

"Every ride undergoes documented safety inspections before opening each day, supported by comprehensive maintenance programs designed to meet or exceed industry safety guidelines," the spokesperson said. "Our ride operators complete a comprehensive, multi-stage training program that includes classroom instruction, hands-on training and supervised, on-the-job experience with additional instruction and evaluation provided whenever necessary."

When riders board the Goliath, they are buckled into the ride's 36 seats using a padded clamshell lap bar, a U-shaped restraint that is typically locked in place over a rider's thighs and waist. Ride operators check restraints to make sure they're locked before the ride begins.

Daniel, a self-described "big roller coaster nerd" who also operates a Goliath at another park, said the coaster is designed so staff can use a control panel with various buttons and a screen to operate the ride.

Daniel, who asked to use his middle name because he is still employed, said it was likely that ride operators used two orange buttons on the control panel to open and close the car restraints. When the sensors detect that every single restraint is closed, two green mushroom-shaped buttons at the bottom start blinking. That means that operators can press on them to dispatch the ride, he said.
Goliath inspection records obtained by CBS News, dating back over a decade, show a smattering of 20 quickly resolved violations between 2016 and 2021, and none since.
However, Troy Richardson, an engineer with experience building and inspecting roller coasters, said the March inspection's note about bushings could be significant.
Bushings are used to keep mechanical pieces in restraints, chassis joints and wheel bogies, positioned correctly amid the repeated friction and bumps of a roller coaster ride.
Even a small defect in a bushing can be a major problem, said Richardson, the founder and CEO of MIT Experts, which provides forensic consulting in amusement park litigation.
"A bushing, if it's slightly off a little bit, now the pin won't go into the hole or it's a little bit loose in the hole," he said.

Richardson added that the manufacturer of the roller coaster most likely laid out a maintenance and replacement schedule for each part in an operation manual. A key question investigators will ask, Richardson said, will be if staff adhered to those instructions.

A person with knowledge of the park's operations said the bushings identified in the March inspection were located on the ride's bogie assemblies, which connect the vehicle to the track, and unrelated to the restraint system. They were changed as recommended, the person said.
Another expert, Kathryn Woodcock, editor-in-chief of the Journal of Themed Experience and Attractions Studies, said investigators will want to know "what exactly is not the way it is expected to be."
"If two parts disconnected (e.g., a latch came undone), it is a different thing than if one part broke (e.g., a crack failed catastrophically)," Woodcock said.
Woodcock described the tricky process behind determining when to replace parts.
"It is not automatically better to replace a part too early," Woodcock, a professor at Toronto Metropolitan University, wrote in an email.

She said the likelihood of failure in roller coaster parts often falls along a "'bathtub curve,' where failure is most common at the start of use due to possible manufacturing defects, and then if it does not fail then, the failure likelihood is very low for a length of time — which depends on its material and shape and loading — when failure likelihood increases again."
"In charge of some very important systems"
Six Flags operates nearly three dozen parks across North America, with more than 47 million guests and 95,000 employees in 2025, according to SEC filings.

At Six Flags Magic Mountain in California, the death of 22-year-old Christopher Hawley after he rode the X2 roller coaster in 2022 prompted questions about ride maintenance and inspection, said Timothy Loranger, an attorney who represented Hawley's family.

"What I did see in having talked to people who maintained the rides, I did not come away from those conversations feeling confident that they were competent in their jobs, I felt like they didn't have appropriate training," Loranger said. "They were in charge of some very important systems and maybe didn't really even understand what they were doing."

Six Flags Magic Mountain settled the wrongful death lawsuit with Hawley's family. The park shuttered X2 permanently in September, after lawsuits alleging riders suffered brain injuries piled up. (The Doan Law Firm, which tracks published claims of theme park-related fatalities, lists two previous deaths on Goliaths in its database: a 2002 brain aneurysm at Six Flags Magic Mountain in California and a 2006 death listed as a likely heart attack on Six Flags Over Georgia's Goliath.)
Loranger said he wouldn't be surprised if the same challenges he saw at Magic Mountain arose at Six Flags Over Georgia.
Ride operators at Six Flags Over Georgia spoke to CBS News about the training and management they received while being tasked with ensuring the safety of thrill-seekers.

Jacobi Edwards, 18, who was a ride operations lead at Six Flags Over Georgia for several months last spring, described it as "a very well-run place," saying he's proud of his work there. But he chose to work on other roller coasters, in part because of Goliath's popularity.
"They have a clock to beat as that is the most famous ride in the park, so they do definitely feel rushed," said Edwards, who was 17 when he worked at the park.
He said when he was on the clock, he prioritized guest safety over trying to get "more cycles in."
Richardson, the MIT engineer, said park supervisors need to trust park staff as "ambassadors … that are trying to keep people safe and be your frontline."

"I don't care if there's 100 people in the line, we don't want somebody to die, you know? And they need to have that ability to come in and say, 'Hey, I have the authority to shut this down if I don't think it's safe,'" Richardson said.
Richard Pretlow, park president of Six Flags Over Georgia, said in a statement after the incident, "our team members receive extensive training to safely operate and maintain our rides."

But Harper Henderson,18, a former employee who started her job at Six Flags Over Georgia when she was 15, said the pressure to keep lines for the Goliath moving was paralleled by the rush to get new employees trained to operate the coaster.
Like Edwards, Henderson said she was promoted to trainer at 17 years old — after six weeks as a ride operator.

"Whenever we got a new employee, I would walk them through the operating procedures for all the rides and then watch them as they pretend they're operating the ride, or pretend to help with the restraints or something," she said. "And I would do that over and over again until I thought they were ready for the test and then I would send them to take the test."
She described it as a process that "could be done in about an hour." Henderson said ride operators needed at least an hour to review all the training.

CBS News reviewed operator tests for two Six Flags Over Georgia rides: Georgia Scorcher and the Log Jamboree. The questions, on a Microsoft Forms sheet, asked about the mechanics of each ride and its safety procedures. For example, in the Georgia Scorcher quiz, operators are asked, "What does it mean when the DISPATCH buttons flash on the main operator?"
Henderson said the rides were often so busy she had to rush the training.
"We would just give them the test answers," Henderson said, adding that new operators would then be ready to work in "15 minutes."
Henderson said she wasn't comfortable with the process. She said she resigned in July 2025.
"The fact that you could just skip, that was not great," she said. "And it was because the managers really pushed to have the minimum amount of people to open every ride."

title: Toledo man describes days-long chemical leak: "Looked like a movie"
summary: Hundreds of people remain evacuated from their homes days after the chemical leak began at a facility in Toledo, Ohio.
story: Hundreds of people in Toledo, Ohio, remain evacuated from their homes as officials work to resolve a fiery chemical leak that began Tuesday.

Residents within a mile of an MC Tank facility were order to evacuate on Tuesday, and everyone within a 3-mile radius was told to shelter in place. On Wednesday, the shelter-in-place was lifted and evacuations were reduced to half a mile. They were reduced further, to a quarter-mile, by Thursday morning. But a chemical plume remains.

City officials have been allowing the chemicals to vent from the 5,500-gallon tank, instead of trying to send in crews to stop the leak. Toledo Mayor Wade Kapszukiewicz said Wednesday that the potential for an explosion made it too dangerous for first responders, including hazardous material teams, to approach the tank. One first responder has sustained injuries, Kapszukiewicz said.

The city and MC Tank Transport Inc. said the substance involved in the leak is glycidyl methacrylate, an industrial chemical that is used in plastics, paints and coatings. State officials said the leak happened due to an error as the chemical was being transferred.

Residents have reported symptoms including burning in the eyes, lungs and sinuses, bad headaches and nausea. One area hospital is treating 35 patients. Resident Travis Williams said he "woke up choking" from overwhelming fumes.
"I've never had these feelings, the burnings, itchy skin, irritated eyes," Williams said. "I am definitely worried about the long-term effect of this."

A dense fog has also descended over Toledo. Officials say the fog was indistinguishable from the chemical plume. The conditions are also affecting visibility. Williams said the scene outside his home "looked like a movie."
"I couldn't even see as far as my car to the curb," Williams said.

Officials are asking residents to ventilate their homes by opening windows and doors. Residents are also being encouraged to wash their hands thoroughly and watch for coughing and eye irritation in people and pets. The Environmental Protection Agency is monitoring air quality.

In May, an industrial tank containing another methacrylate compound ruptured in Orange County, California. That incident displaced thousands until a crack formed in the overheating tank, relieving the pressure and ending the risk of explosion.

title: Omar says she can't keep living in home federal agents searched
summary: The Minnesota Democrat told MS NOW's Chris Hayes that her address is now public and she is facing death threats. She said her children visit on and off, and she doesn't want people tracking them.
story: Rep. Ilhan Omar said she can't keep living in the Washington, D.C., home that federal agents searched, because its address is now public and she is facing death threats.

The Minnesota Democrat described the search and its aftermath in an interview Wednesday night with MS NOW's Chris Hayes. She said she is working out where to move and doesn't want people tracking her children, who visit on and off.
Omar said she is leaning on her faith.
"I'm designed uniquely by God to withstand all of this," she said.

She said those targeting her would be most satisfied if she gave up and left Congress, but she has "a legal right to be a member of Congress." She also said she is confident she "didn't do anything wrong."

Homeland Security Investigations agents searched Omar's home Oct. 12 as part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation. Sources told CBS News the same day that the investigation centered on Omar's immigration paperwork, which dates to her childhood and was completed by her late father, and that investigators were examining potential false statements and immigration fraud.
Omar said Homeland Security Investigations agents arrived at her home at about 6 a.m. Her husband and 20-year-old son were inside.

"You don't show up to somebody's house that early in the morning unless you're trying to freak them out," Omar said. She said she had slept about two and a half hours after traveling and thought something was on fire. Agents surrounded the house and pounded on the front and back doors, she said, as she and her husband hurried downstairs.

Omar said she asked for a search warrant and agents provided one. She said 15 to 25 agents searched room by room for four to five hours, and she couldn't call her attorney until about an hour in. Agents took fewer than 20 items, about half of them notebooks and old phones, Omar said. They also took an old camera her husband's uncle gave him and a Somali phrase book.

Omar said she believes the Trump administration needed to "save face" with right-wing influencers after promising that something would happen to her. She said she believes the broader goal is to scare people from voting, but that she is hearing the opposite: calls about long lines at early voting sites and staff who can't keep up with requests for rides.

Omar's office has said she has done nothing wrong. President Trump told reporters he had nothing to do with the search. Omar rejected that in her Wednesday interview, saying he had "everything to do with it."
In an Instagram video after the search, Omar vowed to keep campaigning in the weeks before the midterm elections.

title: Armed federal agents knock on doors looking for noncitizen voters
summary: Armed and in uniform, agents from the Department of Homeland Security have been knocking on doors to ask residents about their immigration status whether they're registered to vote.
story: Armed and in uniform, federal agents from the Department of Homeland Security have been knocking on doors in several states to ask residents about their immigration status — and to inquire if they have registered to vote or cast votes in past elections, a CBS News Investigation has found.

The operation is part of an effort to root out potential noncitizen voters ahead of the midterms. DHS has alleged that there could be as many as 250,000 citizens illegally registered to vote, although election experts have disputed the accuracy of this figure. Just 156 people have been charged with voting-fraud related offenses since the beginning of the Trump administration, according to the Department of Justice. There are 227 million registered voters in the U.S.
Critics say that sending armed federal agents to the doors of U.S. residents could be intimidating for legal voters.

"What we're seeing now is the federal government is inserting itself into the state process for verifying their voter roles in an unprecedented way," said Jessica Marsden, a lawyer for Protect Democracy, a left-leaning advocacy group that is suing the federal agency over the door-knocking campaign. "And they are doing it in a way that seems maximally designed to scare lawful voters from participating."

The home visits ramped up in September, in the thick of the midterm campaign season, and continued over the past weekend. The Justice Department announced Monday that Homeland Security agents in California arrested more than 20 people, all of them green card holders, on allegations they had illegally registered or cast a vote.

As part of that roundup, dozens of federal agents descended on the residence of a 72-year-old man from Belize, who was taken from his home in his pajamas and arrested on charges he allegedly voted illegally in the past four elections.

"HSI is actively rooting out and investigating election fraud wherever it can be found," said a DHS spokesperson. "Under President Trump, HSI is committed to restoring integrity to our election systems and ensuring that American citizens and only American citizens are electing American leaders."
Eric Balliet, a former Homeland Security Investigations agent, said the door-knocking operation is a significant departure from traditional law enforcement activities.

"In my 23 years with HSI, I never engaged in or was aware of any incident or initiative that sent Special Agents to private residences to verify the eligibility of voters," Balliet said, who served in the federal government under multiple administrations.

In June, the DHS directed U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, to assist in deportations of alleged noncitizen voters. Homeland Security Investigations, the agency conducting the at-home visits, is one of the enforcement arms of ICE and typically focuses on criminal cross border investigations like child exploitation, drug smuggling and money laundering.

Months later after the announcement, hundreds of agents were pulled off their cases and assigned to track down alleged noncitizen voters as part of a "surge" initiative, according to internal documents reviewed by CBS News. The directive, first reported by CNN, describes a "Criminal Voter Fraud " initiative that includes "field reviews" in at least six states including California, Georgia, Missouri, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wisconsin.

Photos and videos posted on X show agents from Homeland Security Investigations, some of whom are carrying firearms, approaching houses and knocking on doors, under captions like, "AMERICAN ELECTIONS ARE FOR AMERICANS."
One photo from Kansas City HSI's account shows four agents at the door of a woman standing on her porch holding a child's hand.

The woman is identified in a Department of Justice press release as Mariana Alexandra Dewey, a Peruvian national who was charged with four counts of voter-fraud related crimes including illegally casting a ballot in the 2024 election. Her case has not yet been heard. Her lawyer declined to respond to CBS News' request for comment.

Hours after this article was published, Democratic Rep. Bennie Thompson, the ranking member of the Homeland Security Committee, wrote to DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin to demand the that DHS immediately cease "law enforcement activity aimed at intimidating the public as the 2026 midterm elections are underway." He said the DHS operations "reflect an anti-democratic departure from the mission Congress set for the Department, and serve only President Trump's voter suppression agenda, not a legitimate enforcement objective."
For civil rights advocates, the show of force has sparked concerns about the chilling effect it could have on legal voters.
"It is sending the signal to a much broader community, do not show up at the polls. Do not vote," said Dr. Carol Anderson, a professor of African American Studies at Emory University.

"And so if you are somebody who has registered to vote and you're a naturalized citizen, what you see in that community is that —  because this is not a regime that makes those discernments — that you're gonna stay away from the voting booth."

A DHS spokesperson said, "DHS and DOJ are laser focused on prosecuting and removing aliens who vote and preventing the dilution of the votes of U.S. citizens. … Those who are here legally and are not breaking other laws have nothing to fear."
"Target List"
In one video, agents are filmed holding a document that says, "Target List."

That list can be far reaching, said a HSI agent familiar with the initiative who asked to speak anonymously. DHS pulls from internal databases, voter rolls, and other datasets. Then employees attempt to match names against citizenship data provided by the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, or USCIS.

In September, a USCIS whistleblower said that employees were asked to review the voter information of tens of thousands of individuals across the country, including citizens. Employees were given quotas to investigate 40 subjects a day, which is a rate of roughly 12 minutes per subject.
DHS has defended the data matching program and the work USCIS has done to identify potential noncitizen voters.

"Far from being rushed or untrained, these investigative efforts are conducted diligently and professionally,"  said a DHS spokesperson. "There is no quota on criminality. DHS will pursue each and every illegal voter to the fullest extent of the law ."
"There's every reason to expect that there are many, many more false positives in these lists," said Marsden.

She noted that Homeland Security officials initially said they had identified nearly 16,000 noncitizens on Nevada's voter rolls, but ultimately they were unable to provide evidence of a single illegally registered voter.

title: Childcare costs are growing faster than rent in the U.S.
summary: A growing share of American families are having to shell out more than $2,000 a month for childcare services, new data shows.
story: The rising cost of childcare in the U.S. is vying with food prices and healthcare expenses in straining household budgets.

Nearly 8% of families are spending more than $2,000 per month on childcare services, including daycare, nanny services and other programs. That's more than double the share of households that spent that much just three years ago, according to new research from the Bank of America Institute.

In September, the cost of daycare and school-related fees rose faster than other essential expenses, such as rent and medical care, compared to the same period a year ago, according to federal labor data.

Families nationwide spent an average of 8% of their monthly incomes on childcare services in September, BofA found. Under federal guidelines, childcare is considered affordable when it consumes no more than 7% of household income.

Assuming a family spends $24,000 annually on childcare, it would need to earn roughly $343,000 to remain below the 7% threshold. In 2025, median household income was $87,460, according to Census Bureau data.
Lower- and middle-income families spend nearly 9% of their annual incomes on childcare payments, while higher-income households spend 7.3%, according to BofA.

Along with facing rising childcare costs, workers have also seen slowing wage growth, heightening the financial pressure on many families, Economic Policy Institute economist Elise Gould told CBS News.
Separate research from AARP shows that families are turning to grandparents, who provide $172 billion per year in direct financial assistance.
Where are childcare costs growing fastest?

In some parts of the U.S., childcare fees are rising even faster, according to BofA. In September, median childcare costs rose fastest in Nashville, Tennessee, followed by Jacksonville, Florida, and Phoenix, Arizona, compared to the same period a year ago, according to BofA's analysis.

"There's been an increase in domestic migration to these areas," BofA Institute economist Taylor Bowley told CBS News, noting that an increase in demand for childcare services is putting pressure on prices.

A shortage of childcare workers also appears to be driving up childcare expenses. Employment in the sector fell 0.7% in September compared to one year earlier, making it harder for providers to deliver such services.
"You see job growth falling and price pressures creeping in, leading to a bit of an availability problem," BofA Institute senior economist David Tinsley told CBS News.

A lack of affordable childcare disproportionately affects women's employment opportunities, according to the researchers. Women are more likely than men to take on childcare responsibilities, according to data from the American Time Use Survey.
"Beyond childcare being a household expense, it's a form of economic enablement," Bowley said.

Edited by
                                        
                                  Alain  Sherter

title: iPhone Duo already backordered until 2027 as pre-order sales soar
summary: Consumer demand for Apple's first foldable phone is strong despite the device's hefty $1,999 price tag.
story: Apple is seeing strong demand for its new foldable iPhone, with supplies quickly selling out after pre-order sales opened on Friday.

"Apple opened iPhone Duo pre-orders this morning, and the early read looks robust in our view, with demand for Cupertino's first foldable running well ahead of supply out of the gates," Wall Street analyst Dan Ives, a partner at Yorkville Ives, said in a research note.

The pre-order window for the Duo opened on Friday at 8 a.m. ET on apple.com and in the Apple Store app. Within minutes, the estimated delivery of the phone was pushed back past Oct. 23, the device's official launch date, and into next year. As of Friday afternoon, the Apple phone was backordered until late January.
"It's been 3 minutes, and it's sold out at every store around the NYC/CT area," Max Weinbach, an analyst for the market research firm Creativestrat, said on X.
Apple did not immediately respond to a request for comment on how many pre-order requests it received.
When the Duo officially launches on Oct. 23, Apple said it will have some inventory at its stores, but noted that supply could sell out quickly.

"On Friday morning, our teams look forward to welcoming customers at Apple Stores to experience iPhone Duo and the incredible iPhone line-up for themselves," an Apple spokesperson said in an email. "Apple Stores will have limited iPhone Duo available for walk-in customers, and we're working hard to get this revolutionary new product into customers' hands as quickly as possible."

Apple's new CEO, John Ternus, announced the iPhone Duo last month. The Duo lets users split the screen to use two different apps on the device, or two windows of the same website for uses such as comparison shopping.

Prices start at $1,999 for a device with 256 GB of storage. When folded, it's about the size of a passport. The full display is the largest of any Apple phone, resembling more of an iPad than an iPhone.
Ternus also announced the iPhone 18 at Apple's annual fall showcase, which went on sale last month.

Ives thinks demand for the Duo will remain strong into 2027, with many iPhone users planning to upgrade. He projects Apple will sell around 10 million Duos in the next few quarters and up to 25 million in 2027.

title: Mark Zuckerberg threatened to leave California over wealth tax
summary: Zuckerberg has agreed to remain in California for eight years as part of a board-approved plan to create new shares he can sell to pay a proposed wealth tax.
story: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg threatened to move out of California if residents of the state approve a first-of-its-kind billionaire wealth tax when voters head to the polls on Nov. 3, the company said in a new regulatory filing.

Because of his concerns over the wealth tax, Zuckerberg told Meta that he was "evaluating relocating his primary residence outside California and that steps toward any such relocation, including any listing of his residential real estate in California on the market, would be public and inevitably noted and commented upon by company employees and, accordingly, raise questions for management of the company going forward," the filing states.

Meta said that because Zuckerberg's presence near the company's Menlo Park, California, headquarters is "critically important" to its success, the company took an unusual step: Its board approved a new class of nonvoting common stock that he can sell to raise cash to pay the wealth tax, if voters approve it.
Without that change, Zuckerberg faced the prospect of having to sell voting shares to raise funds to pay the tax, which would have reduced his control of Meta.

As a result of that decision to issue new stock, Zuckerberg has told Meta he will commit to remaining a California resident for eight years. If Meta moves its headquarters to another state, Zuckerberg will move to that jurisdiction, according to the regulatory filing.

The disclosure highlights the public debate over the proposed billionaire wealth tax, known as Proposition 40, which will be on the Nov. 3 ballot in California. Under the proposal, the tax would impose a one-time 5% state tax on billionaire wealth — about $12.4 billion of Zuckerberg's estimated $247 billion net worth, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.

The company believes "it is critically important to keep Mr. Zuckerberg in a leadership position with our company and that he continue to reside in and manage the company from our headquarters in California to ensure his continued ability to effectively drive our performance during this era of unprecedented challenge and competition in our industry," Meta said in its filing.

The billionaire tax is aimed at raising $100 billion from the state's wealthiest residents, with the money earmarked for shoring up California's healthcare system. Stanford University economists have questioned whether the tax could backfire, given that several billionaires have already moved out of the state. The economists said that could result in lower projected wealth taxes and reduced overall income tax collections.
Nonvoting Class C shares
Creating a new stock class isn't only designed to keep Zuckerberg near Meta's headquarters, according to the filing.

The publicly listed, nonvoting Class C common stock, which will become effective in January, is also intended in part to boost the company's ability to raise capital for AI infrastructure investments. It will also use the new stock to raise capital, compensate employees, make acquisitions and for other general corporate purposes.
"Meta plans to issue nonvoting shares to fund AI investments without diluting CEO Mark Zuckerberg's control," said Andrew Rocco, stock strategist at Zacks Investment Research.

title: Teacher who survived Oregon school shooting recounts playing dead
summary: Becky Drury, the 54-year-old teacher wounded in the shooting at an Oregon elementary school last week, says she was shot before she had "any chance to act."
story: Becky Drury, the 54-year-old teacher wounded in the shooting at an Oregon elementary school last week, is sharing a statement about her experience, saying the gunman shot her before she had "any chance to act."
In the statement Wednesday, Drury recalled running to see what was happening outside her classroom at Silver Rail Elementary School before spotting the shooter.
"I turned to shut the door behind me, but the shooter was already there," Drury wrote. "Before I could do anything more, he shot me at close range and I fell to the ground."

"Lying on the floor, I saw that my left hand was almost completely severed from the gunshot, and my other arm was also severely injured," she continued. "I could not get up, defend myself, or protect anyone else. So, I did the only thing I could do, which was to pretend to be dead in the hope he would not shoot me again."

Drury suffered serious but non-life-threatening injuries from the Oct. 15 shooting that killed three children, ages 5, 8 and 11, and a 25-year-old teacher. Another student, a 7-year-old, was also seriously wounded.

The suspect was identified as 16-year-old Griffin J. John II, a former student at the school. Police said he shot through the school's locked doors before entering a special needs classroom and opening fire.
The gunman was tackled by another teacher and fatally shot by an armed bystander, 36-year-old Kaylub Giamanco, who followed him into the school, according to police.
Drury said Wednesday she was sharing what happened to her because "I want to make sure the events of that day and my actions in particular are reported accurately."
"I know there has been contradictory reporting about my actions that day, but the truth is I was shot before I had any chance to act," she wrote.

She thanked those who have supported her since the shooting, and said, "What happened in that classroom was unimaginable, and like so many in this community, my heart is broken for everyone affected by this tragedy."

title: Stephen Hubbard back in U.S. after release from Russian prison
summary: Hubbard, a Michigan native, spent four years wrongfully imprisoned in Russia before being released on Wednesday.
story: Stephen Hubbard, the Michigan native who spent four years wrongfully imprisoned in Russia before being released on Wednesday, landed back in the U.S. late Wednesday, according to President Trump.

The president said Hubbard had just landed back in the U.S. while Mr. Trump spoke to reporters late Wednesday night as he returned from a rally in South Carolina. He expected Hubbard to visit the White House "in the next day or so."
"He's obviously just got out of prison," Mr. Trump told reporters. "He was there for a long time."

Hubbard's release was announced earlier in the day during a meeting between U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Hubbard was imprisoned in Russia for more than four years after being accused of fighting for Ukraine. The U.S. government had deemed Hubbard wrongfully detained.
In a brief phone call with his father before Hubbard took off from St. Petersburg, his son, friar Joseph Coleman, said he sounded better than he had during their last conversation in May 2025.
"I want to embrace him as a son embraces his father. I want to personally assess his health to make sure he's well," Coleman said.
Hubbard, 74, landed in San Antonio, where he will receive a medical evaluation, as is typical for prisoners released from overseas.

Hubbard, a retired schoolteacher, was captured in Ukraine shortly after Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022 and was accused of manning a checkpoint for mercenaries. He was later sentenced to almost seven years in a penal colony. His family has always disputed the charges.

Mr. Trump said in social media posts that Putin agreed to release Hubbard at his request, with "no 'swap' necessary," though he also said he would not have been released had the White House not halted new sanctions passed by Congress against Russia from taking effect last week.

"It would seem that this is all tethered to short-term interests on the part of the Trump administration that seem to be connected to fuel prices," CBS News national security analyst Elliot Ackerman, a retired Marine and special activities officer at the CIA, told "CBS Mornings."
Witkoff praised Putin after the release, calling him a "humanitarian," a comment that generated bipartisan criticism.
"You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian, you are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that," Witkoff told Putin.
Despite the goodwill expressed after Hubbard's release, Moscow still launched major strikes on Ukraine overnight. Russia launched 21 missiles at Kyiv and nearly half of all of Ukraine's regions.

"I think this hostage release seems to be a much smaller gesture in what's a larger pattern of kind of appeasing actions between President Trump and Putin that are running counter to Ukraine's interest in the war," Ackerman told CBS News.

title: Warren warns of "food insecurity crisis" from SNAP cuts and prices
summary: Sen. Elizabeth Warren is urging the U.S. Department of Agriculture to reverse cuts to the food-stamp program as consumers shoulder $22 billion in additional food costs.
story: Americans are facing a "food insecurity crisis" after shouldering an additional $22 billion in food costs due to rising inflation and billions of dollars in food-stamp cuts, according to Sen. Elizabeth Warren.

In an Oct. 21 letter to U.S. Department of Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins, the Massachusetts Democrat said that the combination of rising food prices and cuts to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program has created a "one-two punch" for millions of households.
Warren also asked the USDA to work with lawmakers to reverse food-stamp policies that have resulted in 5.2 million people losing SNAP benefits since July 2025.

SNAP enrollment, now at its lowest level since 2019, could shrink in the coming months as additional changes to the program take effect, according to anti-hunger experts. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), a tax and spending law signed into law by President Trump in 2025, expanded SNAP's work requirements and shifted more of the program's costs onto states. Those changes have created new hurdles for enrollment, according to experts.

The USDA halted its annual study on food insecurity in 2025, saying at the time that the report was "redundant, costly [and] politicized." But a May analysis from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York found "a remarkable increase in food insecurity, particularly among lower-educated and lower-income households and households with young children."

The New York Fed found earlier this year that 10% of U.S. families reported they didn't have enough food and that their children sometimes missed meals, more than double the 4% share in 2020. Almost 20% of families with annual income of less than $50,000 reported not having enough food, up from about 7% six years ago.

"My office developed a 'food misery index' to measure how much the combination of rising food prices and declining SNAP participation is costing American households," Warren said in her letter to the USDA. "The index combines the more than $17.2 billion in rising grocery prices — calculated by inflation-adjusting consumer expenditures — with the more than $5.1 billion in lost household SNAP benefits."
The USDA and White House didn't return a request for comment.

Changing SNAP policies would require lawmakers to pass new rules for the food-stamp program. Some anti-hunger advocates and state organizations are now lobbying Congress to delay some of the OBBBA's changes to SNAP, including a rule that would require states with high payment error rates to absorb billions in additional costs starting in October 2027.

The USDA serves as the primary federal regulator and rule-maker for SNAP, giving it some leeway in administering the program. For instance, the agency allowed some states to ban enrollees from using food stamps to buy soda and candy, although a federal judge earlier this year ruled that the Agriculture Department exceeded its authority in implementing the rules.

Warren also pointed to President Trump's tariffs as contributing to higher food prices. Higher import duties last year boosted U.S. inflation by about 2.9 percentage points through February, according to recent research from the New York Fed. Without those tariffs, the price of goods would have declined, the researchers said.

title: John Anderson, country music Hall of Famer, dies at 71
summary: John Anderson, a country music Hall of Famer with a distinctive voice, died on Wednesday, his family said. He was 71 years old.
story: John Anderson, a country music Hall of Famer with a distinctive voice, has died, his family said Wednesday. He was 71 years old.
"It is with the heaviest of hearts that we share the passing of our beloved husband, father, grandfather, and best friend," his family said in a statement on Instagram.

"To the world, he was a gifted country music singer whose voice and songs touched countless lives," they said. "To us, he was so much more. He was the heart of our family, the one who made us laugh, loved us fiercely, and made every ordinary moment feel special."
"His music will live on, but for us, his greatest legacy will always be the love he gave his family and the memories we will carry with us forever," they said.

Anderson's unmistakable voice helped make him a country music legend. And for some of Nashville's biggest names, he was required listening, with stars like Blake Shelton collaborating with him. Others, including Luke Combs and Ashley McBryde, recorded his songs for his tribute album, "Something Borrowed, Something New."
The Florida native arrived in Nashville as a teenager, playing clubs and working construction — even helping build the roof of the Grand Ole Opry.
But before long, he was the one raising it.
"Swingin'" became a no. 1 hit and the CMA Single of the Year in 1983.
A decade later, "Straight Tequila Night" and "Seminole Wind" brought Anderson's distinctive sound to another generation.
But years later, a mysterious life-threatening illness nearly silenced him, taking away his hearing and leaving him wondering whether he would ever make music again.
Anderson told CBS News in 2022 that the first part of the illness brought severe, terrible headaches, starting in 2016. Then, he said, his hair fell out and he lost his hearing "almost completely."
"They never really figured out just what it was," he said.
His return to music included the 2020 album "Years." Then, in 2024, came country music's highest honor: a place in its Hall of Fame.
"It's a long long road from Apaka, Florida, to standing right here on this stage, but I must say, behind all of that there was a lot of adventure, and I got to choose my own way," he said.
Anderson died just days after attending a Hall of Fame ceremony in Nashville on Sunday.

"I was talking with John Sunday night at the HOF ceremony," country star McGraw wrote on social media. "He was in such good spirits. We talked, we laughed, we sang his songs that I loved so much together, just goofing off. I am completely heartbroken by his passing. There will never be a stylist in music, any music, that was so defining as his."

title: Man who halted runaway school bus credits "Grey's Anatomy" inspiration
summary: A quick-thinking bystander came to the rescue of the students and driver aboard a runaway school bus in Saint Paul, Minnesota.
story: A quick-thinking man who came to the rescue of the students and driver aboard a runaway school bus in Saint Paul, Minnesota, on Monday afternoon credited the television series "Grey's Anatomy" for inspiring his actions.
Ebro Ahmed, 27, told CBS News that he leaped into action after noticing the Battle Creek Middle School bus rolling down the street at about 10 mph with its doors wide open and its lights flashing.
Ahmed said it caught his attention because the lights of a school bus normally don't flash unless it is at a complete stop.
"When he drove past me, it really shook me," Ahmed told CBS News Wednesday. "I was like, 'What is going on?'"
As captured on nearby security cameras, Ahmed, who works at a nearby store, sprinted from the sidewalk and jumped onto the moving bus.
"I saw the bus driver obviously having a medical emergency," Ahmed said. "All I looked at was the gear control and I was trying to put it into park."

Ahmed, who told CBS News he had never been behind the wheel of a bus before, said he briefly got confused between the reverse and park selections on the gear shift and accidentally put the bus into reverse.
"I started hearing beeps and we were going backwards," Ahmed explained. "And then I said, 'That is not right,' and I threw it into neutral and pulled the [parking] brake."
He went on: "When I looked behind me, I saw all of the kids kind of a little scared, crying with their phones out getting ready to call the police."
Saint Paul Public Schools said there were 19 students aboard the bus at the time. None of them were hurt in the incident. The district did not provide information on the condition of the driver.

"After everything, he was coming to, but he's still kind of out of it," Ahmed said of the driver. "And so I just let him be. Even when the police came, he was already done having his medical emergency. He was getting a little bit better, but I just didn't want to rush and start asking him questions."
Ahmed doesn't have any medical experience, but he does credit his favorite TV show, "Grey's Anatomy," for inspiring him.
"In 'Grey's Anatomy,' you never see doctors panic. I know it is all acting and stuff, so I just knew to be calm and just think everything through," Ahmed said.
The district said a second bus eventually came to pick up the students and continue the route.
Asked if he feels like a hero, Ahmed responded, "I feel like any person in my situation would have done the same thing."
