title: Pope Leo welcomed back as he delivers Angelus prayer days after lung cancer surgery
summary: Thousands gathered in St. Peter's Square as Pope Leo XIV made a surprise early return from Gemelli hospital following cancerous tumor removal.
story: A crowd of supporters greet Pope Leo XIV outside of Gemelli Hospital in Rome, Italy, on Saturday, Oct. 17 as the pontiff returns to the Vatican following surgery to remove a cancerous node in his right lung. Credit: Reuters.

Pope Leo XIV made a remarkable return to the Vatican on Sunday, appearing before thousands of Catholic faithful in St. Peter's Square just five days after undergoing surgery to remove a cancerous tumor from his lung.

The 71-year-old pontiff delivered his traditional Angelus prayer from a window overlooking the square, marking his first official engagement since being discharged Saturday from Rome's Gemelli hospital, where doctors removed the lower lobe of his right lung.

Leo thanked the faithful for their prayers and support throughout his hospitalization, saying his recent health struggles had brought him closer to those suffering from illness. He also expressed gratitude to the doctors, nurses and hospital staff who cared for him following the operation.
POPE LEO XIV DISCHARGED FROM HOSPITAL, WILL RETURN TO VATICAN AFTER SURGERY TO REMOVE LUNG CANCER

Pope Leo XIV appears at the window of his study in the Apostolic Palace overlooking St. Peter's Square at the Vatican for the traditional noon blessing after praying the Angelus, Sunday, Oct. 18, 2026, a day after he returned from the hospital, where he had lung cancer removed on Tuesday. (AP Photo/Alessandra Tarantino)
The first American-born pope said he planned to gradually resume his regular activities with God's help and the continued prayers of the faithful.

During his Angelus address, Leo reflected on one of Jesus' best-known teachings, "Give therefore to the emperor the things that are the emperor's, and to God the things that are God's," urging Christians to live with integrity and resist hypocrisy.
His return came sooner than expected after doctors initially anticipated a hospital stay of approximately one week following Tuesday's surgery.
As he departed the hospital on Saturday, the pope told a reporter in English that he was doing "much better."

Faithful watch Pope Leo XIV appearing at the window of his study in the Apostolic Palace overlooking St. Peter's Square at the Vatican for the traditional noon blessing after praying the Angelus, Sunday, Oct. 18, 2026, a day after he returned from the hospital, where he had lung cancer removed on Tuesday. (AP Photo/Gregorio Borgia)
Claire Holland, visiting from Jacksonville, Fla., told The Associated Press she felt "very blessed" to witness the pope's return.
"I think there have been millions and millions of prayers. And he is a strong determined man, and I am so happy that he is feeling well enough to do this," Holland said.
POPE LEO UNDERGOES BLOOD TESTS, X-RAY FOLLOWING CANCER SURGERY, VATICAN SAYS
The surgery marked the first major health crisis of Leo's 17-month pontificate. Doctors confirmed that the tumor was adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer.

Doctors are conducting further testing on the tumor and surrounding lymph nodes to determine the extent of the disease and whether additional treatment, including chemotherapy, immunotherapy or targeted therapy, may be necessary.

Pope Leo XIV appears at the window of his study in the Apostolic Palace overlooking St. Peter's Square at the Vatican for the traditional noon blessing after praying the Angelus, Sunday, Oct. 18, 2026, a day after he returned from the hospital, where he had lung cancer removed on Tuesday. (AP Photo/Alessandra Tarantino)
The pope is scheduled to visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from Nov. 6 through Nov. 17, a demanding itinerary that includes a dozen flights and two helicopter rides to high-altitude destinations.
His surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora, told Vatican News on Saturday that the pope appears well enough to go on the trip.
"The Holy Father has put his heart and soul into his recovery," Margaritora said, adding that he expected Leo to recover fully from the surgery "in another 10 days or so."

"As for a long trip involving air travel in about three weeks, I would say there are no clinical reasons why it should not take place," Margaritora said.
Fox News’ Courtney Walsh and The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: European Parliament votes to confront Muslim Brotherhood, 'Islamist entryism' in overwhelming vote
summary: The European Parliament voted 'historic' 381-167 to condemn Islamist entryism and Muslim Brotherhood influence as critics say the hard part will be converting the resolution into legislation.
story: George Washington University Program on Extremism director Lorenzo Vidino joins 'Fox & Friends' to discuss the Senate's examination of the Muslim Brotherhood's quiet, long-term influence in American institutions.
Following the sanctioning of foreign Muslim Brotherhood groups by the Trump administration, the European Parliament recently took its own action against the transnational radical Islamist group.

As Europe begins to respond to the threat of radical Islam across the continent, an overwhelming majority of the European Parliament voted for a resolution that condemned the Muslim Brotherhood and its actions.

European Parliament member Céline Imart of France, who sponsored the resolution, called the vote "a historic victory because it is a European first. For the first time, Europe has voted on a text that tackles Islamist entryism and the Muslim Brotherhood."
EUROPE’S LEFT COURTS MUSLIM VOTERS AS ANTI-ISRAEL POLITICS RESHAPE CONTINENT
MEP Céline Imart at European Parliament session confronting the Muslim Brotherhood and Islamist entryism for the first time on Oct. 7 (Jeremy Baumert / European Parliament )

Imart posted on X that she had "broken a taboo that Europe has been dragging around like a chain: this victory signifies a major doctrinal shift in the institutions… We were able to transcend partisan divides on a major issue for our societies and our youth."

Lorenzo Vidino, director of the program on extremism at George Washington University, told Fox News Digital that, "This is something that the French and the Austrian governments have been pushing for almost a decade," noting a growing consensus across Europe that wants action.
Protesters attend an anti-Israel demonstration in Leipzig, Germany Jan. 17, 2026. (Christian Mang/Reuters)

The resolution was led by the European People’s Party, or EPP, a center-right coalition that is the largest group in the European Parliament. "The voting does reflect a gap between the right and the left," said Vidino, "with the right voting almost entirely in favor of the resolution, and a good part of the left, although with some notable exceptions, voting against it."

As part of her post on X, Imart made it a point to thank "the negotiators from the other groups with whom I had the pleasure of working - excluding the socialists and the far left, who boycotted the text."
Vidino said, "The Brotherhood remains something that is seen through the political lenses of our own political debates, where it shouldn't be... because it's a challenge to our societies."
DENMARK'S LEFT-WING PM WARNS: 'BIG ENEMY HAS STARTED TO GROW FROM WITHIN' AS EUROPE FACES MIGRANT RECKONING
Veiled women walk in a street of Monfalcone, on April 26, 2024. (Alberto Pizzoli via Getty Images)

A press release on the resolution issued by the European Parliament's news website stated that Islamist entryism targets "democratic institutions, the rule of law, equality between women and men and fundamental freedoms." It stressed that Muslim citizens must be protected from discrimination as "a democratic obligation," while "warning against treating organized Islamist networks as representative interlocutors."

The release also stated, "While Europe must remain free, open and faithful to its principles, it can ‘no longer fund, consult or legitimize networks that use its language, procedures and funding to weaken its values from within,’" but "MEPs stress that anti-discrimination policies must not be used to shield Islam from criticism or legitimize organized Islamist networks."
Flags from the 27 countries of the EU fly in the wind in front of the European Parliament on April 5, 2025, in Brussels, Belgium.  (Thierry Monasse/Getty Images)

The resolution was slammed by ENAR, a pan-European anti-racism network, which released a statement following its passage. "ENAR condemns in the strongest possible terms the racist and Islamophobic resolution "on the need for an EU strategy to counter Islamist entryism and the influence of the Muslim Brotherhood network" proposed by the European People’s Party (EPP) and passed by the European Parliament today, including its targeting of ENAR and its members like FEMYSO through sham allegations and falsehoods seeking to associate our network with the Muslim Brotherhood. ENAR categorically rejects these claims."

It added in part, "This resolution is a stain on the European Parliament and marks a profoundly shameful day in Europe’s history. A Parliament that should defend democracy, equality and fundamental rights has instead given institutional legitimacy to a racist politics of suspicion that casts Muslim communities, Muslim-led civil society, organizations combating Islamophobia, and those who defend their rights as inherently suspect."

Edmund Fitton-Brown, a senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies (FDD), told Fox News Digital "This resolution is where the pushback begins against Islamist entryism in Europe. It is admirably clearly worded. The task of converting it into binding legislation begins now and will be difficult."

The former UK ambassador to Yemen, Fitton-Brown added, "Europe regularly imagines that "legal", "non-violent" Islamism is in conflict with, and a potential antidote to, violent Islamist terrorism. It is not, it is a gateway to it, it creates the climate for it, and the two are pursuing the same goals, only via different tactics."

Migrants wait to board the Coast Guard ship "Diciotti" before being transferred to Porto Empedocle from the so-called "Hotspot" operational facility, containing over 1,700 people, on August 3, 2022, in Lampedusa, Italy.  (Photo by Antonio Masiello/Getty Images)

He added, "Europe fails to prioritize subversion as a threat, whereas during the Cold War it understood that threat and took serious measures to counter it. Europe also seeks to appease Islamist entryism by adopting hostile policies towards Israel, and sometimes by passing blasphemy-adjacent and anti-"Islamophobia" laws, thinking they are protecting the Muslim community. In fact, the main victims of these laws are liberal Muslims trying to escape the confines of their community and enjoy Western freedoms."

Asked about the differences between Europe and the U.S. approach to the Brotherhood, Vidino said the European way is "a bit more nuanced" than that of the U.S., where the Trump administration has designated the Muslim Brotherhood and 4 of its branches as terrorist organizations. He says Europe sees the Muslim Brotherhood "mostly through the lenses of entryism, of subversion, of a group that destroys the fabrics of society… a matter of a threat to democracy, but a lot of the activities of the Brotherhood might be legal if taken individually."
TRUMP ADMIN ACCUSES HAMAS OF BACKING GAZA FLOTILLA, SANCTIONS ACTIVIST AND MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD NETWORKS
European flags fly outside the European Parliament on Feb. 7, 2024 in Strasbourg, eastern France. (AP Photo/Jean-Francois Badias, File)

While noting that numerous security services across Europe have been warning about the Muslim Brotherhood for some time, Vidino says the resolution "sets the tone. It gives a political push," suggesting agencies and governments "might feel more legitimized in seeing the Brotherhood in negative ways."

"I'm a bit skeptical on whether this resolution would have a major tangible impact," Vidino added. "Islamist groups are very good at camouflaging their activities." While there is "no organization that calls itself Muslim Brotherhood in Europe," he said if and when funding is pulled from an Islamist organization by the EU, "They will make a fuss… They fight back. They have an ability to also leverage what could be a crisis, but turn it to their advantage by playing the victim card and the Islamophobia card."

A man is led by two federal police officers to two waiting emergency vehicles. The Federal Public Prosecutor General had three suspected members of the Islamist terrorist organization Hamas arrested. The men will be brought before the investigating judge of the Federal Court of Justice in Karlsruhe in Oct, 2 2025. (Philipp von Ditfurth/Picture Alliance via Getty Images.)

As part of the resolution, the European Council was asked to assess whether entities or individuals linked to the Muslim Brotherhood should be added to the EU list of terrorist organizations. It called for full traceability of EU funding and a European Commission overview of EU funds awarded to people or entities suspected of links to the Muslim Brotherhood or political Islam.

It also welcomed initiatives by member states to draw up national lists of hate preachers and calls for the establishment of such a list at EU level, while also calling for stronger scrutiny of foreign funding and transnational partnerships, particularly involving actors linked to Qatar or Turkey and greater use of Schengen tools and EU databases.
"This vote is a victory, but it is also a starting point," Imart said. "The Commission and the Council must now take action, and I will make sure they do."

title: Supreme Court says New Hampshire student IDs can’t be used to vote in November
summary: In a win for Republicans, the court said a federal judge should not have changed the rules so close to the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
story: WASHINGTON — In a win for Republicans, the Supreme Court said Thursday that student IDs cannot be used in New Hampshire for the midterm elections.
The justices granted an emergency request filed by the state, which had the backing of the Republican National Committee.

The ballot in New Hampshire includes a closely watched Senate race that could play a key role in deciding control of the chamber.  Republican former Sen. John E. Sununu is pitted against Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas for the seat held by retiring Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen.
The brief court order said a federal judge should not have ordered a change in voting rules so close to the Nov. 3 election, citing existing precedent on that point.
“Here, the District Court did not point to anything that would justify deviating from that principle,” the unsigned order said.
Liberal Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was the sole dissenter.
“I would not disturb a clearly justifiable federal court order issued to ensure that the public receives accurate information about a State’s electoral processes,” she wrote.

While a state law restricting use of student IDs as a primary form of identification was already on the books, the decision means potential voters also cannot use them as backups when they seek to establish their identities.
The dispute arises from a state law enacted in April that removed student IDs from the list of forms of identification that election officials would accept when someone requests a ballot.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
The measure was challenged by a nonprofit voting rights group called Coalition for Open Democracy, which argued that it unlawfully burdened the right to vote and discriminated against young voters.
U.S. District Judge Joseph Laplante declined to block the law, but on Oct. 2 he weighed in again, putting guidance from New Hampshire Secretary of State David Scanlan, a Republican, on hold.
Scanlan’s guidance said student IDs could not be used for any purpose when people seek ballots, which Laplante said went further than the law itself, which only barred them as a primary source of ID.

A separate provision of state law allows people to establish their identities using other, unofficial forms of ID. It says people can use “any other evidence that reasonably establishes that it is more likely than not that the person is who they claim to be.”
Under Laplante’s ruling, election officials could still take a student ID into account in trying to determine whether someone is a valid voter.
The Boston-based 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals declined to put Laplante’s ruling on hold, prompting the state to ask the Supreme Court to intervene.

title: Tom Skerritt, star of ‘Alien’ and ‘Top Gun,’ dies at 93
summary: Skerritt, a prolific actor with dozens of screen credits, was also an Emmy winner for his lead role on the cult favorite series “Picket Fences.”
story: Tom Skerritt, a prolific actor who won an Emmy playing a hardworking sheriff in “Picket Fences” and appeared in hit Hollywood movies like “Top Gun” and “Alien,” has died, his family confirmed Thursday. He was 93.
Skerritt died Wednesday of natural causes, his family said in a statement.

“While the world knew Tom through his remarkable acting career, we knew him for his humor, curiosity, wisdom, generosity, and the love he brought into our lives,” his family said. “He cared deeply about imagination, creativity, storytelling, service, veterans, the natural world, and helping others find and share their own voices.”
Born Aug. 25, 1933, in Detroit, Skerritt landed in Hollywood after having served four years in the Air Force, intending to become a director.
But with his lean frame and weather-beaten good looks, Skerritt quickly found his place in front of the camera.
His breakthrough role was playing Capt. Duke Forrest in Robert Altman’s 1970 satirical war movie “M*A*S*H.”
That led to starring roles in a string of successful movies, like “The Turning Point,” “Up in Smoke,” “The Dead Zone” and “Steel Magnolias.”
But Skerritt was best known to moviegoers as Tom Cruise’s no-nonsense flight instructor in the 1986 blockbuster “Top Gun” and the doomed Capt. Dallas in the 1979 science fiction classic “Alien.”
Skerritt was also widely praised for his role as a stern minister in the 1992 Robert Redford movie “A River Runs Through It,” which won an Oscar for best cinematography.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
Later, Skerritt made his mark on the small screen playing Sheriff Jimmy Brock on the family dramedy “Picket Fences” from 1992 to 1996.
In later years, Skerritt branched out and started Heyou Media in 2016, a digital entertainment and content-aggregation company based in Seattle. He was 84 at the time.
“This is a new era and we’re positioning ourselves to bring some light to new media and digital entertainment,” he told The Seattle Times. “My frame of reference is as big as this room.”
Skerritt is survived by his wife, Julie; five children; five grandchildren; and two great-grandchildren.
“We are heartbroken by his loss,” his family said in their statement.

title: Atlanta Falcons post of retro team symbol draws Nazi imagery comparisons
summary: The Atlanta Falcons on Wednesday showed off a retro team symbol on their social media platforms, which sparked backlash across social media from fans who said the image bore an uncomfortable resemblance to World War II-era German Nazi imagery.
story: The Atlanta Falcons on Wednesday showed off a retro team symbol on their social media platforms, which sparked backlash across social media from fans who said the image bore an  uncomfortable resemblance to World War II-era German Nazi imagery.
Red, white and black stripes adorned the familiar Falcons logo on the team’s Instagram and X accounts
It was called “New PFP” on X, shorthand for “new profile picture.”
A team representative, reached late Thursday afternoon, said the Falcons do not have a “new logo” and declined any further comment.
The Reichskriegsflagge-like imagery triggered a wave of taste-challenged World War II-themed comments and jokes to the Falcons social media pages.
The artwork appeared to be an ill-advised effort to honor the expansion 1966 Atlanta Falcons.
The Dirty Birds next take the field on Sunday, welcoming the San Francisco 49ers to Mercedes-Benz Stadium in an old school NFC West showdown that Atlanta is set to wear throwback threads.

“Absolutely there was no ill intent and I can’t imagine in a million years the Atlanta Falcons would do something like that (seek Nazi alignment),” sports logo historian Chris Creamer told NBC News on Thursday.
For Subscribers

“It’s throwback weekend for the team, and the social media team just wanted to dress up like the players were going to, and it’s a very common thing that social media accounts do across all sports. If a team’s wearing a throwback uniform, usually their profile photo will be updated to match that.”
For Subscribers
Creamer didn’t fault the Falcons for posting the image originally, but wondered if the team could’ve avoided some of the blowback.
“I think if I was in the room with the Falcons, honestly, I wouldn’t have noticed it (any possible offensive Nazi connection) when I hit send,” he said.

“But I would have, once the replies started coming in as fast as they were coming in and it spiraled out of control, at that point they could have taken it down and tried a different one. At this point it just sort of seems kind of stubborn to keep it up.”

title: Hackers appear to be struggling to exploit PHP flaws after global cybersecurity crisis
summary: There were few, if any, reports of widespread damage by hackers exploiting PHP flaws, experts said, one day after officials warned of severe vulnerabilities.
story: One day after governments around the world warned that newly publicized software vulnerabilities were so severe that websites should consider going offline until they could fix them, experts and insiders said there are few, if any, reports of widespread damage.

That could still change, of course, and cybersecurity experts warn that the threat will remain for weeks, if not longer. Still, there were early signs Thursday that hackers were finding it difficult to capitalize on the vulnerabilities.

“Across all our telemetry, and we are looking hard, we have only seen a couple of real exploitation attempts,” said Don Smith, vice president of threat research at the British software security firm Sophos.
Experts agree that that was in part because of a behind-the-scenes, global effort that identified the flaw and quietly designed a fix to address it.

The effort was aided, inadvertently, by the current limits of some widely available AI models, which did not appear to be very helpful at exploiting the vulnerabilities. And perhaps, they said, a little bit of luck.
“My sense is that these [vulnerabilities] are harder to exploit than folks thought at first, so this could be a slow burn,” Smith said.

The flaws were in PHP, a website programming language that is used in an estimated 69% of all websites. After researchers quietly found two devastating software vulnerabilities in August, they worked across borders and disciplines to develop patches that were released to the world Wednesday morning.

That led to an unusual circumstance in which government agencies from the FBI and the National Security Agency to European cybersecurity authorities and Australian intelligence agencies all recommended that websites go dark until they could implement the patches. And dozens of major websites around the world did just that.
Experts say there is plenty of evidence that hackers have been relentlessly scanning the flaws for ways to use them to attack targets.

But researchers and spokespeople from nine industry-leading companies — CrowdStrike, ESET, Google Threat Intelligence Group, Huntress, Palo Alto Networks, Recorded Future, SecureWorks, Sophos and Trail of Bits — told NBC News that as of Thursday evening, they had not seen any successful attacks.
“We have not yet seen these PHP vulnerabilities exploited in the wild yet,” said Sherrod DeGrippo, vice president of threat intelligence at Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42.

“We have seen over 200 examples of proofs-of-concept exploit code, and we’re actively investigating them all,” she said, referring to programs that claimed they could exploit the PHP flaws. “Whether or not there are current, active exploits is only a matter of time.”
For Subscribers
While the vulnerability itself was devastating in theory, it was also technically very difficult to hack, said Dan Guido, CEO of the cybersecurity research and consulting firm Trail of Bits.
For Subscribers
Guido said it took one of his employees, a 10-year veteran, an entire day to hack the vulnerabilities with an advanced AI model.

Amazon Web Services said it used honeypots — fake websites that cybersecurity researchers set up to trick and monitor hackers — to find evidence that hackers were trying to exploit the PHP vulnerability at least four days before it was made public.
“Technical analysis is ongoing, and it’s unclear if any of these attempts would have succeeded in real-world systems,” the company said in a blog post.

Matthew Prince, the CEO of Cloudflare, one of the internet’s most popular hosting companies, said that the company had been in talks for months about how to patch the flaw and that none of his customers were affected.

“The scary thing here is that something could have gotten compromised very quietly,” he said. “There may not be any public evidence that the server was compromised, and the hacker could just be hanging out there.”

While dormant intruders are always a potential threat in any hacking scenario, Guido, of Trail of Bits, said it was important to keep in mind that it takes more than just an experimental code and a little luck to hack a sophisticated web property.
That is especially true for hackers who rely on open-weight AI models — ones they can tinker with and remove guardrails from to assist with their operations.
Those models are not as powerful as those available to front-line cybersecurity researchers — and they typically struggle with complicated vulnerabilities like the PHP flaws.
“A lot of people are confusing proof of concept with exploit,” he said. “Turns out that writing exploits still requires expertise. You can’t just fake it.”

The measure was challenged by a nonprofit voting rights group called Coalition for Open Democracy, which argued that it unlawfully burdened the right to vote and discriminated against young voters.
U.S. District Judge Joseph Laplante declined to block the law, but on Oct. 2 he weighed in again, putting guidance from New Hampshire Secretary of State David Scanlan, a Republican, on hold.
Scanlan’s guidance said student IDs could not be used for any purpose when people seek ballots, which Laplante said went further than the law itself, which only barred them as a primary source of ID.

A separate provision of state law allows people to establish their identities using other, unofficial forms of ID. It says people can use “any other evidence that reasonably establishes that it is more likely than not that the person is who they claim to be.”
Under Laplante’s ruling, election officials could still take a student ID into account in trying to determine whether someone is a valid voter.
The Boston-based 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals declined to put Laplante’s ruling on hold, prompting the state to ask the Supreme Court to intervene.

title: Ramaswamy’s ad splits the GOP in Ohio’s closing stretch: From the Politics Desk
summary: In today’s edition, Jonathan Allen digs into the fallout from a controversial ad that has roiled Ohio politics.
story: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.
In today’s edition, Jonathan Allen digs into the fallout from a controversial ad that has roiled Ohio politics. Plus, we explore two Senate races where Black voters are playing a critical role.
— Adam Wollner
Ramaswamy’s ad splits the GOP in Ohio’s closing stretch
If there’s one notion that Republican Vivek Ramaswamy reinforced with an ad featuring his opponent’s estranged mother this week, it’s that he is trailing in his bid to become Ohio’s governor.

In the ad, Donna Arthur calls her daughter, Democratic gubernatorial nominee Amy Acton, a “liar.” Acton has previously talked about how, as a child, she was sexually abused by her mother’s husband. Her brother said in a video released by Acton’s campaign this week that their “birth mother stayed married to Amy’s rapist until he died.” Acton has also said that she has not seen or spoken to her mother in nearly 50 years.

Democrats roundly condemned Ramaswamy for turning this chapter of Acton’s life into a political attack. Many Republicans also distanced themselves from the ad, including Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine, whom Ramaswamy is vying to succeed, and Sen. John Husted, R-Ohio, who is also on the ballot next month.
“The ad, on its face, is deeply, deeply troubling,” DeWine said today, calling on Ramaswamy to take it down.

But Ramaswamy had some defenders in the GOP. Vice President JD Vance, a former Ohio senator, admonished fellow Republicans to quit “whining” about the ad and focus on winning the election. And in a Truth Social post today, President Donald Trump criticized DeWine while praising Ramaswamy’s “very powerful” ad.
Most candidates try to unify their own party and divide the other party, especially in the final stretch of a campaign. Ramaswamy has managed to do the opposite.
As the fallout continues to scatter across the Buckeye State, there are a couple of conclusions to draw from Ramaswamy’s controversial move and the state of the race.

First, it appears he thinks he’s running behind Acton, but not by a wide margin. No one with a lead would take such a big risk, in the same way no one who was trailing by a lot would in the hopes of losing by a little less.

Second, his team seems to have concluded the ad was the best way to help him close the gap. That would be counterintuitive, but it could be that they see more value in the fight surrounding the ad than in its content. Sometimes, when a campaign looks like it is playing checkers, it is really playing chess. And sometimes, it’s just playing checkers and losing.
Most strategists think the Ramaswamy ad fits in the latter category. And some believe that Husted and other Republicans could suffer collateral damage because they share the ticket with Ramaswamy.
Ramaswamy couldn’t afford to do nothing if he felt he was headed toward defeat. Whether he made the right move remains to be seen. That’s up to Ohio voters.
Black voters play a crucial role in the battle for the Senate

In the final days before the election, Senate candidates from both parties are aggressively vying for the support of Black voters, a key bloc that could determine who controls the chamber. Michigan: Former Rep. Mike Rogers opened an office for his Senate campaign last weekend in Detroit, a city where 75% of the population is Black and is known for helping Democrats secure and pad their victories. It’s also an area where Rogers’ general election opponent, Abdul El-Sayed, underperformed and lost in the Democratic primary.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

In a race that could be decided by a slim margin, Rogers is making a late run for Black voters who ordinarily wouldn’t consider him, but who also have doubts about casting their ballot for El-Sayed, Henry J. Gomez and Allan Smith write. Rogers recently turned up at a Detroit bar, where he served drinks and snapped photos with several Black patrons. His wife, Kristi Rogers, posted up in the parking lot of a Detroit gas station last week to hand out $10 gift cards.

Underscoring the stakes, former President Barack Obama will headline a Saturday rally in Detroit for El-Sayed and other Democrats. Even that potentially helpful development could not spare El-Sayed scrutiny over his past criticism of the nation’s first Black president, who in his opinion fell short of delivering change.
Rogers has impressed some Democrats with his efforts, including Rep. Haley Stevens, who lost to El-Sayed in a bitterly fought primary, while others have accused Rogers of pandering.
Texas: Meanwhile, state Rep. James Talarico is leaning on Black voters to help him pull off an elusive Democratic Senate, Natasha Korecki reports from Arlington.

A recent gathering of mostly Black activists and community members featured Rep. Jasmine Crockett, who lost to Talarico in the Democratic primary. While sitting for a panel-style conversation, Crockett sang Talarico’s praises, calling him “our amazing Senate nominee” and urging the room to back him and others on the ballot.

But in an interview with NBC News afterward, Crockett revealed some tensions still existed in the wake of that hard-fought primary. She would not explicitly say whether she believed Talarico was doing enough to mobilize Black voters, answering, “It is my hope.” She noted candidates in other states had invited her to campaign with them, but Talarico has not.

Crockett pointed to her ability to dominate the Black vote in the primary and revealed the Talarico team had not taken up an offer by one of her top campaign lieutenants to assist on the campaign “specifically by having the person that led us to really a historic African American turnout.”

title: Tom Skerritt, star of ‘Alien’ and ‘Top Gun,’ dies at 93
summary: Skerritt, a prolific actor with dozens of screen credits, was also an Emmy winner for his lead role on the cult favorite series “Picket Fences.”
story: Tom Skerritt, a prolific actor who won an Emmy playing a hardworking sheriff in “Picket Fences” and appeared in hit Hollywood movies like “Top Gun” and “Alien,” has died, his family confirmed Thursday. He was 93.
Skerritt died Wednesday of natural causes, his family said in a statement.

“While the world knew Tom through his remarkable acting career, we knew him for his humor, curiosity, wisdom, generosity, and the love he brought into our lives,” his family said. “He cared deeply about imagination, creativity, storytelling, service, veterans, the natural world, and helping others find and share their own voices.”
Born Aug. 25, 1933, in Detroit, Skerritt landed in Hollywood after having served four years in the Air Force, intending to become a director.
But with his lean frame and weather-beaten good looks, Skerritt quickly found his place in front of the camera.
His breakthrough role was playing Capt. Duke Forrest in Robert Altman’s 1970 satirical war movie “M*A*S*H.”
That led to starring roles in a string of successful movies, like “The Turning Point,” “Up in Smoke,” “The Dead Zone” and “Steel Magnolias.”
But Skerritt was best known to moviegoers as Tom Cruise’s no-nonsense flight instructor in the 1986 blockbuster “Top Gun” and the doomed Capt. Dallas in the 1979 science fiction classic “Alien.”
Skerritt was also widely praised for his role as a stern minister in the 1992 Robert Redford movie “A River Runs Through It,” which won an Oscar for best cinematography.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
Later, Skerritt made his mark on the small screen playing Sheriff Jimmy Brock on the family dramedy “Picket Fences” from 1992 to 1996.
In later years, Skerritt branched out and started Heyou Media in 2016, a digital entertainment and content-aggregation company based in Seattle. He was 84 at the time.
“This is a new era and we’re positioning ourselves to bring some light to new media and digital entertainment,” he told The Seattle Times. “My frame of reference is as big as this room.”
Skerritt is survived by his wife, Julie; five children; five grandchildren; and two great-grandchildren.
“We are heartbroken by his loss,” his family said in their statement.

title: Despite security concerns, NFL plans to stage Paris game amid French protests
summary: The NFL will host its first game in Paris on Sunday between the New Orleans Saints and Pittsburgh Steelers despite widespread protests across France.
story: As nationwide protests continue across France, raising security concerns, the NFL says it still plans to stage its first regular-season game in Paris on Sunday.

When the New Orleans Saints arrived in France after they beat the New York Giants on Sunday and the Pittsburgh Steelers arrived Thursday, they came to a country that has been roiled by protests since early October over the high cost of living and deteriorating conditions in the country’s schools. French officials have said the unrest has led to thousands of arrests. The French government estimated that 550,000 people took part in demonstrations Saturday, and a curfew has been in effect in some parts of Paris. Though many of the protests have been peaceful, some have turned violent as masked looters clashed with riot police.

In one instance, the mayor of the Paris suburb Saint-Denis, the site of the Stade de France, where the Steelers-Saints game will be played, stood between police officers and protesters. A league spokesman wrote Wednesday that “preparations continue as scheduled.”

The security and events team the league uses to host events such as the Super Bowl is also staging the international game in the Stade de France, the spokesman said, adding, “There’s been no disruption or impact at league sites.”

The NFL has moved the locations of some games because of natural disasters, such as a Los Angeles Rams game in January 2025, as wildfires raged across Southern California. Peter O’Reilly, the NFL’s executive vice president of club business, international and league events, told reporters after league owners’ meetings Tuesday that no such discussions had taken place in this case.

“We have never been close to that point,” O’Reilly said. “We’ve always got contingency plans for every game, every single one of them. But no, we were not at that point at any point in the conversation.”

O’Reilly said officials from the league had been in Paris for several days to oversee operation plans, including Cathy Lanier, the NFL chief security officer, who used to run the Washington, D.C., police department.

The protests have altered at least one event surrounding the game, however. The Steelers said Thursday that they were canceling plans to host a “Steelers House” for fans “following recent events in the Bastille neighborhood, and after careful consideration.”

Asked about his comfort level regarding security around the game, NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell said Wednesday, “Very high is my comfort level.” Goodell said that he had spoken with Secretary of State Marco Rubio and that the league was “involved at the highest levels, both in France on a global basis, with our officials here in the United States.”

“We’ve made all the preparations,” he said. “We’ve been in touch with the appropriate authorities. Protests are not unusual in France, as you know. And that’s something that we will be aware of and make sure that the appropriate arrangements are made.”
Goodell said he was looking forward to attending the game.
Paris officials prep for NFL game amid civil unrest
“We’re guests in the country, we’re going to be good guests, and we’re going to do our thing, and I’m confident they’re going to do theirs,” Goodell said.

Amid the unrest in France, Paris has already hosted one major sporting event this week without incident. On Tuesday, the two-time reigning European champion soccer club Paris Saint-Germain hosted Barcelona in a Champions League match, which some Saints players attended.

“NFL does feel comfortable in sending us over,” Steelers defensive lineman Cam Heyward said Wednesday on “The Rich Eisen Show.” “That’s the trust we have to believe in. Hopefully we’re not going into a firestorm, but for us, we have to be smart about what we’re doing out there. No traveling alone, make sure we stay in groups and don’t wander off too far.”
“The NFL likes money,” Heyward added, “so we’re not missing that opportunity.”

title: Top adviser to Kennedy resigns from Trump administration
summary: Means, a key advocate for the “Make America Healthy Again” movement, had grown frustrated with a lack of progress on his policy goals, a source familiar with his departure said.
story: Calley Means, a top adviser to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and central advocate for the “Make America Healthy Again” movement, has resigned from the Trump administration.

“I am resigning from the White House with tremendous respect for President Trump and RFK — two historic figures who are committed to confronting a corrupt DC bureaucracy that is doing everything possible to protect the status quo,” Means said in a statement to NBC News. He posted a similar one on X.

Means was an adviser on Kennedy’s 2024 presidential campaign and a key architect of his MAHA agenda. He joined the White House early last year as a special government employee. He transitioned to a full-time role as senior adviser to the Health and Human Services Department after divesting from his wellness company, Truemed.
A person familiar with Means’ decision to resign said Means had been growing increasingly frustrated as he realized how little he could get done in Washington to advance his MAHA goals.

The final straw, the source said, was the lack of progress on rolling out a federal definition of ultraprocessed foods — one of Means’ biggest priorities. The administration teased a definition in August but has yet to release it.

The source also mentioned Trump’s executive order to boost the supply of the weed killer glyphosate in the U.S. (glyphosate is the key ingredient in Roundup), as well as some actions at the Environmental Protection Agency that have clashed with Kennedy’s agenda.
Trump’s EPA has, for example, weakened mercury emissions standards and rolled back drinking water limits for certain PFAS chemicals — actions the MAHA movement has largely opposed.
“We are grateful for Calley Means’ time in the Trump Administration. He has done a fantastic job for the MAHA movement,” White House spokesperson Allison Schuster said in a statement.

Frustrations over a lack of progress on MAHA goals have reverberated throughout the movement. Earlier this month, some supporters — including former members of Kennedy’s presidential campaign — accused the Trump administration of breaking nearly every promise made to them on food, agriculture and environmental health.

With less than two weeks left until the midterm elections, some dissatisfied MAHA supporters have threatened to abstain from voting. Some Democrats are seeking to make inroads with the movement in the final days of campaigning.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

One of the MAHA movement’s central beliefs is that corporations hold too much influence over the food supply and healthcare system. Many of its supporters, including Means, had hoped to see a greater crackdown on pesticides and artificial dyes, as well as more significant changes to vaccine policy that emphasize what some describe as “medical freedom” over universal recommendations.

On pesticides, a particular setback for the MAHA cause came in June, when the Supreme Court ruled that Bayer, the manufacturer of Roundup, didn’t need to warn consumers about a potential cancer risk associated with its product. The Trump administration had backed Bayer in the case.

President Donald Trump last year nominated Means’ sister, Casey Means, for surgeon general, but she faced scrutiny at her confirmation hearing over her lack of an active medical license and past comments questioning the safety of vaccines and birth control. Trump chose a new nominee, Dr. Nicole Saphier, in April.
Last month, at a talk Means gave at a MAHA summit in Washington, he said he was inspired by the way federal agencies had collaborated to advance the MAHA agenda, but he also acknowledged roadblocks.

“D.C. is a tough place. It’s a toxic place, and there’s a lot of complaints you can make about D.C.,” Means said. “But I am more optimistic today than I’ve ever been about what I feel is my life’s work of evangelizing the chronic disease crisis and empowering Americans who want to be healthy to address the root cause of disease.”

In his statement on Thursday, Means highlighted several policy wins for the MAHA movement during his tenure, including restricting soda purchases through the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, fast-tracking research and review of psychedelics, urging food companies to voluntarily phase out certain dyes and overhauling the federal dietary guidelines to recommend less ultraprocessed food and more protein.
“More policy and cultural change has happened around these goals in the past 2 years than any time in history,” he wrote.

title: Blanche won’t rule out DOJ post-election action in a ‘doomsday’ scenario
summary: The attorney general’s comments come in the middle of a broader campaign by the Trump administration to zero in on what elections experts say is a relatively rare phenomenon of voting by noncitizens.
story: NORFOLK, Va. — Attorney General Todd Blanche on Thursday left open the possibility that the Justice Department could seek to block states from certifying votes in the midterm elections, though he said it wasn’t his intention to “improperly interfere with elections.”

NBC News reported this week that the Justice Department is weighing more election-related litigation against states after it sued California to compel state officials to review 18,000 registered voters it suspected could be noncitizens seeking to cast fraudulent ballots. California has an all-mail election and sends out ballots automatically.
Blanche does not rule out DOJ post-election action

Washington, D.C., and seven other states do, too: Colorado, Hawaii, Nevada, Oregon, Utah, Vermont and Washington. Mail voting has frequently been a target for President Donald Trump’s voter fraud claims, which have escalated ahead of the 2026 midterms, even as he uses the voting method to cast his ballot in Florida.
On Thursday, Blanche was asked whether he could rule out any action by the Justice Department that could seek to delay the counting of ballots.
Blanche said there could be some “doomsday” scenario in which it would seek to get involved.

“It is not DOJ’s intention to, and it’s never our intention to, improperly interfere with elections or the state confirmation process or certification process,” he told reporters before he boarded a plane.
Blanche’s comments come in the middle of a broader campaign by the Trump administration to zero in on what voting experts say is a relatively rare phenomenon of voting by noncitizens.
The Justice Department’s role in U.S. elections is limited by law, chiefly allowing it to safeguard civil rights and prosecute people who violate election law.

While private citizens and candidates can sue to challenge ballots or election results, no U.S. laws say the Justice Department can challenge ballots or delay certification. U.S. elections are run by state and local officials, who are charged with certifying results.

Blanche said he couldn’t say there were zero circumstances under which the Justice Department wouldn’t get involved. “Of course, I’m not going to say that,” he said. “But am I planning my days around the election to be somewhere to not certify? Of course not.”
Blanche and FBI Director Kash Patel traveled to Norfolk for a news conference Thursday to announce racketeering charges against an 82-year-old Virginia state senator.

At that news conference, when he was pressed about the Justice Department’s litigation against states, Blanche said the Justice Department was “not trying to create chaos.” He said it was trying to alert officials to potential issues.

“I’m not trying to not have an election certified. Of course not,” Blanche said. “What we’re trying to do is guarantee to the American people that the only people that are voting are people that are eligible to vote.”

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., reacted to Blanche’s comments, saying Senate Democrats “have been preparing for this for months and will be ready for whatever” the Trump administration tries.
“As Trump and his cronies attempt to steal this election, we are fighting them at every turn,” Schumer posted on X. “Our elections must always belong to the voters — not Donald Trump.”

title: Airbnb hosts can no longer ask guests to clean dishes or make beds
summary: Customers don’t have “to complete tasks that require significant effort or time, or would typically be performed by a cleaner,” according to the home-sharing app.
story: Airbnb hosts can set only “reasonable” housecleaning duties for guests, according to new guidelines rolled out by the tech giant, with tasks such as dishwashing and bed stripping now the sole responsibility of homeowners.
While Airbnb bookings have always included cleaning fees, there hadn’t been universal policies on what hosts can ask their renters to complete.

But now, starting with rentals on Nov. 20, Airbnb will limit those guest responsibilities to “set clear expectations” for hosts whose house rules must be “reasonable and comply with” the new requirements.

Hosts cannot ask “guests to complete tasks that require significant effort or time, or would typically be performed by a cleaner, including stripping the bed, taking trash offsite, or washing and putting away dishes,” Airbnb said.
The new guidelines come after years of customer complaints, travel industry expert Clint Henderson told NBC News.
“So this is pretty major for consumers,” said Henderson, managing editor and spokesperson for the travel industry website The Points Guy.

“The complaints have been really ramping up lately with owners asking guests to do the most ridiculous things, like stripping beds, washing dishes, doing all the laundry and taking the trash out,” Henderson said.
“It’s just gotten really out of hand,” he said. “And from a consumer’s perspective, it’s like, ‘Why am I going to stay at Airbnb when I have to do chores?’”
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

While Airbnb host Gabriel Valk, of Greenville, South Carolina, believes small tasks like dishwashing and bed stripping should be “common courtesy” performed by guests, he understands why Airbnb would institute the clearer guidelines.
“But I do understand the pushback,” Valk said, citing the service fees that are supposed to cover cleaning costs.
“OK, you guys are paying, whatever, $100 for the cleaning. ‘We shouldn’t have to do anything,’” he imagined the guests saying. “So totally makes sense to me.”
Airbnb had to give guests a break or risk consumers’ flocking back to traditional hotels, according to Henderson.

“Why [stay at an Airbnb] when I can stay at a hotel and not have to do all that busywork?” he said. “And these days, Airbnb is as expensive, with all the fees and everything, as a hotel is. So I think Airbnb has lost some of its competitive edge over the years.”

title: Ohio governor calls on Vivek Ramaswamy to take down ad featuring opponent’s estranged mother
summary: DeWine, a Republican, said he still endorses Ramaswamy over Democrat Amy Acton in the race to succeed him as Ohio’s governor.
story: Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine on Thursday called for Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican he endorsed to succeed him as governor, to stop airing an ad that features the estranged mother of Ramaswamy’s Democratic opponent, Amy Acton.
“The ad, on its face, is deeply, deeply troubling,” DeWine said at a news conference he called to address what has become a boiling controversy in the final days of a hostile race.
His comments drew a rebuke later Thursday from President Donald Trump, who chastised him on Truth Social and called the Ramaswamy spot a “very powerful Ad.”
DeWine, for his part, reaffirmed his support for Ramaswamy.

“Look, today is about the ad, but I’m not — no, I’m not changing my endorsement,” he said when reporters pressed him at the Ohio Statehouse. “I endorse the whole ticket, as you know. I’m a Republican. I endorse the whole ticket. On that ticket are some amazing people, almost all of whom I have worked with in the past.”

The Ramaswamy campaign ad, backed by a $4 million purchase of statewide airtime, features Donna Arthur, who calls her daughter a “liar” in the minutelong spot and urges Ohioans not to vote for her. Acton has talked about having been sexually abused by her mother’s husband as a child. Her brother, Philip Stearns, has corroborated her account, saying in a video for Acton’s campaign that their “birth mother stayed married to Amy’s rapist until he died.”
Acton has said she has not seen or spoken to her mother in nearly 50 years. Arthur has not responded to requests for comment.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

The ad did not refer to the abuse claims. But DeWine on Thursday talked about prosecuting sexual assault cases earlier in his career in public service and said he found the ad troubling given the family history.

“When you know the rest of the story, when you know the backstory, when you know that the husband of the mom was indicted by a grand jury after hearing testimony and that he took off along with the mother ... and that two children never saw, I guess, the mother after that — when you know that, it just to me makes it more serious,” he said. “It makes it just more wrong.”
He added, “So it’s wrong to run this ad, and even at this late time — my wife, Fran, saw the ad run this morning on TV — I would just urge the Ramaswamy campaign to take this down.”
In his lengthy post on Truth Social, Trump suggested Ramaswamy and Republicans were being held to a different standard. He also mocked DeWine.

“If my mother, the legendary Mary MacLeod Trump, said anything bad about me, the Fake News would play it up,” Trump wrote. “The Dumocrats would be totally supportive, and it would go down as the Ad of the Decade — Maybe the Century!”

DeWine, Trump added, “was, as usual, disloyal to the Republican Party. He strongly suggested that Vivek should, ‘take down the Ad.’ He probably wants a Dumocrat to win, and certainly doesn’t want someone who will do a much better job than he is capable of doing.”

DeWine joins a growing list of Republicans who have condemned an ad that has been criticized on both sides of the political aisle. Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, said Wednesday that he “would not have run that ad.”

But there also has been a split in the Republican Party. Others, including Trump and Vice President JD Vance, whose old Senate seat Husted was appointed to last year, have downplayed the outrage over the spot.

“Politics is a tough business, and my message to my fellow elected Republicans is if you actually believe in the things you say you believe in, stop whining about an advertisement and go win the race in 13 days,” Vance told reporters Wednesday in Cincinnati.
Asked about Vance’s remarks Thursday, DeWine said, “Look, I’m not going to comment on what someone else said.”
“I mean, this is Mike DeWine, with my life experiences, saying what I think about this ad,” he added. “So I’m going to keep it just to that.”

DeWine’s life experiences aside, his willingness to reprimand Ramaswamy is not entirely surprising. He worked closely with Acton when she was his health director during the early days of the Covid pandemic. DeWine has defended her against attacks from Ramaswamy and his allies on her leadership during that crisis.

DeWine also was not initially sold on Ramaswamy’s candidacy for governor. He had originally wanted Husted, who was his lieutenant governor, to be his successor. And last year he expressed interest in his new lieutenant governor, former Ohio State football coach Jim Tressel, challenging Ramaswamy in the Republican primary. Tressel passed, and DeWine eventually backed Ramaswamy.

Ramaswamy spokesperson Connie Luck noted that DeWine expressed concern Thursday over how Acton’s campaign has attacked Ramaswamy’s mother in its messaging. DeWine also emphasized that it was Ramaswamy’s attack that had a $4 million push behind it.

“Governor DeWine is correct that the first and only candidate to attack the mother of her opponent in this race was Amy Acton,” Luck said in a statement. “We refuse to accept the media’s double standards when Democrats have regularly used family members of President Trump, RFK Jr., and other Republicans in ads. Voters shouldn’t buy it.”

title: Everything tool you need to bake a perfect batch of cookies, according to pastry chefs
summary: Professional bakers break down everything you need to make homemade cookies, especially during the holidays. Here are their top tips for beginner to advanced bakers.
story: Cookies are one of the most low-stress, beginner-friendly desserts you can make, and they’re always a crowd pleaser whether they melt in your mouth or crunch as you take a bite. There’s room to grow, too — as you become confident in the kitchen, you can pick more complex recipes that require a bit more skill.
